items.label: Run with Healthcheck
items.command: docker run -d --health-cmd "curl -f http://localhost/ || exit 1" --health-interval 30s --name hc nginx:alpine

items.label: Clean After Build
items.command: docker build -t app:dev . && docker image prune -f

items.label: Backup Volume
items.command: docker run --rm -v dbdata:/data -v C:/backup:/backup alpine tar czf /backup/vol.tar.gz -C /data .

items.label: Exec in Service
items.command: docker compose exec db psql -U app

items.label: Exec: List Databases
items.command: kubectl exec -it mysql-0 -- mysql -u root -p -e 'SHOW DATABASES;'

items.label: Exec: List Users
items.command: kubectl exec -it mysql-0 -- mysql -u root -p -e 'SELECT user,host FROM mysql.user;'

items.label: Exec: Show Variables
items.command: kubectl exec -it mysql-0 -- mysql -u root -p -e 'SHOW VARIABLES;'

items.label: Exec: Check Version
items.command: kubectl exec -it mysql-0 -- mysql -u root -p -e 'SELECT VERSION();'

items.label: Dump to File
items.command: kubectl exec mysql-0 -- mysqldump -u root -p appdb > backup.sql

items.label: Exec: List Tables
items.command: kubectl exec -it postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres -d appdb -c '\dt'

items.label: Exec: Show Version
items.command: kubectl exec -it postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres -c 'SELECT version();'

items.label: Exec: Activity
items.command: kubectl exec -it postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres -c 'SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity;'

items.label: Dump to File
items.command: kubectl exec postgres-0 -- pg_dump -U postgres appdb > backup.sql

items.label: Dump All Databases
items.command: kubectl exec postgres-0 -- pg_dumpall -U postgres > backup-all.sql

items.label: Run Every SAST Check
items.command: bandit -r src && semgrep --config auto && gitleaks detect

commands.label: Explain OWASP Top 10
commands.command: echo Start with the OWASP Top 10, then read the Security Testing chapter

items.label: Allow HTTP and HTTPS
items.command: sudo ufw allow 80/tcp && sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

items.label: Add a Rich Rule
items.command: sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv4 source address={arg} port port=443 protocol=tcp accept'

items.label: Allow Established Traffic
items.command: sudo iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

items.label: Show Firewall Rules
items.command: netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name=all

items.label: Enable All Profiles
items.command: netsh advfirewall set allprofiles state on

items.label: Allow Inbound a Port
items.command: netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="Allow {arg}" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport={arg}

items.label: Block Outbound for a Program
items.command: netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="Block {arg}" dir=out action=block program={arg}

items.label: Render Every File in a Folder
Count Lines of a Diagram File
Explain a Query
items.command: mysql -u root -p -D {arg} -e 'EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email="a@b.c";'

items.label: Find Duplicate Values
items.command: psql -U postgres -d {arg} -c 'SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;'

items.label: Find Rows With Nulls
items.command: psql -U postgres -d {arg} -c 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL;'

items.label: Check Relationship Cardinality
items.command: psql -U postgres -d {arg} -c 'SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 10;'

items.label: Show Row Counts
items.command: psql -U postgres -d {arg} -c 'SELECT relname, n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_live_tup DESC;'

items.label: Find Unused Indexes
items.command: psql -U postgres -d {arg} -c 'SELECT relname, indexrelname FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0;'

docs.Docker:
Docker packages applications into lightweight containers.
Key concepts:
- Image: read‑only template containing filesystem layers.
- Container: a running instance of an image.
Common commands:
    docker ps            – list running containers
    docker ps -a        – list all containers
    docker images       – list local images
    docker run IMAGE    – start a new container from IMAGE
    docker exec -it CONTAINER /bin/bash – open an interactive shell inside a running container.
docs.Minikube/Kind:
Minikube and Kind provide local Kubernetes clusters for development.
- Minikube uses a VM or Docker driver to run a single‑node K8s cluster.
- Kind runs Kubernetes inside Docker containers (great for CI).
Typical commands:
    minikube start      – start the cluster
    kind create cluster – spin up a cluster with default config.
docs.Pods:
Pods are the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. They encapsulate one or more containers that share the same network namespace and storage volumes.
Important fields in a pod YAML:
- `metadata.name`: unique pod name.
- `spec.containers`: list of container specs (image, ports, env).
- `spec.restartPolicy`: `Always`, `OnFailure`, or `Never`.
docs.Deployments:
Deployments manage stateless workloads, ensuring a desired number of pod replicas. They provide declarative updates and roll‑backs.
Key YAML fields:
- `spec.replicas`: number of desired pod replicas.
- `spec.selector.matchLabels`: label selector matching the pods.
- `spec.template`: pod template used for new pods.
- `spec.strategy.type`: `RollingUpdate` (default) or `Recreate`.
docs.Services:
Services expose a set of Pods via a stable network endpoint.
Types:
- **ClusterIP** (default): internal cluster‑only IP. Use when pods talk to each other.
- **NodePort**: exposes the service on each node’s IP at a static port (30000‑32767).
- **LoadBalancer**: provisions an external load balancer (cloud providers).
Key fields:
- `spec.type`: `ClusterIP`|`NodePort`|`LoadBalancer`.
- `spec.ports`: list of ports (port, targetPort, nodePort).
docs.ReplicaSets:
ReplicaSets ensure that a specified number of pod replicas are running at any time. They are usually managed by Deployments, but can be used directly for simple scaling.
Key fields:
- `spec.replicas`: desired replica count.
- `spec.selector`: label selector.
- `spec.template`: pod template.
docs.StatefulSets:
StatefulSets manage stateful workloads that require stable network IDs and persistent storage. Ideal for databases.
Key concepts:
- Stable pod names (ordinal index).
- Ordered, graceful deployment and scaling.
Important fields:
- `spec.serviceName`: headless service governing DNS.
- `spec.volumeClaimTemplates`: template for PersistentVolumeClaims per pod.
docs.Volumes & PVC:
A **PersistentVolume (PV)** represents a piece of storage in the cluster (NFS, cloud disk, etc.). A **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** is a request for storage by a pod.
Common PVC fields:
- `spec.accessModes`: `ReadWriteOnce`, `ReadOnlyMany`, `ReadWriteMany`.
- `spec.resources.requests.storage`: size (e.g., `5Gi`).
- `spec.storageClassName`: optional storage class.
docs.MySQL:
MySQL on Kubernetes

MySQL is a stateful, transactional database. In Kubernetes it must run as a
StatefulSet so each replica gets a stable identity and its own persistent
volume. A stateless Deployment would lose data every time a pod is rescheduled.

Key concepts:
- StatefulSet gives pods stable hostnames (mysql-0, mysql-1) tied to PVCs
- headless Service (clusterIP: None) provides per-pod DNS resolution
- PersistentVolumeClaim keeps data across pod restarts and rescheduling
- Secret stores the root password; never bake it into an image or a manifest
- mysqldump is the backup tool, mysql is the interactive client

Getting started:
1. Click 'Write MySQL Manifest' to drop a ready-to-apply YAML file into the
   working directory, then edit it in the built-in YAML editor.
2. Apply it, then check the pods with the Pods list button.
3. Use 'Exec Shell' to open the mysql client inside the container.
4. Port-forward to connect from your machine with any SQL GUI.

Key commands:
    kubectl apply -f mysql.yaml
    kubectl get statefulset mysql
    kubectl get pods -l app=mysql
    kubectl exec -it mysql-0 -- mysql -u root -p
    kubectl logs mysql-0 -f
    kubectl port-forward svc/mysql 3306:3306
    kubectl scale statefulset mysql --replicas=3
    kubectl delete statefulset mysql

Connect from your machine:
- Port-forward first, then use host 127.0.0.1 port 3306 in DBeaver or Navicat
- From another machine use the NodePort and the node IP

Important notes:
- mysqld is the server, mysql is the client - they are different binaries
- Deleting a StatefulSet leaves the PVCs behind; remove them explicitly with
  'Delete PVCs' when you really want the data gone
- Back up with mysqldump before any destructive operation
docs.Postgres:
PostgreSQL on Kubernetes

Postgres follows the same pattern as MySQL - a StatefulSet, a headless Service
and persistent volumes. What differs is the tooling: the server is 'postgres',
the client is 'psql', and backups are taken with pg_dump and pg_dumpall.

Key concepts:
- Init containers or an init script create databases and roles on first boot
- PGDATA must live on the PVC, never on the container filesystem
- pg_dump is logical and portable, pg_basebackup is physical and faster
- Postgres listens on 5432 and uses the pg_hba.conf ruleset for auth
- Connection strings look like postgres://user:pass@host:5432/dbname

Getting started:
1. Click 'Write Postgres Manifest' to create a StatefulSet with a PVC.
2. Apply it and watch the pods come up.
3. Exec into the pod and run psql.
4. Port-forward to reach it from pgAdmin or DBeaver.

Key commands:
    kubectl apply -f postgres.yaml
    kubectl get statefulset postgres
    kubectl exec -it postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres
    kubectl port-forward svc/postgres 5432:5432
    kubectl logs postgres-0 -f
    kubectl scale statefulset postgres --replicas=2

Backup and restore:
    kubectl exec postgres-0 -- pg_dump -U postgres dbname > backup.sql
    kubectl cp postgres-0:/tmp/backup.sql ./backup.sql
    kubectl exec -i postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres dbname < backup.sql

Important notes:
- A single-writer database means one replica unless you add a replication
  tool such as Patroni or CloudNativePG
- Quote the database name when it contains upper case characters
- Never store the password in plain text; use a Secret and envFrom
docs.MongoDB:
MongoDB on Kubernetes

MongoDB is a document database. It is usually deployed as a StatefulSet and
scaled with a replica set so reads can be distributed and failover is fast.
Unlike MySQL and Postgres, MongoDB has no schema and no fixed table layout.

Key concepts:
- Replica set = one primary and N secondaries; writes only hit the primary
- WiredTiger is the default storage engine with journaling
- mongosh is the modern shell; mongo was the legacy shell
- mongod is the server, mongos is the sharding router
- Connection strings look like mongodb://host:27017/?replicaSet=rs0

Getting started:
1. Click 'Write MongoDB Manifest' to create a single-node replica set.
2. Apply it and confirm the pod is Running.
3. Exec into the pod and open mongosh.
4. Port-forward 27017 for Compass or Atlas tooling.

Key commands:
    kubectl apply -f mongodb.yaml
    kubectl get statefulset mongodb
    kubectl exec -it mongodb-0 -- mongosh --quiet
    kubectl port-forward svc/mongodb 27017:27017
    kubectl logs mongodb-0 -f

Data operations inside mongosh:
    show dbs
    use mydatabase
    db.collectionName.find().pretty()
    db.collectionName.insertMany([{a:1},{a:2}])
    db.collectionName.createIndex({field:1})
    db.collectionName.dropIndexes()

Important notes:
- A single-node replica set is fine for development, never for production
- Authentication is off by default in the plain image - enable it before
  exposing the pod outside the cluster
docs.CI/CD & GitHub Actions:
CI/CD and GitHub Actions

CI/CD is the pipeline that turns a commit into a running artifact. In a
Kubernetes context the pipeline builds an image, pushes it to a registry,
then applies it to a cluster and verifies the rollout.

Key concepts:
- Workflow lives at .github/workflows/<name>.yml and triggers on events
- steps run on a runner; each step is a shell command in a container
- Secrets are stored in GitHub and injected as environment variables
- needs defines job dependencies; jobs without it run in parallel
- act runs a workflow locally before you push it

Pipeline stages:
1. Lint and unit test on every pull request
2. Build the Docker image and tag it with the commit SHA
3. Push the image to a registry
4. Deploy to the cluster with kubectl apply or a Helm upgrade
5. Verify with kubectl rollout status and smoke tests

Key commands:
    gh workflow list
    gh workflow run deploy.yml --ref main
    gh run list --limit 10
    gh run view 123456789 --log-failed
    gh run rerun 123456789 --failed
    gh secret set DOCKER_PASSWORD
    act -l
    act -j build
    docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
    docker push myregistry/myapp:1.0
    kubectl apply -f k8s/deploy.yaml
    kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp
    kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp

Important notes:
- Never put secrets in the workflow file - use secrets or environments
- Pin runner versions such as ubuntu-22.04 for reproducible builds
- A pipeline that cannot be re-run from a clean checkout is not a pipeline
docs.GitHub:
GitHub and Git

Git is a distributed version control system: every clone is a full repository
with history. GitHub is a hosted platform around it that adds pull requests,
issues, Actions and releases. The commands below cover the everyday workflow
plus the GitHub CLI.

Setup and configuration:
    git config --global user.name "Your Name"
    git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
    git config --global init.defaultBranch main
    git config --list --show-origin

Repository lifecycle:
    git init
    git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
    git clone git@github.com:user/repo.git
    git remote -v
    git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
    git remote set-url origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
    git remote remove origin
    git remote prune origin

Everyday work:
    git status
    git status -sb
    git add .
    git add -p
    git commit -m "message"
    git commit -am "message"
    git commit --amend --no-edit
    git diff
    git diff --staged
    git restore file.txt
    git restore --staged file.txt
    git mv old.txt new.txt
    git rm file.txt
    git pull --rebase
    git push -u origin main

Branching:
    git branch
    git branch -a
    git branch -d feature
    git branch -D feature
    git switch -c feature
    git switch main
    git checkout -b hotfix
    git merge feature
    git rebase main
    git rebase --continue
    git rebase --abort

History and inspection:
    git log
    git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
    git log -p file.txt
    git show abc1234
    git blame file.txt
    git shortlog -s
    git reflog
    git describe --tags
    git tag
    git tag -a v1.0 -m "release"
    git push --tags

Undo and recovery:
    git restore --staged .
    git reset --soft HEAD~1
    git reset --mixed HEAD~1
    git reset --hard HEAD~1
    git revert abc1234
    git cherry-pick abc1234
    git stash
    git stash push -m "wip"
    git stash list
    git stash pop
    git stash drop
    git clean -n
    git clean -fd

Advanced:
    git bisect start
    git bisect bad
    git bisect good abc1234
git bisect reset
    git worktree add ../hotfix hotfix
    git gc --prune=now
    git fsck

GitHub CLI:
    gh auth login
    gh auth status
    gh repo view
    gh repo create myrepo --private --push
    gh repo clone user/repo
    gh pr create --fill
    gh pr list
    gh pr checkout 42
    gh pr merge 42 --squash
    gh issue list
    gh issue create --title "bug" --body "details"
    gh release create v1.0 --generate-notes
    gh api /repos/user/repo
    gh browse

Important notes:
- git reset --hard and git clean -fd destroy uncommitted work irrecoverably
- Use git reflog to recover anything you reset away
- Never commit directly to main on a shared repository; use a feature branch
docs.Jenkins:
Jenkins

Jenkins is a self-hosted automation server. It runs pipelines defined in a
Jenkinsfile, triggered by webhooks, timers or manual builds. Running it in
Docker is the fastest way to get a working controller locally.

Key concepts:
- Controller runs the UI, executor and agent orchestration on port 8080
- Agent (node) executes the actual build steps
- Jenkinsfile declares stages, each with steps that run shell commands
- The initial admin password is generated on first start
- Plugins extend everything: GitHub, Kubernetes, Docker Pipeline, Credentials

Getting started:
1. Click 'Start Jenkins Container' to launch a detached container.
2. Click 'Get Initial Admin Password' and paste it into the unlock screen.
3. Choose 'Install suggested plugins', then create your first job.
4. Click 'Open Jenkins UI' to reach http://localhost:8080

Key commands:
    docker run -d --name jenkins -p 8080:8080 -p 50000:50000 -v jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk17
    docker exec jenkins cat /var/jenkins_home/secrets/initialAdminPassword
    docker logs -f jenkins
    docker restart jenkins
    docker stop jenkins
    docker rm jenkins
    docker exec -it jenkins bash
    docker inspect jenkins
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/json

Important notes:
- Mount a volume or you lose every job on container removal
- Port 50000 is the inbound agent port; keep it open for agents
- Pin the image tag rather than using 'latest'
docs.Terraform:
Terraform

Terraform manages infrastructure as code. You describe the desired state in
HCL files and Terraform works out the exact API calls needed to reach it,
recording everything it creates in state.

Key concepts:
- init downloads providers and prepares the .terraform directory
- plan shows what would change without changing anything
- apply executes the plan; destroy tears resources back down
- state is the memory of what exists - back it up and never edit by hand
- workspaces let you manage several states (dev, staging, prod) separately

Core workflow:
    terraform init
    terraform validate
    terraform plan
    terraform plan -out=tfplan
    terraform apply tfplan
    terraform destroy
    terraform fmt
    terraform fmt -recursive
    terraform show
    terraform providers
    terraform version

State management:
    terraform state list
    terraform state show aws_instance.web
    terraform state rm aws_instance.web
    terraform refresh
    terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID
    terraform workspace list
    terraform workspace new staging
    terraform workspace select staging

Importing and debugging:
    terraform import aws_instance.web i-0123456789
    terraform graph -type=plan
    terraform console
    terraform output
    terraform output -json
    terraform taint aws_instance.web
    terraform untaint aws_instance.web
    terraform apply -auto-approve
    terraform apply -target=aws_instance.web

Important notes:
- Commit the lock file .terraform.lock.hcl, ignore the .terraform directory
- Never run terraform apply without reviewing the plan first
- Keep state in a remote backend for any real team
docs.Ansible:
Ansible

Ansible is agentless configuration management. It connects over SSH, reads an
inventory of hosts, and applies playbooks that describe the desired state of
those machines. No agent to install, no daemon to maintain.

Key concepts:
- inventory lists the hosts and groups you manage
- playbook is a YAML file of plays, each with tasks and handlers
- module is the unit of work: copy, apt, service, template, lineinfile
- --check (or --dry-run) reports changes without applying them
- --diff shows the exact before/after for file modules
- handlers run once at the end of a play, triggered by notifications

Common commands:
    ansible all -m ping
    ansible webservers -m ping
    ansible-playbook site.yml
    ansible-playbook site.yml --check --diff
    ansible-playbook site.yml --syntax-check
    ansible-playbook site.yml --limit webservers
    ansible-playbook site.yml --tags deploy
    ansible all -m shell -a "uptime"
    ansible all -m command -a "df -h"
    ansible webservers -b -m apt -a "nginx"

Inventory and configuration:
    ansible-inventory --graph
    ansible-inventory --list
    ansible-inventory --host web1
    ansible -i production.ini all -m ping
    ansible-config dump
    ansible-config list
    ansible --version

Vault and collections:
    ansible-vault create secrets.yml
    ansible-vault edit secrets.yml
    ansible-vault decrypt secrets.yml
    ansible-galaxy collection install community.general
    ansible-galaxy role init myrole
    ansible-doc -l
    ansible-doc user.add

Important notes:
- Keep inventory in source control but secrets in ansible-vault
- Always run --syntax-check in CI before a real run
- Use --check --diff in pull requests to preview infrastructure changes
docs.Port Manager:
Port Manager

Port Manager lists every TCP and UDP port currently in use on this PC, maps
each one to the owning process, and lets you terminate that process.

Key concepts:
- netstat -ano shows the connections plus the owning PID for each one
- tasklist resolves those PIDs into readable process names
- LISTENING means the process accepts inbound connections on that port
- taskkill /F force-kills a process; /T also kills its children
- PID 0 and PID 4 are kernel-owned and can never be terminated

Common ports you will recognise:
- 135 RPC, 445 SMB, 3389 RDP, 53 DNS, 8080 Jenkins, 5432 Postgres
- 3306 MySQL, 27017 MongoDB, 6379 Redis, 9090 many dashboards
- 6443 Kubernetes API server, 3000 Grafana

Key commands:
    netstat -ano
    netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING
    netstat -ano | findstr :8080
    netstat -ano -p TCP
    tasklist /FI "PID eq 1234"
    tasklist /FO CSV /NH
    taskkill /PID 1234 /F
    taskkill /PID 1234 /F /T
    taskkill /IM node.exe /F

How to use it:
1. Press Refresh to load the live table.
2. Filter by protocol or search a port number to narrow the list.
3. Select a row and press Kill Port.
4. Confirm the dialog; the table refreshes automatically afterwards.

Important notes:
- Killing a system service can trigger a reboot or lose unsaved work
- The Kill button blocks PID 0, PID 4 and core Windows services
- Admin rights are required to terminate protected processes
docs.Custom: Enter any free‑form command you want to run – useful for resources not covered by the built‑in shortcuts, such as `ReplicationController` or custom `kubectl` plugins.
docs.Networking Masterclass:
Open the Learning Centre for the full study guide.

43 chapters covering networking fundamentals, IP addresses, subnetting, ports, TCP vs UDP, protocols, network devices, the Linux command line and permissions, software engineering, Linux and Windows sysadmin, and DevOps.

Every chapter explains the theory in plain English, shows the real commands, gives memory tricks, includes a Learning vs Production comparison, and ends with an exercise you can run on this machine.

Press the button below to open it in its own window.
docs.Security Testing:
Find and fix security problems before users find them for you.

The buttons are grouped by the kind of test, which is also the order tests usually run in:
• Reconnaissance - map the target with nmap, nikto and whatweb
• Application scanning - OWASP ZAP, nuclei and sqlmap against a running app
• Static analysis (SAST) - read the source without running it (bandit, semgrep, gitleaks)
• Dependency scanning (SCA) - find known CVEs in what you imported (pip-audit, npm audit, trivy)
• Container and host - check images and Kubernetes configuration
• CI/CD gates - the checks that should fail a build automatically

Only ever scan systems you own or have written permission to test.
docs.Firewalls:
A firewall is the rulebook that decides which network traffic is allowed in, allowed out, or dropped silently.

This panel covers the four you will actually meet:
• ufw - the simple front end on Ubuntu
• firewalld - the zone-based equivalent on RHEL, CentOS and Fedora
• nftables - the modern kernel rule engine underneath both
• Windows Defender Firewall - the same idea via netsh on Windows

Read the rules before you change them. Enabling a firewall with the wrong rules can lock you out of your own machine over SSH, so always confirm port 22 (or 3389 for Windows) is allowed first.
docs.Diagrams:
A diagram is an explanation that fits on one screen. Drawing one finds the gaps in your thinking faster than talking does.

These buttons render and check diagrams rather than draw them by hand:
• PlantUML - architecture, UML and sequence diagrams from text
• Graphviz - graph layout, good for dependency and flow graphs
• Mermaid - diagrams that live in Markdown documentation
• dbdiagram.io - database schemas, and it can generate the SQL

The Diagrams chapter explains which diagram to reach for, what each one is for, and when in the project you should draw it.
docs.Databases:
Designing and querying a database properly is most of what separates a working application from a fast one.

• Postgres, MySQL and Mongo clients for day-to-day work
• Schema design and normalisation - finding duplicate values, stray nulls and unused indexes
• Relationships and cardinality - which tables point at which, and how many rows each may have
• The Databases chapter covers normalisation from 1NF to BCNF, joins, indexes, and full SQL and NoSQL

The MySQL, Postgres and MongoDB categories deploy those engines on Kubernetes. This category administers a database you already have.

chapters.title: Start Here
chapters.html:
How to Use This Guide

This guide is written for someone starting from nothing. Each chapter follows the same shape, so you always know what comes next:

SectionWhat you get
What it isA plain-English analogy with no jargon
How it worksStep-by-step, with real numbers
How to rememberA mnemonic or shortcut that actually sticks
CommandsReal, copy-pasteable commands
Try it yourselfA short hands-on exercise
Learning vs ProductionWhat changes when it is real

Where to start

  • Never touched networking? Chapters 1 to 4, in order. Do the exercises, they matter more than the reading.
  • Know the basics, want depth? Chapters 5 to 7 cover protocols and devices that most people half-understand.
  • Learning Linux? Chapter 8 takes the command line from navigation through permissions, pipes and services.
  • New to how teams work? Chapter 11 covers the SDLC, Agile and the full Scrum framework.
  • Learning AWS? Chapter 12 starts from regions and IAM and works through to cost control.
  • Learning the delivery toolchain? Chapter 13 covers CI/CD, GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Terraform and Ansible.
  • Managing Windows servers? Chapter 10 shows every command side by side with its Linux equivalent.
  • Building for the cloud? Chapter 21 covers VPCs, subnets, IAM, high availability, disaster recovery and FinOps across AWS, Azure and GCP.
  • Running things in production? Chapters 15 to 20 cover security testing, firewalls, diagrams, databases, observability and SRE. Read them in that order; each one assumes the one before it.
  • New to how money and companies work? Chapters 22 and 23 cover payments, receipts, invoices, how shops and SaaS work, and the web security vocabulary every developer is expected to know.
  • Want depth beyond the basics? Chapters 24 onward go deeper: testing, deployment strategies, auth and TLS, advanced Python and its internals, FastAPI, email, cryptography, advanced networking, CCNA and Packet Tracer, Linux and Windows administration, the kernel, diagnostics, machine learning and AI, platform engineering, and a Docker deep dive.

How to actually learn this

  • Type every command yourself. Reading code is not the same as running it.
  • Break things on purpose. Seeing a real error teaches more than a success.
  • Explain each concept out loud in one sentence. If you cannot, reread it.
  • Spaced repetition beats cramming. Revisit the memory tricks tomorrow.
  • Build something small. A server on your laptop beats any amount of reading.

A note on the command examples

Commands are shown for Windows PowerShell and Linux where they differ. Port scanning, killing processes and DNS lookups are all covered in the Port Manager category of this app, so you can try them without a second machine.

chapters.title: Networking Fundamentals
chapters.html:
1. What Is a Network?

A network is simply two or more computers that can talk to each other. That is the whole idea. Everything else - routers, subnets, protocols, DNS - exists only to make that conversation reliable, fast and private.

The best analogy: a city. Houses are computers, streets are networks, house numbers are IP addresses, and postal codes are subnet masks. The postman is the router. A phone book is DNS.

Why bother connecting machines?

  • Share resources - one printer, one disk, one licence.
  • Share data - your web browser fetches pages from servers.
  • Separate concerns - the database runs on a different machine so it can be scaled and secured independently.
  • Reliability - if one machine dies, the service keeps running somewhere else.

2. Packets: How Data Actually Moves

When you send data it is not sent as one giant lump. It is chopped into small pieces called packets. Each packet carries a label saying where it came from and where it is going.

Analogy: posting a book. You do not courier the whole book in one van. You split it into chapters, put each in an envelope with an address, and a courier delivers them. The envelopes may arrive in any order, but the reader reassembles the book.

Why split it?

  • If one packet is lost, you resend only that packet, not the whole file.
  • Different packets can take different routes across the internet.
  • Several computers can share the same cable at the same time.

The layers of a packet

Every packet is built in layers, like envelopes inside envelopes. Each layer only talks to the layers above and below it, which is why you can replace a cable without rewriting the application.

OSI LayerWhat it doesExample protocolsTypical device
7 ApplicationWhat the data meansHTTP, DNS, SSH, SMTPYour computer
6 PresentationEncoding, compression, encryptionTLS, JPEG, ASCIIYour computer
5 SessionStart, sync and end conversationsNetBIOS, RPC, SocketsServer
4 TransportReliable delivery, ports, segmentationTCP, UDPFirewall, load balancer
3 NetworkLogical addressing and routing between networksIP, ICMP, BGPRouter, L3 switch
2 Data LinkLocal delivery using MAC addresses and framesEthernet, Wi-Fi, ARPSwitch, NIC, access point
1 PhysicalActual signals on wire or radioCables, fibre, radioCable, transceiver

Memory trick for OSI, bottom up: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.

1 Physical, 2 Data Link, 3 Network, 4 Transport, 5 Session, 6 Presentation, 7 Application.

3. The Two Models You Must Know

OSI (7 layers) - the teaching model

OSI is what textbooks and interviews use. Excellent for reasoning, rarely used in real configuration.

TCP/IP (4 layers) - the real internet

This is what actually runs on the internet, and what you will configure.

TCP/IP layerMaps to OSIReal protocols
ApplicationLayers 7, 6, 5HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SSH, FTP, DHCP
TransportLayer 4TCP, UDP
InternetLayer 3IP, ICMP, ARP, BGP
Network AccessLayers 2, 1Ethernet, Wi-Fi, cables, MAC addresses

4. Key Words You Will Hear Immediately

WordPlain EnglishWhy you care
LatencyDelay before data arrivesUsers judge a site as slow even when throughput is fine
BandwidthMaximum capacity of a linkThe size of the pipe, not the flow speed
ThroughputActual useful data per secondAlways lower than bandwidth because of overhead
JitterVariation in latencyKills VoIP and video quality more than high latency does
MTULargest packet allowed on a linkA mismatch causes silent fragmentation or drops
SubnetA slice of a bigger networkHow an organisation splits into departments
GatewayDoorway into another networkWhere your traffic leaves
NATTranslation of private IPs to a public IPHow thousands of devices share one public address
Subnet maskWhich part of the IP is the streetDecides who is local and who needs a router

5. Latency vs Bandwidth - The Classic Confusion

Bandwidth is the width of the pipe. Latency is the length of the pipe. A fat but very long pipe (high bandwidth, high latency) feels slow. A thin but short pipe (low bandwidth, low latency) feels instant.

This is why a satellite link can offer more bandwidth than fibre yet feel slower: roughly 600 ms round trip just for the signal to bounce off a satellite.

6. Try It Yourself (10 minutes)

ping 8.8.8.8
tracert google.com
ipconfig /all
nslookup github.com
  • ping tests reachability and shows round-trip time in ms.
  • tracert shows every hop a packet passes through.
  • ipconfig /all shows your IP, mask, gateway and DNS servers.
  • nslookup asks a DNS server to turn a name into an address.

7. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
Network sizeOne laptop, maybe a Raspberry PiVPCs or VLANs across regions
LatencyNegligible, everything localMilliseconds accumulate; users abandon slow pages
BandwidthHome Wi-Fi, gigabitShaped, metered and billed per GB
FailureUnplug and restartRedundant paths, health checks, automated failover
SecurityOpen ports on your home routerFirewalls, least privilege, network segmentation
VisibilityNone at allMetrics, logs and alerts on latency, loss and errors
DocumentationIt is all in your headWritten network diagrams and runbooks

8. Key Takeaways

  • A network is just computers talking; everything else is detail.
  • Data travels as small labelled packets, not one lump.
  • OSI has 7 layers for theory; TCP/IP has 4 for reality.
  • Bandwidth is pipe width, latency is pipe length, and users feel latency.
  • The concepts are identical in production; failure and visibility are not.

chapters.title: IP Addresses
chapters.html:
1. What Is an IP Address?

An IP address is a unique number given to every device that joins a network. Its only job is to act as a delivery address.

Analogy: your home address. "Flat 4B, 22 Baker Street, London, NW1 6XE." The flat and number find the exact door, the street and city locate you quickly, and the postcode helps the postman route efficiently. An IP works the same way.

2. IPv4: The Dotted Decimal Form

An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four numbers between 0 and 255 separated by dots, such as 192.168.10.25.

Why four groups? Because 32 bits split into four chunks of 8 bits gives four numbers, and each 8-bit chunk can represent 0 to 255.

OctetDecimalBinary (8 bits)
119211000000
216810101000
31000001010
42500011001

Converting decimal to binary by hand

Each set bit is worth a power of two counted from the right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. For 192 that is 128 plus 64:

128  64  32  16  8  4  2  1
 1    1   0   0   0  0  0  0   = 11000000

Memory trick: memorise that single row as 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. Any decimal number is just a sum of those values. Once you can read that row both ways, binary is finished.

3. IPv6 - Why It Exists

IPv4 offers about 4.3 billion addresses and the internet ran out. IPv6 is 128 bits, giving roughly 3.4 x 10 to the power 38 addresses.

VersionBitsWritten asTotal space
IPv432Dotted decimal, for example 192.168.10.25About 4.3 billion
IPv6128Eight hex groups, for example 2001:db8::1About 3.4 x 10^38

The address 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001 shortens to 2001:db8::1. The double colon means "fill the rest with zeros" and may appear only once.

4. Public vs Private Addresses

This is the single most important idea for a beginner. Not every IP reaches the internet.

RangeNameReachable from the internet?
10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255Private, 10/8No, only inside your network
172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255Private, 172.16/12No, only inside your network
192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255Private, 192.168/16No, only inside your network
127.0.0.1LoopbackNo, means this machine
0.0.0.0Any / unspecifiedMeans all interfaces when binding
169.254.x.xLink-local, APIPASelf-assigned when DHCP fails
Everything elsePublicYes, if routing allows it

Memory trick: 10 is the easy one, 172 is the middle one, 192 is the one you see at home. Learn them as 10, 172, 192 and they will not slip.

Why private addresses exist: IPv4 ran short. NAT lets thousands of private devices share one public IP. Your laptop uses 192.168.1.42, the router owns 203.0.113.7, and the router swaps the numbers as packets leave and return.

5. How an IP Address Splits - The Core Concept

This is what subnetting rests on. Every IP is divided into two parts:

  • Network portion - which street you are on
  • Host portion - which house number on that street

The subnet mask is the rule that says where the split falls. In binary it is a run of 1s followed by a run of 0s.

Take 192.168.10.25/24 whose mask is 255.255.255.0:

PartAddressMaskBinary maskMeaning
Network192.168.10255.255.25511111111.11111111.11111111The street
Host25000000000The house number

The rule you will use forever

Write the mask in binary, count the 1s, and that number is the CIDR prefix.

255.255.255.0
11111111 . 11111111 . 11111111 . 00000000
 24 ones -> /24

255.255.254.0
11111111 . 11111111 . 11111110 . 00000000
 23 ones -> /23

Memory trick: the prefix length is simply the count of 1s in the mask. Nothing else. Count the ones and you have your answer.

How a computer decides local or remote

To send a packet, your machine ANDs the destination address with the mask. If the result equals its own network portion, the destination is local and it uses a MAC address. Otherwise it hands the packet to the gateway.

My IP:       192.168.10.25
Mask:        255.255.255.0
My network:  192.168.10.0

To 192.168.10.99 -> same network  -> send directly using MAC
To 8.8.8.8       -> other network -> send to the gateway

That single comparison is why your printer at 192.168.1.50 answers directly, while a website has to go through the router.

6. Special Addresses Worth Memorising

AddressMeaningNote
0.0.0.0Any address, all interfacesUse when a server should bind everywhere
127.0.0.1Localhost, this machineNever leaves your computer
255.255.255.255BroadcastEvery device on the local network
x.x.x.0 for a /24Network address of the subnetCannot be assigned to a host
x.x.x.255 for a /24Broadcast for that subnetCannot be assigned to a host

7. Commands

ipconfig /all
ip addr show
ping 192.168.10.1
tracert 8.8.8.8
nslookup google.com

8. Try It Yourself (15 minutes)

  • Run ipconfig /all and find your IPv4 address and subnet mask.
  • Count the 1s in your mask and write the CIDR beside it.
  • Work out your network address by ANDing your IP with the mask.
  • Ping your own IP; it replies instantly without leaving the machine.
  • Compare your IP with your router gateway. Matching first three octets means traffic never touches the internet.

9. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
Addressing192.168.1.x handed out by your home routerPlanned CIDR blocks reserved per environment
OverlapsOverlap with home and ignore itOverlapping VPCs break VPN routing and must be planned
Public IPsNone, everything stays privateRarely used; load balancers and NAT gateways instead
IPv6Often switched off entirelyFrequently mandatory on cloud providers
AllocationTyped manually in a terminalIPAM, DHCP scopes, Terraform, Kubernetes Services
Source of truthYour memoryIPAM, so no engineer guesses

10. Key Takeaways

  • An IP address is a delivery address split into network and host parts.
  • IPv4 is 32 bits as four numbers; IPv6 is 128 bits as eight hex groups.
  • The prefix length is just the count of 1s in the subnet mask.
  • 10, 172.16-31 and 192.168 are private and never route to the internet.
  • Same network means direct delivery; a different network means via the gateway.

chapters.title: Subnetting
chapters.html:
1. Why Subnet at All?

One flat network is simple until it breaks. In a single subnet every device sees every other device, broadcast traffic floods everywhere, and you cannot apply different rules to different teams. Subnetting slices one big network into smaller logical networks.

Analogy: one giant open-plan floor versus a building divided into departments. They share the same postal address, but each has its own internal number range and its own secured door.

Subnets give you:

  • Segmentation - a breach in one subnet does not expose all.
  • Efficiency - smaller broadcast domains, less wasted space.
  • Organisation - engineering, finance and guests look different.
  • Flexibility - separate policies, routes and DHCP scopes.

2. CIDR Notation

CIDR is an address followed by a slash and the prefix length, for example 10.0.0.0/16. The number after the slash says how many of the 32 bits belong to the network. A /24 means 24 network bits and 8 host bits, and those 8 host bits decide how many addresses exist.

3. The Magic Number Table - Memorise This

This single table answers almost every subnetting question.

PrefixMaskHost bitsTotalUsable hosts
/24255.255.255.08256254
/25255.255.255.1287128126
/26255.255.255.19266462
/27255.255.255.22453230
/28255.255.255.24041614
/29255.255.255.248386
/30255.255.255.252242
/31255.255.255.254122 point to point
/32255.255.255.255011 single host

Memory trick: 255.255.255.0 is /24. Every step down halves it: 254, 126, 62, 30, 14, 6, 2. Learn that sequence and you can answer instantly.

4. Usable Hosts = 2 to the power n, minus 2

Two addresses are always wasted: the network address and the broadcast address.

Hosts needed: 50
Smallest power of two above 50 is 64  ->  2^6
Add 2 back for network and broadcast  ->  64 + 2 = 66
Next power of two above 66 is 128      ->  2^7
So we need 7 host bits -> prefix = 32 - 7 = /25

Why minus 2? .0 is the name of the street itself and .255 means "everyone on this street". Neither can be a real house.

5. Subnetting Step by Step - A Worked Example

You own 192.168.0.0/24 and need to split it into four /26 subnets.

SubnetNetwork addressUsable rangeBroadcast
1192.168.0.0/26192.168.0.1 - 192.168.0.62192.168.0.63
2192.168.0.64/26192.168.0.65 - 192.168.0.126192.168.0.127
3192.168.0.128/26192.168.0.129 - 192.168.0.190192.168.0.191
4192.168.0.192/26192.168.0.193 - 192.168.0.254192.168.0.255

Memory trick: start at .0 and add the block size each time. For /26 the block size is 64, so: 0, 64, 128, 192.

6. The Borrow 2^n Trick

For a /26 you borrow 6 bits, so the block size is 2 to the power 6, which is 64. You never need to look it up.

Bits borrowed1234567
Block size248163264128

Equivalently, the block size is 256 minus the last octet of the mask. For 255.255.255.192 that is 256 minus 192, which is 64.

7. VLSM - Variable Length Subnet Masking

Old subnetting gave every subnet the same size and wasted enormous address space. VLSM gives each subnet only what it needs, largest first.

DepartmentHosts neededPrefixUsableWasted
Engineering500/221022522
Marketing100/2512626
Support50/266212
Router link2/3120

Why biggest first: if you allocate the small subnets first, the large one no longer fits into what is left. Always work downwards from the largest requirement.

8. Scenarios Worth Memorising

ScenarioWhat to doAnswer
Give a PC and a router addresses on 192.168.1.0/24Never use .0 or .255PC 192.168.1.10, router 192.168.1.1
Usable hosts on 10.0.0.0/272^5 = 32, minus 230 hosts, .1 to .30
Split 172.16.0.0/24 into twoBorrow 1 bit/25 and /25, 126 hosts each
Link between two routersSmallest useful subnet/30, 4 addresses, 2 usable
One address on a loopbackZero host bits/32, for example 10.0.0.1/32
Kubernetes Service CIDRServices are virtual IPsCommonly 10.96.0.0/12

9. Commands

# Windows
ipconfig /all
route print
netsh interface ip show address

# Linux
ip addr show
ip route

10. Try It Yourself (20 minutes)

  • You need subnets for 100, 50 and 10 hosts. Find the prefix for each.
  • Split 10.0.0.0/24 into four equal subnets and write out the ranges.
  • Why is 192.168.1.255 unusable on a /24? Because it is the broadcast address.
  • Write /24, /25, /26, /27 and their usable counts from memory.
  • Drill the row 254, 126, 62, 30, 14, 6, 2 until it is automatic.

11. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
ExampleA tidy 10.0.0.0/24 split into four /26Whole /16 blocks carved across many VPCs
OverlapsOverlapping home causes no visible problemBreak VPN tunnels and on-prem routing
RoutingOne flat table and the default routeDynamic protocols with summarisation and BGP
AllocationDone by hand in a terminalTerraform, VPC CNI, IPAM with strict tagging
WasteNot a concernSome clouds bill per allocated address
DocumentationYou remember itIPAM plus a network diagram reviewed in pull requests
ErrorsRedo the tableCause outages, so changes need review and rollback

12. Key Takeaways

  • The CIDR number equals the count of 1s in the mask.
  • Usable hosts is 2 to the power n, minus 2 for network and broadcast.
  • Block size is 2 to the power the bits borrowed, or 256 minus the last mask octet.
  • /24 gives 254 hosts and every step down halves it.
  • In VLSM always allocate the largest subnet first.
  • In production a subnet mistake is not homework; it is an outage.

chapters.title: Ports and Sockets
chapters.html:
1. What Is a Port?

An IP address gets a packet to the right machine. A port gets it to the right program on that machine.

Analogy: the IP is the building address and the port is the flat number inside. 22 Baker Street (IP), flat 4B (port). Many apps can run on one machine only because their doors have different numbers.

Both numbers fit into one value, a socket: an IP address plus a port. A TCP socket is written as 192.168.1.10:8080.

2. Why Not One Service Per Machine?

Before ports existed, a machine could run one network service at a time. Ports let many programs share one IP. Your laptop is simultaneously running a web server on 8000, a database on 5432 and a remote shell on 22.

3. Port Ranges

RangeNamePurposeExamples
0 - 1023Well-knownStandard services, need admin rights to bind22 SSH, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS
1024 - 49151RegisteredApplications registered with IANA3306 MySQL, 5432 Postgres, 27017 MongoDB
49152 - 65535Dynamic or ephemeralTemporary client ports chosen by the OSA browser picks a random source port

Memory trick: the ones you will see constantly number under 1000, and the number usually hints at the service. 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS.

4. Ports You Will Meet Every Day

PortProtocolUsed by
20, 21FTPFile transfer, insecure
22SSH, SFTPSecure remote shell and file transfer
25SMTPSending mail between servers
53DNSTurning names into IP addresses
80HTTPUnencrypted web traffic
443HTTPSEncrypted web traffic, also many APIs
3306MySQLMySQL database
5432PostgresPostgreSQL database
6379RedisIn-memory cache and datastore
8080HTTP altJenkins, proxies, dev servers
27017MongoDBMongoDB database
6443HTTPSKubernetes API server

5. Connections Use Two Ports - This Confuses Everyone

When you browse to a site on port 443, your machine also opens an ephemeral port of its own. Every connection needs a port at each end.

Your machine (192.168.1.10:54321)  -->  Website (93.184.216.34:443)
          source port                          destination port

Your OS picks the source port automatically from the ephemeral range, and the server replies back to 192.168.1.10:54321. Many simultaneous connections are possible because each uses a different source port.

6. One IP Can Only Use a Port Once, Per Protocol

Two processes cannot both listen on 192.168.1.10:8080 over TCP. The second fails with address already in use. That is why you must stop the old process before starting a new one on the same port.

TCP and UDP are tracked separately, so TCP 8080 and UDP 8080 can coexist on the same machine.

7. Finding and Killing a Process by Port

Use the Port Manager in this app, or work from the command line:

# Windows: find what is using a port
netstat -ano | findstr :8080
tasklist /FI "PID eq 1234"
taskkill /PID 1234 /F /T

# Linux and macOS
lsof -i :8080
netstat -tulnp | grep 8080
kill -9 1234

Worth remembering: -ano shows all, numeric and owning PID. /F forces the kill. /T also kills child processes.

8. Reading netstat States

StateMeaningWhat to do
LISTENINGA server is waiting for connectionsUsually a service you started
ESTABLISHEDAn active conversationLeave it alone unless you know why
TIME_WAITClosed, waiting to be sure nothing returnsNormal after a short connection closes
CLOSE_WAITRemote side closed but we have notOften a sign of a buggy application
SYN_SENTConnection attempt in progressNormal during connect, or a firewall dropping you

9. Try It Yourself (10 minutes)

  • Open the Port Manager in the sidebar of this app and press Refresh.
  • Search for a port you know, such as 5432 or 3306.
  • Run netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING and compare with the table.
  • Notice how many processes share port 80 and explain why.
  • Start a small server and watch it appear: python -m http.server 8080

10. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
ExposureServer on localhost, fire and forgetBound to 0.0.0.0 behind a load balancer and firewall
Ingresskubectl port-forward for everythingIngress controller plus a managed load balancer and TLS
Port choiceAnything freeWell-known ports, documented and reserved
Discoverynetstat by handService mesh, metrics, automated port inventory
Many replicasOne process, one portMany pods share a Service that load balances
SecurityAssume everyone is friendlySecurity groups, NetworkPolicy, least exposure

11. Key Takeaways

  • IP finds the machine, port finds the program.
  • Well-known ports are 0-1023; ephemeral ports are chosen automatically.
  • Every connection uses one source port and one destination port.
  • Two TCP programs cannot share one port on one IP.
  • netstat -ano with taskkill is how you free a stuck port.
  • In production you rarely expose a port directly; you put a proxy in front.

chapters.title: TCP vs UDP
chapters.html:
1. What Are They?

TCP and UDP are the two transport protocols at OSI layer 4. TCP is careful and reliable; UDP is fast and careless. Both move data between two ports.

Analogy: TCP is registered post with tracking and a signature. UDP is a courier who sprints to your door and hands over the parcel without checking any ID.

2. The TCP Three-Way Handshake

Before any data flows, both sides confirm they can hear each other. That buys reliability and ordering.

Client                          Server
  | ---- SYN -------------------> |   I would like to connect
  | <--- SYN + ACK -------------- |   Yes, and I would like to connect
  | ---- ACK -------------------> |   Great, we agree
  | ---- DATA ------------------> |   The conversation starts
  • SYN - I want to open a connection.
  • SYN + ACK - I agree, and I also want to connect.
  • ACK - Confirmed by both sides.

UDP sends data immediately, with no handshake at all.

3. Side by Side Comparison

FeatureTCPUDP
ConnectionHandshake first, then dataNone, just send
ReliabilityLost packets are resentNo resending
OrderingReassembled in orderArrival order not guaranteed
SpeedSlower, more handshakingVery fast, no waiting
Header size20 bytes or more8 bytes
Congestion controlYes, slows down when congestedNo, can flood the network
Flow controlYes, protects the receiverNo
Broadcast and multicastNot possibleSupported
Data unitA byte streamDiscrete messages

4. How to Remember the Choice

Use TCP when losing data would be wrong: web pages, email, file transfers, databases, SSH.

Use UDP when being late is worse than losing something: live video, voice calls, gaming, DNS lookups.

Memory trick: TCP is Trouble-free, Cautious, Patient. UDP is Unreliable but Dazzlingly quick.

5. Real Examples - Know Which One Each Uses

ApplicationProtocolWhy
HTTP and HTTPSTCPA page must arrive complete
SSH and SFTPTCPInteractive commands cannot be lost
Email, SMTP, IMAPTCPPartial mail is useless
Database trafficTCPCorrupt queries are unacceptable
DNS lookupUDPOne small question, one small answer
DHCPUDPBroadcast discovery before any IP exists
Video and voice callsUDPA late frame is worthless, drop it
Online gamingUDPPosition updates must be current
Streaming live TVUDPContinuity beats completeness

DNS is the classic surprise. People assume DNS uses TCP, but ordinary lookups use UDP port 53 because the question and answer are tiny. TCP is used when the response is too large for a single packet and for zone transfers between DNS servers.

6. Flow Control and Congestion Control

Flow control stops a fast sender drowning a slow receiver. TCP uses a sliding window and signals "I have room for N more bytes right now".

Congestion control stops the network being overwhelmed by too many senders. TCP increases its rate cautiously and backs off when it detects loss, which it treats as a sign of congestion.

UDP does neither, which is why large UDP floods are dangerous to a network.

7. Seeing It in Practice

# Windows: test a TCP port
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName example.com -Port 443

# Windows: test a UDP port
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 1.1.1.1 -Port 53 -Udp

# Linux and macOS
nc -vz example.com 443
ss -tan state established

8. Try It Yourself (15 minutes)

  • Run Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443 and read TCPTestSucceeded.
  • Compare the timing against a filtered port. Notice the difference between connection refused and a timeout.
  • Run the UDP variant against port 53 and observe the speed.
  • Run nslookup and notice how instant it is, because DNS uses UDP.

9. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
Handshake costHardly noticed on localhostDominates at scale, so connections are reused
HTTPNew connection every requestHTTP/2 or HTTP/3 multiplex over one connection
UDP usageMostly DNS and gamesAlso QUIC, service meshes, telemetry and load testing
CongestionSingle flow, no issueLatency and loss actively managed and monitored
TimeoutsLong, just retryTight budgets with backoff and circuit breakers
Default choiceTCP everywhereStill TCP, with UDP only where latency is critical

10. Key Takeaways

  • TCP handshakes first, then guarantees order and resends losses.
  • UDP sends immediately with no guarantees at all.
  • TCP when losing data would be wrong; UDP when lateness is worse.
  • Web, SSH and databases use TCP; DNS, video calls and gaming use UDP.
  • TCP has flow and congestion control; UDP has neither.
  • Production mostly runs TCP, using UDP where latency really matters.

chapters.title: Protocols: DNS, HTTP, SSH, TLS
chapters.html:
1. DNS - The Phone Book of the Internet

People remember google.com, not 142.250.185.78. DNS translates names into addresses. It is the first thing that happens when you press Enter in a browser.

Analogy: you know a friend's name, not their phone number. DNS is you opening the phone book, finding the entry and dialling.

The full resolution journey

Type www.example.com and the following happens:

StepWho is askedWhat they say
1Your OS resolver"Do I already know this?" Usually from cache
2Recursive resolverYour ISP or a public resolver like 1.1.1.1
3Root server"Ask the .com server" (a.root-servers.net)
4.com TLD server"Ask the example.com server"
5Authoritative server"It is 93.184.216.34"
6Back up the chainResolver caches it, then you get the answer

Memory trick: Root, TLD, Authoritative - in that order, and each one narrows the search. The resolver does all the walking; your machine only ever asks the resolver.

Record types

TypePurposeExample
AName to IPv4 addressexample.com A 93.184.216.34
AAAAName to IPv6 addressexample.com AAAA 2606:2800:220::1
CNAMEAlias to another namewww.example.com CNAME example.com
MXMail serverexample.com MX 10 mail.example.com
TXTFree text, used for SPF and domain verificationexample.com TXT "v=spf1 -all"
NSWhich DNS server is authoritativeexample.com NS ns1.provider.com
PTRAddress back to name, the reverse lookup34.216.184.93 PTR example.com

The hosts file

DNS caching can get in the way while testing. Add an entry to the hosts file to override it. On Windows that file is C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts.

93.184.216.34  example.com
127.0.0.1     myapp.local

2. HTTP and HTTPS

HTTP is a request and response conversation over TCP. The client asks, the server answers, and they are done. HTTP is stateless, meaning each request stands alone and the server remembers nothing between them.

Methods

MethodMeaningSafeRepeats
GETRead somethingYesYes
POSTCreate or submitNoNo
PUTReplace entirelyNoYes
PATCHPartially updateNoYes
DELETERemoveNoYes

Memory trick: Safe methods never change anything, so a browser may retry them. POST and DELETE change things, so they must never be retried automatically.

Status codes grouped by first digit

RangeMeaningCommon codes
1xxInformational, still working100 Continue, 101 Switching Protocols
2xxSuccess200 OK, 201 Created, 202 Accepted, 204 No Content
3xxRedirection301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified
4xxClient error, your fault400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found
5xxServer error, our fault500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Unavailable, 504 Timeout

Memory trick: 4xx is you to fix, 5xx is the server. On call, a flood of 5xx means the service is broken, not that users mistyped.

3. TLS and SSL - Encryption on the Wire

SSL is the obsolete name; the modern standard is TLS. They encrypt data so that anyone in the middle sees only gibberish, and they prove the server is who it claims to be.

Analogy: posting a letter in a locked box, with a wax seal. The seal proves the sender is genuine and the box prevents reading en route.

The TLS handshake, simplified

Client                                 Server
  | --- ClientHello: version, ciphers ---> |
  | <-- ServerHello + certificate ------- |   Here is my identity
  |     Client verifies the certificate    |   Issued by a CA I trust?
  | --- ClientKeyExchange ----------------> |   Here is the shared secret
  | --- Finished -------------------------> |
  | <== All later traffic is encrypted ===>
  • Asymmetric encryption (public and private keys) agrees on a shared secret without ever sending it.
  • The certificate binds a public key to a domain, signed by a Certificate Authority the browser already trusts.
  • Symmetric encryption (AES) is then used for the actual data, because it is far faster.

Memory trick: public key opens, private key proves. Public keys are fine to hand out, private keys must never leave your machine.

What HTTPS does not protect

Encryption hides the content. It does not hide the fact that you visited a site, it does not stop a phishing page that has its own valid certificate, and it does not make a slow site fast.

4. SSH - Encrypted Remote Access

SSH gives you an encrypted terminal on another machine over port 22. It replaced Telnet, which sent passwords in plain text.

Authentication is either a password or, far better, a key pair. Your private key stays on your machine and the public key is copied to the server's authorized_keys file. The server sends a challenge, you sign it with the private key, and it verifies against the public key it already holds. The private key is never sent.

ssh user@10.0.0.5
ssh -p 2222 user@host          # non-standard port
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 user@host
scp file.txt user@host:/tmp/   # encrypted copy
rsync -avz ./dist user@host:/var/www  # efficient sync

5. Other Protocols You Will Meet

ProtocolPortPurpose
ICMPnoneping and traceroute, no ports because it does not use TCP or UDP
DHCPUDP 67 and 68Automatically hands out IP addresses to devices joining the network
NTPUDP 123Keeps clocks synchronised, which logs and certificates depend on
FTPTCP 20 and 21File transfer, unencrypted and now discouraged
SFTPTCP 22File transfer tunnelled inside SSH, encrypted
SMTPTCP 25Sending email between mail servers
IMAPTCP 143 or 993Reading mail on a server
POP3TCP 110 or 995Older way of downloading mail
LDAPTCP 389 or 636Directories, also used by Kubernetes for authentication
SyslogUDP 514Sending logs to a central collector

6. Commands

# DNS
nslookup example.com
dig example.com A
dig example.com MX
dig +short example.com

# Connectivity
ping 8.8.8.8
tracert example.com
Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443

# TLS inspection
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com
curl -v https://example.com

7. Try It Yourself (20 minutes)

  • Run dig example.com and read the ANSWER SECTION for the A record.
  • Run dig example.com MX to find where its mail is handled.
  • Run curl -v https://example.com and find the TLS version and certificate issuer.
  • Add 127.0.0.1 myapp.local to your hosts file and see a browser honour it.
  • Compare ping example.com with ping 93.184.216.34.

8. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
DNSLocal machine, hosts file overridesManaged resolvers, health checks, TTLs tuned for failover
TLSSelf-signed and clicked throughAutomated renewal, short-lived certs, TLS everywhere
HTTPhttp://localhost:3000HTTPS only, HTTP redirected, HSTS enabled
SSHPassword login to a boxKey only, no root, bastion host, session logging
CertificatesHand-installed, long livedACME automation with alerting on expiry
SecretsIn a file next to the codeSecret manager, rotated regularly
Protocol choiceWhatever installs quicklyDeliberate, reviewed, version pinned

9. Key Takeaways

  • DNS walks Root, TLD, Authoritative, and the resolver caches the answer.
  • 4xx status codes are the client's fault; 5xx are the server's.
  • TLS uses asymmetric keys to agree, then symmetric AES for the data.
  • Public keys can be shared; private keys must never leave the machine.
  • SSH key authentication never transmits your private key.
  • In production, TLS is automated and SSH is key-only through a bastion.

chapters.title: Network Devices
chapters.html:
1. The Devices, Side by Side

Each device has one main job and one OSI layer it belongs to. Learn the table and the rest follows.

DeviceOSI layerIts one jobKnows aboutDoes not know
Repeater or hub1 PhysicalBoost the signalElectrical signalsAnything above
Bridge or switch2 Data LinkConnect devices, forward by MACMAC addressesIP addresses, networks
Router3 NetworkMove traffic between networksIP addresses, routing tablesWhich application is talking
Modem1 PhysicalConvert digital data to a line signalSignal modulationNothing above
Access point2 Data LinkBridge Wi-Fi to wired EthernetMAC addressesRouting
Firewall3 and 4Allow or block traffic by ruleIP, ports, sometimes app dataContent unless it inspects deeply
Load balancer4 and 7Spread requests across serversPorts, and at L7 URLs and headersData correctness
Proxy7 ApplicationTerminate a connection and forward itThe application protocolRouting

2. Switch vs Router - The Classic Question

A switch connects things in the same network. A router connects different networks. That is the entire difference.

AspectSwitch, layer 2Router, layer 3
UsesMAC addressesIP addresses
Keeps a table ofMAC address tableRouting table
ConnectsDevices on one subnetDifferent subnets or networks
BroadcastsFloods within the VLAN, never routedDoes not forward them by default
Typical deviceAccess switch in a rackHome router, core router, gateway
AnalogyA corridor inside one buildingThe street between two buildings

Memory trick: a switch moves data within a street using house numbers; a router moves it between streets using postcodes.

3. A Packet's Journey Through a Home Network

1. Laptop 192.168.1.10 wants example.com
2. Laptop builds the packet, destination 93.184.216.34
3. Laptop checks its mask: 93.184.216.34 is NOT local
4. Laptop sends the frame to its gateway 192.168.1.1, using the
   gateway's MAC address which it found with ARP
5. Switch forwards that frame to the router port, by MAC lookup
6. Router rewrites the frame header, decrements the TTL and looks
   up the destination in its routing table
7. Router hands the packet to the ISP
8. ISP routers hop by hop until the packet reaches the server
9. The reply returns along the same path in reverse

Each device rewrites only the part it understands: the switch changes the MAC header, the router changes the IP TTL and checksum.

4. How MAC and IP Work Together

ARP asks "who has 192.168.1.1?" on the local network and the reply carries a MAC address. ARP works only inside one subnet, because it is a broadcast and broadcasts do not cross routers.

AddressLayerScopeChanges at
IP3End to end across the whole internetEvery router decrements the TTL
MAC2One local link onlyEvery switch and router rewrites it

Memory trick: IP is the parcel address and stays the same end to end. MAC is the label on the van, rewritten at every depot.

5. VLANs - Virtual LANs

A VLAN splits one physical switch into several logical ones. Ports in VLAN 10 cannot reach ports in VLAN 20 without a router. That is segmentation without running extra cables.

A trunk port carries several VLANs at once using 802.1Q tags, which is how switches connect to each other and to routers.

6. NAT - Why Private IPs Work

NAT rewrites the source address on the way out and reverses it on the way back. Your laptop uses 192.168.1.42, the router owns 203.0.113.7, and everyone outside sees only the router. Thousands of devices can share one public address.

The trade-off is that unsolicited inbound traffic has nowhere to go, which is why inbound servers need port forwarding or a public address.

7. DHCP - Addresses on Tap

DHCP hands out addresses automatically in four steps, remembered as DORA:

StepLetterMeaning
1DiscoverClient broadcasts "is there a DHCP server?"
2OfferServer offers an address from its pool
3RequestClient asks for that specific address
4AcknowledgeServer confirms and records the lease

Memory trick: DORA. Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

8. Try It Yourself (15 minutes)

  • Run ipconfig and find your default gateway.
  • Run arp -a to see the MAC addresses your machine has learned.
  • Run tracert 8.8.8.8 and notice which hop is your router.
  • On Windows use ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew to watch DORA happen.
  • Log into your home router and list connected devices to see the switch table.

9. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
SwitchingOne home router doing everythingAccess, distribution and core layers, all redundant
SegmentationProbably none at allVLANs per environment plus NetworkPolicy in Kubernetes
RoutingStatic routes onlyBGP between sites and clouds, with summarisation
AddressingDHCP straight from the routerCentral IPAM with strict ownership per team
RedundancyNoneRedundant links, spanning tree or MLAG, dual-homed uplinks
VisibilityNoneSNMP, streaming telemetry, flow logs

10. Key Takeaways

  • Switch means layer 2 and MAC; router means layer 3 and IP.
  • MAC addresses are local and rewritten; IP addresses are end to end.
  • ARP only works inside one subnet because broadcasts do not cross routers.
  • VLANs give segmentation over a single physical switch.
  • NAT lets many private devices share one public address.
  • DHCP is DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

chapters.title: Linux Command Line
chapters.html:
1. What Linux Is, in One Paragraph

Linux is an operating system: the layer between your programs and the hardware. It is built from four ideas you will meet everywhere - users, files, processes and permissions - and almost everything in this chapter exists to work with one of them.

The one mental model to keep: Linux is one big folder tree starting at /. There is no "C drive" and no "D drive". Everything, including your USB stick and every hard disk, hangs off that single root.

/
├── home      your personal files
├── etc       system-wide configuration
├── var       logs and data that grow
├── tmp       temporary files, cleared on reboot
├── usr       programs and libraries
├── bin       essential commands
└── proc      a live view of running processes

Memory trick: /etc holds configuration, /var holds variable data that grows, /usr holds user programs. They are the three you will visit most.

2. Getting Around - pwd, cd, ls

pwd                 # where am I? prints /home/alice/project
ls                  # list this folder
ls -l               # long format: permissions, owner, size, date
ls -la              # long format plus hidden files
ls -lh              # human readable sizes: 4.0K instead of 4096
cd ..               # go up one level
cd ~                # go home
cd -                # go back to the folder you were just in
cd /etc             # absolute path, from the root
cd ../sibling       # relative: up one, then into sibling

Reading ls -l output

Every line has ten fields. The first is the permission string:

-rw-r--r--  1 alice alice  4096 Mar  3 10:22 notes.txt
drwxr-xr-x  2 root  root   4096 Mar  3 10:20 project
FieldExampleMeaning
Type- or ddash for a file, d for a directory, l for a symlink
Ownerrw-permissions for the file's owner
Groupr--permissions for the file's group
Othersr--permissions for everyone else
Links1how many hard links point at it
Owneralicethe user that owns it
Groupalicethe group that owns it
Size4096size in bytes
ModifiedMar 3 10:22last change time
Namenotes.txtthe file name

Memory trick: hidden files start with a dot, like .bashrc. ls -a reveals them.

3. Paths: Absolute vs Relative

KindStarts withExampleBased on
Absolute//etc/nginx/nginx.confAlways the root, no matter where you are
Relativeanything else../logs/app.logYour current folder
Home~~/documentsYour home folder, wherever you are
Current../run.shThe folder you are in right now
Parent..../One level up from where you are

Use absolute paths in scripts and configuration, because relative paths break the moment the script runs from a different folder.

4. Creating, Copying, Moving, Deleting

touch notes.txt              # create an empty file
mkdir project                # create a directory
mkdir -p a/b/c               # create nested folders, no error if they exist
cp notes.txt backup.txt      # copy a file
cp -r source/ destination/   # copy a directory and everything in it
mv old.txt new.txt           # move or rename
rm notes.txt                 # delete a file
rm -r project                # delete a directory and its contents
rm -i bigfile                # ask before each delete
mkdir /tmp/backup && cp app.log /tmp/backup/   # only if the first worked

Be careful with rm -rf. There is no undo and no recycle bin. Always rm -i until you are confident.

5. Viewing File Contents

cat notes.txt                # print the whole file
less notes.txt               # scroll with arrows, q to quit
head -n 5 notes.txt          # first 5 lines
tail -n 5 notes.txt          # last 5 lines
tail -f /var/log/syslog      # follow new lines as they arrive
wc -l notes.txt              # count lines
grep -c error notes.txt      # count matching lines
sort names.txt | uniq        # sorted unique values
cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd      # print field 1 using : as the separator

Memory trick: tail -f is how you watch a log file live. Learn falling for follow.

6. Pipes and Redirection - Where Everybody Gets Stuck

Every command in Linux writes its result to something called standard output. Redirection decides where that output goes, and a pipe sends it to another command's input.

Redirection: changing where output goes

SymbolMeaningUse it to
>Write to a file, replacing itSave output, discarding the old file
>>Append to a fileAdd to a log without losing previous lines
<Read input from a fileFeed a file into a command
2>Redirect errors to a fileKeep errors separate from results
2>&1Send errors to normal outputCapture everything in one stream
|Pipe one command into the nextChain commands together
echo "hello" > file.txt        # file now contains hello
echo "world" >> file.txt       # file now contains hello then world
ls > listing.txt               # save the listing
ls > /dev/null                  # throw the output away
command < input.txt# read input from a file
ls 2> errors.txt               # save errors separately
ls 2>&1 | grep denied# catch errors AND results together

Why 2>&1 works: file descriptors are numbered. Descriptor 1 is normal output, 2 is errors. 2>&1 means "take descriptor 2 and send it wherever descriptor 1 is going".

Memory trick: > points right into a file, < points left out of one, | is a pipe between two commands.

Pipes - chaining commands

The real power of Linux is that each command does one small thing well, and pipes let you combine them.

ls -l | grep "Jul" | wc -l          # count files modified in July
cat access.log | grep "404" | wc -l  # count errors in a log
ps aux | grep nginx | grep -v grep # find nginx, hide the grep itself
cat file | sort | uniq | sort -rn | head   # top 10 most common values
find . -name "*.log" -exec du -h {} ";" | sort -rh | head
# Command substitution: run one command and use its output as an argument
cd "$(dirname /etc/nginx/nginx.conf)"
echo "Today is $(date)"
tar -czf backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz /etc
for file in $(ls *.txt); do echo "Found $file"; done

Conditionals that chain commands

SymbolMeaningExample
&&Run the second only if the first succeededmkdir x && cd x
||Run the second only if the first failedcd x || echo "no such folder"
;Run the second regardlessecho a; echo b

Memory trick: && is "success leads to", || is "failure leads to".

7. grep - Searching Text

grep "error" app.log              # lines containing error
grep -i "error" app.log           # ignore capitalisation
grep -v "error" app.log           # lines NOT containing error
grep -n "error" app.log           # show line numbers
grep -c "error" app.log           # count matching lines
grep -r "apiKey" .                # search a whole directory tree
grep -r -l "apiKey" .             # list only files that match
grep -E "error|warning" app.log   # alternation, like a regex or
grep -r "^root" /etc/passwd       # lines starting with root
grep "user.$" app.log             # end-of-line anchor

Memory trick: invert case, verse the match, number the lines, recursive, count.

8. File Permissions - The Full Picture

Linux has no concept of files you cannot see. Every file has an owner, a group, and three permissions for each of three classes of user. Once you can read the ten characters of ls -l you can manage any file on the system.

The three classes

ClassWho it applies toSymbol
Owner, the userThe single user who owns the fileu
GroupEveryone in the file's assigned groupg
OthersAnybody else on the systemo
All threeOwner, group and others togethera

The three permissions

PermissionLetterValueOn a file it meansOn a directory it means
Readr4You can open and view itYou can list the contents
Writew2You can change the contentsYou can create and delete files inside
Executex1You can run it as a programYou can enter it and reach files deeper inside
None-0No access at allNo access at all

This is the part that confuses everyone: the same letter means different things for a file and a directory. Execute on a file means "runnable script". Execute on a directory means "you may travel through it to reach files deeper inside". Without it you can list a folder but not enter it.

Reading the permission string

-rw-r--r--  1 alice alice 4096 notes.txt
drwxr-xr-x  2 root  root  4096 project
-rwxr-xr-x  1 alice alice 4096 run.sh
ExampleOwnerGroupOthersWhat it is
-rw-r--r--read writereadreadA normal text file, mode 644
drwxr-xr-xread write executeread executeread executeA normal folder, mode 755
-rwxr-xr-xread write executeread executeread executeA script anyone can run, 755
-rw-------read writenonenoneA private file, 600, such as an SSH key
drwx------read write executenonenoneA private folder, 700, such as ~/.ssh

9. chmod in Numeric Mode

Numeric mode gives one digit per class. Each digit is the sum of the values you want: read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1. Read and write without execute is 6, and all three together is 7.

DigitLettersHow you get it
0---Nothing
1--xExecute only
2-w-Write only
3-wx2 + 1, write and execute
4r--Read only
5r-x4 + 1, read and execute
6rw-4 + 2, read and write
7rwx4 + 2 + 1, everything

Memory trick for the digits: 4ead, 2rite, e1xecute. Add them up. Learn 644 and 755 first, because those two cover almost everything.

Why 644 for files and 755 for directories

ModeApplies toOwnerGroupOthersWhy
644Filesread writereadreadAnyone can read it, only the owner edits it
755Folders and scriptsread write executeread executeread executeEveryone can pass through it, only the owner changes it
600Private filesread writenonenoneSSH keys, passwords, tokens
700Private foldersread write executenonenone~/.ssh and similar
750Team readableread write executeread executenoneShared with a group only
775Team writableread write executeread write executeread executeGroup members can edit

The logic is always the same: give the owner everything, give the group what they genuinely need, and give everyone else read-only so they can see but not change.

chmod in practice

chmod 644 notes.txt       # readable by all, writable by owner
chmod 755 run.sh           # anyone can execute it
chmod 600 config.yaml      # only the owner
chmod 700 ~/.ssh           # only the owner
chmod 644 config.yaml      # standard for data and config files
chmod -R 755 public_html/ # -R applies recursively to subfolders

The habit to build: start from 644 for a file or 755 for a directory or script, then narrow permissions only where there is a real reason. Never start from 777.

10. chmod in Symbolic Mode

Numeric mode sets all nine permissions at once. Symbolic mode changes one piece at a time, which is safer when you only want to adjust a single permission.

Who - the classes

SymbolMeans
uuser, the owner
ggroup
oothers
aall three at once

What - the operators

SymbolMeansExample
+add a permissionchmod u+x run.sh
-remove a permissionchmod g-w notes.txt
=set exactly these, clearing the restchmod o=rx file

The permissions being added or removed

LetterMeaningNumeric value
rread4
wwrite2
xexecute1
chmod u+x run.sh             # owner can now execute it
chmod g+w report.txt         # group can now write
chmod o-r secrets.txt        # others can no longer read
chmod a+r public.txt         # everyone can read
chmod u=rwx,go=rwx private.txt  # set everything exactly
chmod o= file.txt            # others get no permissions at all
chmod -R u+w folder/         # owner can write, recursively

Memory trick: read the symbol as a sentence. u+x is "add execute to the user". o-r is "remove read from others". = is the only operator that resets everything it touches before setting it.

11. chown, chgrp and umask

sudo chown alice notes.txt          # change the owner
sudo chown alice:developers app/    # change owner and group
sudo chgrp developers shared.log    # change just the group
sudo chown -R alice:alice /var/www  # recursively fix a whole tree

Changing a file's permissions is a lesser risk than changing its owner, but both are powerful. The rule of least surprise says: prefer adding a user to a group over making a file world-writable.

chmod o+w file.txt     # anyone can now change it, avoid this
chmod -R a+w /etc      # dangerous and rarely ever correct
usermod -aG developers alice   # the better answer: join the group instead

umask - the default for newly created files

The umask is subtracted from the maximum. A umask of 022 turns new files into 644 and new folders into 755, which is exactly why those modes are so common on most systems.

umaskNew files getNew folders getTypical use
022644755The sensible default on most systems
002664775Shared team folders
077600700Private work, keys and secrets
000666777Almost always a mistake
umask                                # show the current umask, usually 0022
umask 077                            # make new files private from now on
touch newfile && ls -l newfile    # verify it is now 600
