12. Troubleshooting Permission Denied

SymptomLikely causeCorrect fix
Permission denied reading a fileMissing read bit for your classchmod o+r or better, add the user to the group
Permission denied in a folderMissing execute bit on a parent folderchmod u+x or 755 on the folder
Permission denied running a scriptFile has no execute bitchmod +x script.sh
Not allowed to sudoUser is not in the sudo groupusermod -aG sudo alice as root
Read-only file systemMounted read-only, or immutable flagCheck with mount, remount or clear the attribute

Diagnose in this order: check who you are with whoami and your groups with id, then read the file with ls -l, then walk the whole path with namei -l /full/path. A readable file inside an unreadable folder is still unreachable.

13. Users, Groups and sudo

whoami                     # which user am I
id                         # my user id, group ids and group names
groups                     # which groups I belong to
su - alice                 # switch to another user, - loads their environment
sudo command               # run one command as root
sudo -u postgres command   # run as a specific user
sudo -i                    # start a full root login shell

Memory trick: su switches user and keeps your current directory unless you add -. sudo runs a single command with elevated rights and leaves you as yourself.

Group membership gotcha

Adding yourself to a group does not update your current session. Log out and back in, or start a new shell, or the change appears to do nothing.

sudo usermod -aG docker alice   # add alice to the docker group
newgrp docker                   # pick up the new group without logging out

14. Processes and Signals

ps aux                  # every process on the machine
ps -ef                  # same idea, system-wide format
top                     # live view sorted by CPU, press q to quit
htop                    # prettier version, often not installed by default
pgrep -f nginx          # find a process by name
kill 1234               # ask process 1234 to stop politely
kill -9 1234            # force it, cannot be caught or ignored
jobs                    # background jobs in this shell
command &                # run in background
nohup command &          # keep running after you log out
SignalNumberMeaningCan the program catch it?
SIGHUP1Terminal closedYes, usually used to reload config
SIGINT2Ctrl and C pressedYes, request a clean exit
SIGTERM15Normal shutdown requestYes, this is the polite way
SIGKILL9Force killNo, the kernel ends it immediately

Always try plain kill before kill -9. SIGTERM lets a server finish in-flight requests and close files properly. SIGKILL gives it no chance, which is how you corrupt databases.

15. Services with systemd

systemctl status nginx            # is it running, and what happened
systemctl start nginx             # start it now
systemctl stop nginx              # stop it now
systemctl restart nginx           # stop then start
systemctl reload nginx            # apply config without dropping connections
sudo systemctl enable nginx       # start automatically at boot
sudo systemctl disable nginx      # do not start at boot
systemctl is-enabled nginx# check whether it starts at boot
systemctl list-units --type=service

Memory trick: enable controls boot behaviour, start controls right now. A service can be running without being enabled, and enabled without running. This trips everyone up.

16. Logs and Troubleshooting

journalctl -u nginx                # everything from one service
journalctl -u nginx -n 50          # last 50 lines only
journalctl -u nginx -f             # follow live, the equivalent of tail -f
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago"
journalctl -p err -n 20            # only errors
journalctl -b                       # this boot, useful after a crash
journalctl --disk-usage             # how much space logs are using

Traditional log files live in /var/log. Common ones worth knowing: /var/log/syslog for everything, /var/log/auth.log for logins and sudo attempts, and /var/log/nginx/ for a web server's own logs.

17. Disk and Storage

df -h                 # free space per mounted filesystem
df -h /               # the filesystem holding the current folder
du -sh *              # size of each item in the current folder
du -sh /var/* | sort -rh | head   # what is eating the most space
lsblk                 # block devices as a tree
mount                 # what is mounted where
free -h               # memory and swap
nproc                 # how many CPU cores

Memory trick: df is for filesystems, du is for directories. They answer different questions and you will need both when a disk fills up.

18. sed and awk - Editing Text at Scale

These two do most of what you would open Notepad for, but across thousands of files or hundreds of thousands of lines in seconds.

sed - stream editor, one line at a time

sed -n '5p' file.txt              # print line 5
sed -n '1,10p' file.txt           # print lines 1 to 10
sed 's/old/new/g' file.txt        # replace every occurrence
sed 's/old/new/' file.txt         # replace the first occurrence per line
sed -i 's/old/new/g' file.txt     # edit in place, always keep a backup first
sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' f.txt   # in place, saving f.txt.bak for you
sed '/^#/d' config.ini            # delete every line starting with a hash
sed -n '10,20p' access.log | grep error   # errors between lines 10 and 20
ExpressionMeaning
s/old/new/gSubstitute every match
-iEdit the file in place
-nSuppress default printing, used with p
/pattern/dDelete matching lines
/pattern/pPrint only matching lines

awk - columns, like a spreadsheet

awk '{print $1}' access.log          # first column
awk '{print $1, $9}' access.log     # first and ninth, separated by a space
awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd    # use a colon instead of whitespace
awk '$3 > 1000 {print $1}' file   # only rows where column 3 is over 1000
awk -F, 'NR>1 {sum += $2} END {print sum}' sales.csv   # total column 2
awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (ip in c) print ip, c[ip]}' access.log

Memory trick: sed changes lines, awk reads columns. If you are counting or totalling you want awk. If you are replacing text you want sed.

19. Archives, Compression and Transfers

tar -czf backup.tar.gz /etc        # create a gzipped tar of a folder
tar -xzf backup.tar.gz             # extract it
tar -tf backup.tar.gz              # list contents without extracting
zip -r files.zip folder/            # the Windows-friendly alternative

rsync -avz src/ user@host:/dest/   # copy, transferring only what changed
rsync -avz --delete src/ dest/     # mirror, removing extra files
scp file.txt user@host:/tmp/       # simple copy over SSH
wget https://example.com/file      # download a file
curl -O https://example.com/file   # same job, different tool

Memory trick: create, xtract, test, file. tar -czf creates, tar -xzf extracts and tar -tf lists without extracting.

20. Package Management

apt update                          # refresh the package lists
apt upgrade                         # upgrade everything installed
apt install nginx                   # install a package
apt remove nginx                    # remove it
apt purge nginx                     # remove it and its config files too
apt install --only-upgrade openssl  # security updates only
apt search nginx                    # search the repositories

# Red Hat family
dnf install nginx
dnf update
dnf info nginx

Never run apt upgrade on a production server without a plan. It can pull in a new library version and restart services in the middle of a working day.

21. Shell Fundamentals Worth Knowing

TopicSyntaxWhat it does
Single quotesecho '$HOME'Literal, nothing is expanded
Double quotesecho "$HOME"Variables are expanded
Historyhistory, press UpRecall past commands
Tab completionpress TabComplete paths and command names
Environment variableexport PATH=$PATH:/opt/binSet for this shell and its children
Aliasalias ll='ls -la'A shortcut command
Exit statusecho $?0 means success, anything else failed
Script header#!/bin/bashTells the kernel which shell to use

Memory trick: single quotes are safe, double quotes are powerful. If unsure about a variable's contents, single-quote it.

22. A Realistic Shell Session

# "the site is slow. why?"
ping -c 5 example.com                          # can we even reach it
dig example.com                                # does DNS resolve
curl -o /dev/null -s -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}
" https://example.com
ss -tulnp | grep 443                           # what is listening on 443
systemctl status nginx                         # is the web server healthy
journalctl -u nginx -n 50 --no-pager          # read the recent logs
free -h && df -h                           # out of memory, or out of disk?

This is the order a real sysadmin works in: reachability, then name resolution, then the application, then logs, then resources. Check from the outside in.

23. Try It Yourself (30 minutes)

  • Run ls -l in a folder and decode all ten fields of every line.
  • Create a file, note its mode, set it to 644 with numeric mode, then add only the execute bit with chmod u+x and compare.
  • Compute 777 by hand as 4+2+1 three times, then set it and set it back.
  • Make a folder, remove its execute bit, and try to cd into it. Notice what breaks.
  • Run ls /etc | wc -l, then ls /etc | grep ssh, then chain both into a single line.
  • Run ps aux --sort=-%mem | head to find the hungriest process.

24. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
Permissionschmod 777 until it works644 and 755 by default, least privilege everywhere
User accountsEverything runs as rootEvery service has its own unprivileged user
AccessSSH as root with a passwordKey only, no direct root, sudo with logging
ChangesTyped straight into the serverChange management, then Ansible, then audit
Config editingnano over SSHConfiguration management or a controlled rollout
Upgradesapt upgrade wheneverScheduled window, tested in staging first
DiskChecked when something breaksAlerting at thresholds, capacity planned ahead
Logstail -f on the consoleCentralised, searchable, retained, alerted on
Knowing whyReboot and hopeDocumented runbook, then post-incident review
chmod -R on a system pathSounds reasonableNever. One wrong path can break the whole machine

25. Key Takeaways

  • Linux is one tree starting at /; there are no drive letters.
  • Permissions are owner, group and others, crossed with read, write and execute.
  • 4 read, 2 write, 1 execute; 644 for files, 755 for folders.
  • Execute on a folder means you may enter it, not that you may run it.
  • Combine small commands with pipes before writing scripts.
  • Try kill before kill -9, and check status before restarting.
  • In production, least privilege and running as non-root are the whole game.

chapters.title: Software Engineering
chapters.html:
1. What Software Engineering Actually Means

Writing code that works once is easy. Writing code that still works in six months, after four other people have edited it, is engineering. Engineering is about making code cheap to change.

2. The Four Pillars

PillarQuestion it answersPractical meaning
ReadabilityCan a stranger understand it?Clear names, small functions, consistent structure
ReliabilityDoes it do what it promises?Tests, error handling, safe defaults
EfficiencyIs it fast and cheap to run?Right data structures, sensible queries, caching
MaintainabilityCan it be changed safely?Version control, small diffs, automation

Memory trick: code is written to be read, by someone who has never met you. Optimise for the reader.

3. The Four Pillars of OOP

PillarMeaningExample
EncapsulationHide internal state, expose behaviourA BankAccount with deposit() rather than a public balance field
AbstractionShow what, hide howA PaymentProcessor interface, not the payment API calls
InheritanceReuse by extendingAdminUser extends User. Use sparingly, it couples tightly
PolymorphismOne name, many behavioursDifferent payment types behind one call

4. SOLID - The Five Rules

LetterNameMeaningSmell it fixes
SSingle responsibilityOne reason to changeA class that both validates and emails
OOpen, closedOpen to extension, closed to modificationA chain of if-else that grows forever
LLiskov substitutionSubtypes must be usable as the parentA subclass that throws when used normally
IInterface segregationSmall interfaces beat one huge oneA class forced to implement methods it never uses
DDependency inversionDepend on abstractions, not concrete classesHard to test because you cannot swap the dependency

Memory trick: read the letters as a phrase: "Super Superior, Superior, Leave, Interface, Dependency". Concretely, remember: one job per class, extend rather than edit, and depend on interfaces.

5. Common Design Patterns

PatternProblem it solvesReal example
SingletonExactly one instanceA database connection pool, a logger
FactoryCreating objects of the right typeChoosing a payment provider by country
StrategySwappable algorithmSorting by name, date or price
ObserverNotify many when one changesEvent listeners, webhooks, pub/sub
RepositoryHide database accessUserRepository so services never write SQL
AdapterMake incompatible things workWrapping a third-party payment SDK

Do not over-apply them. A pattern that makes the code harder to read than the problem it solved is a mistake.

6. Data Structures You Must Know

StructureWhat it is forLookup speed
Array or listOrdered items, fast iterationIndex O(1), search O(n)
Dictionary or mapKey to value lookupGet and set O(1)
SetUnique items, fast membershipContains O(1)
StackLast in, first outO(1)
QueueFirst in, first outO(1)
TreeHierarchies and ordered rangesO(log n)
GraphRelationships between thingsVaries

Memory trick: if you are always scanning a list to find something, you probably wanted a dictionary.

7. The N+1 Query Problem

You fetch a list of 100 users, then loop over them and fetch each one's orders. That is 101 queries instead of 1. It is the most common performance bug in real applications and it hides easily in development because the data set is tiny.

# Bad: 1 + N queries
for user in users:
    user.orders = db.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ?", user.id)

# Good: 1 query with a join
users = db.query("SELECT * FROM users")
orders = db.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (...)")
# attach in memory

8. REST and API Design

REST designs APIs around resources, not around actions. The HTTP method expresses the action.

GET    /users        list users
GET    /users/1      get one user
POST   /users        create a user
PUT    /users/1      replace a user
PATCH  /users/1      update part of a user
DELETE /users/1      delete a user

Memory trick: the URL names the noun, the HTTP method names the verb. Never put a verb in the URL such as /getUser.

9. Authentication vs Authorization

ConceptQuestion it answersCommon methods
AuthenticationWho are you?Passwords, MFA, OAuth 2.0, OIDC, SAML
AuthorizationWhat may you do?RBAC roles, ABAC policies, ACLs
Encryption in transitIs the wire safe?TLS
Encryption at restIs the disk safe?Disk encryption, encrypted volumes

Memory trick: authentication is the bouncer checking your ID. Authorization is the bouncer deciding which rooms you may enter.

10. Testing

LevelScopeSpeedCatches
Unit testOne function or classMillisecondsLogic mistakes
Integration testSeveral parts togetherSecondsWiring and config problems
End-to-end testThe whole system as a userMinutesBroken user journeys

Test behaviour, not implementation. A test that breaks whenever you rename a private helper is a test of the wrong thing.

11. Layered Architecture

Presentation (UI)  ->  Service (business logic)  ->  Repository (data access)
        HTTP layer             domain rules                 SQL and queries

Each layer only talks to the one below it. This is why you can swap the database without touching the UI.

12. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
Code styleWhatever runsLinters, formatters and hooks in CI
TestsA few happy pathsCoverage targets, integration tests, flake detection
ErrorsPrint and move onStructured logging, error tracking, retries with backoff
SecretsIn a .env file that is committedSecret manager, rotated, never in git
DeploysManual, wheneverAutomated pipelines with rollback
DatabaseMigrations run by handVersioned migrations gated in the pipeline
ReviewsNobody checksPeer review, branch protection, CODEOWNERS

13. Key Takeaways

  • Write code for the person who reads it later, which is usually not you.
  • SOLID keeps classes small and dependencies replaceable.
  • Design patterns are tools, not a goal.
  • The N+1 problem is the most common hidden performance bug.
  • URLs name nouns; HTTP methods are the verbs.
  • Authentication is who you are; authorization is what you may do.

chapters.title: Sysadmin: Linux and Windows
chapters.html:
1. What a Sysadmin Actually Does

A system administrator keeps other people's machines working. Concretely, that means five things all day:

JobWhat it means in practiceHow you know it is going wrong
AvailabilityServices stay up and users can workAlerts when a service or host goes down
SecurityPatching, accounts, least privilegeFailed logins, unexpected privilege changes
CapacityDisk, memory and CPU will not run outThresholds reached before they are full
BackupRestorable copies of everything importantRestores tested on a schedule
ChangeUpdates and config applied safelyChange records and rollback plans

Memory trick for the priorities: restore first, then update, then patch. A backup you have never restored is not a backup.

2. Users and Groups, Side by Side

TaskLinuxWindows
Create a usersudo useradd -m aliceNew-LocalUser alice
Delete a usersudo userdel -r aliceRemove-LocalUser alice
Set a passwordsudo passwd alicenet user alice *
Lock the accountsudo usermod -L alicenet user alice /active:no
Add to a groupsudo usermod -aG sudo aliceAdd-LocalGroupMember Administrators alice
See a user's groupsid alicenet user alice
Who am Iwhoamiwhoami
List all userscat /etc/passwdGet-LocalUser
Raise privilegessudoRun PowerShell as Administrator

Memory trick: Linux stores users in /etc/passwd and hashed passwords in /etc/shadow. Windows keeps them in the registry and the SAM database. Both use the idea of a local account plus group membership for permissions.

The sudoers file on Linux

On Linux, which commands a user may run as root is defined in /etc/sudoers, edited with visudo so syntax errors are caught. Never grant ALL casually; grant the specific binary.

alice ALL=(ALL) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx   # good, narrow
alice ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL                # bad, defeats the purpose

3. Services, Side by Side

TaskLinux, systemdWindows, PowerShell
Is it running?systemctl status nginxGet-Service W3SVC
Startsudo systemctl start nginxStart-Service W3SVC
Stopsudo systemctl stop nginxStop-Service W3SVC
Restartsudo systemctl restart nginxRestart-Service W3SVC
Start at bootsudo systemctl enable nginxSet-Service -StartupType Automatic
Do not start at bootsudo systemctl disable nginxSet-Service -StartupType Disabled
List everythingsystemctl list-unitsGet-Service
Apply config without dropping connectionssystemctl reload nginxiisreset

Memory trick: on Linux, enable means "start at boot" and start means "right now". On Windows the equivalent of enable is Set-Service -StartupType. These are genuinely different concepts and getting them confused causes outages.

4. File Permissions, Side by Side

Both systems answer the same question, "who may do what to this file", with the same three classes: owner, group, everyone else. Only the notation differs.

TaskLinuxWindows
See permissionsls -l fileicacls file
Add read for everyonechmod a+r fileicacls file /grant *S-1-1-0:(R)
Change ownersudo chown alice filetakeown /f file
Change groupsudo chgrp admins fileicacls file /setgroup "Domain Admins"
Remove permissionschmod o-r fileicacls file /remove:g Everyone
Apply to subfolders toochmod -Ricacls folder /t
Copy permissions onto a filegetfacl / setfaclicacls file /save acl.txt

The key difference

AspectLinuxWindows
Built-in groupsroot, sudo, and groups you createAdministrators, Users, Guests, SYSTEM
Everyoneothers, written as o or aThe "Everyone" principal, usually represented by a SID
InheritanceOptional, via ACLsOn by default and deeply baked in
Typical default644 files, 755 foldersInherited from the parent folder
Getting it wrong"Permission denied""Access is denied", and inheritance fights you

Memory trick: Linux gives the owner everything and others the minimum. Windows inherits permissions down from the parent folder, so the answer to "why can I not delete this" is usually "the parent folder will not let you", and you must take ownership first with takeown.

5. Host Networking, Side by Side

TaskLinuxWindows
Show IP configurationip addr showipconfig /all
Show the routesip routeroute print
Listening portsss -tulnpnetstat -ano
Who owns a portlsof -i :8080tasklist /FI "PID eq 1234"
DNS lookupdig example.comnslookup example.com
Test reachabilityping -c 4 hostping host
Trace the routetraceroute hosttracert host
Test a TCP portnc -vz host 443Test-NetConnection -Port 443
Firewall, view rulessudo ufw statusGet-NetFirewallRule
Firewall, allow a portsudo ufw allow 443/tcpNew-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName HTTPS -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 443 -Protocol TCP -Action Allow
Active firewallsudo ufw enableSet-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Public -Enabled True

The Port Manager in this app uses netstat -ano and tasklist, which is exactly this Windows column, so you can practise it on your own machine right now.

6. Processes, Side by Side

TaskLinuxWindows
List processesps aux or topGet-Process
Live view by CPUtopGet-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Desc
Find by namepgrep -f nginxGet-Process nginx
Stop politelykill 1234Stop-Process -Id 1234
Force stopkill -9 1234taskkill /PID 1234 /F /T
System loadtop, uptimeGet-Counter
Memoryfree -hGet-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem

Memory trick: on both platforms the polite stop lets the program clean up, and the force stop does not. Prefer the polite one.

7. Disk and Storage, Side by Side

TaskLinuxWindows
Free space per filesystemdf -hGet-Volume
Size of a folderdu -sh /var/logGet-ChildItem -Recurse | Measure-Object
List disks and partitionslsblkGet-Disk, Get-Partition
What is mounted wheremount, df -hGet-Volume
Partition a diskfdisk /dev/sdb, parteddiskpart
Filesystem typemkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1Format-Volume -FileSystem NTFS
Mount a filesystemmount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/dataMount-DiskImage, or assign a drive letter
Mount at bootedit /etc/fstabSet-Partition -NewDriveLetter
Check disk healthsmartctl -a /dev/sdaGet-PhysicalDisk

Warning: partitioning and formatting destroy data. In production nobody does this interactively; a storage system manages it.

8. Logs and Troubleshooting, Side by Side

TaskLinuxWindows
Where logs live/var/log, the journalC:\Windows\System32\LogFiles, Event Viewer
Logs for one servicejournalctl -u nginxGet-WinEvent -LogName Application
Follow livejournalctl -u nginx -fGet-Content -Wait log.txt
Recent errors onlyjournalctl -p err -n 50Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{Level=2}
Search a log filegrep -i error /var/log/syslogSelect-String -Path log.txt -Pattern error
Boot logjournalctl -bGet-WinEvent -LogName System
Rotate old logslogrotateBuilt in, configured per application

A troubleshooting order that works on both

  • Is the machine up? Check uptime or Task Manager.
  • Is the service running? systemctl status or Get-Service.
  • Is it listening on the right port? ss -tulnp or netstat -ano.
  • What do the logs say? journalctl or Event Viewer.
  • Are resources fine? df -h, free -h, or the Task Manager performance tab.
  • Did anything change? Recent updates, config edits, deploys.

9. Scheduling, Side by Side

TaskLinuxWindows
Run daily at 2am0 2 * * * in crontabTask Scheduler with a daily trigger
Edit the schedulecrontab -eschtasks /create /tn "Task" /tr cmd /sc daily /st 02:00
List scheduled jobscrontab -l, ls /etc/cron.dGet-ScheduledTask
Long-running schedulesystemd timersTask Scheduler, or a service
Run once, detachednohup cmd &Start-Process cmd -WindowStyle Hidden

Memory trick for cron: five fields in the order minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. A * means "every", so 0 2 * * * reads "at minute 0 of hour 2, every day".

10. Package Management, Side by Side

TaskLinux, DebianLinux, Red HatWindows
Refresh listsapt updatednf check-updatewinget update
Installapt install nginxdnf install nginxwinget install nginx
Removeapt remove nginxdnf remove nginxwinget uninstall nginx
Security patchesunattended-upgradesdnf update --securityWindows Update, or a patching tool
Other repositoriesadd-apt-repositorydnf config-managerchoco, or a company feed

11. Backup and Transfer, Side by Side

TaskLinuxWindows
Copy preserving timestampsrsync -avz src/ dest/robocopy src dest /E /Z
Archive a foldertar -czf backup.tar.gz /etcCompress-Archive -Path data -DestinationPath data.zip
System backuprsnapshot, or Baculawbadmin, or Veeam
Secure copyrsync -e ssh, scpscp, available via OpenSSH
Verify the backuptar -tzf backup.tar.gzGet-FileHash backup.zip

The rule that matters: a backup is only real once you have restored it. Schedule a restore test, not just a backup.

12. Command Equivalence Cheat Sheet

What you wantLinuxWindows
Where am Ipwdcd
List filesls -ladir /a
Change foldercd /etccd C:\Windows
Copy a filecp a.txt b.txtcopy a.txt b.txt
Move or renamemv a bmove a b
Deleterm a.txtdel a.txt
Create a foldermkdir newmkdir new
View a filecat a.txttype a.txt
Search textgrep -r "x" .findstr /s "x" *.*
Count lineswc -l a.txt(Get-Content a.txt).Count
Set permissionschmod 644 ficacls f /grant *S-1-1-0:(R)
Disk spacedf -hGet-Volume
Free memoryfree -hsysteminfo
List processesps auxGet-Process
Kill a processkill 1234taskkill /PID 1234 /F
IP addressip addripconfig
Ports in usess -tulnpnetstat -ano
Pingping -c 4 hostping host
DNS lookupdig hostnslookup host
Trace routetraceroute hosttracert host
Download a filecurl -O urlcurl.exe -O url
Archivetar -czf f.tar.gz dirCompress-Archive
Who am Iwhoamiwhoami
UptimeuptimeGet-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem

13. Remote Access and SSH

TaskLinuxWindows
Connect to a serverssh user@10.0.0.5ssh user@10.0.0.5, or OpenSSH client
Use a keyssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 user@hostssh -i C:\keys\id_ed25519 user@host
Non-standard portssh -p 2222 user@hostssh -p 2222 user@host
Copy files securelyscp f user@host:/tmp/scp f user@host:C:/tmp/
Tunnel a local portssh -L 5432:db:5432 user@hostSame command works
Server config/etc/ssh/sshd_configC:\ProgramData\ssh\sshd_config
Reload the SSH servicesudo systemctl reload sshdRestart-Service sshd

SSH is identical on both platforms, which makes it the easiest bridge when moving between a Linux server and a Windows workstation.

14. Try It Yourself (30 minutes, Windows)

You can practise most of the Windows side immediately, without installing anything:

  • Open the Port Manager in this app and compare it with netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING.
  • Run Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'}.
  • Run Get-LocalUser and whoami /groups.
  • Run Get-NetFirewallProfile and see which profiles are on.
  • Run Get-WinEvent -LogName System -MaxEvents 10 to see the Windows equivalent of journalctl.

15. Try It Yourself (45 minutes, Linux)

Use WSL, a VM, or a free cloud instance:

  • Run ls -l in /etc and decode five lines fully.
  • Create a file and set it to 644, then 600, checking with ls -l each time.
  • Create a folder, chmod 644 it, and prove you cannot cd into it. Explain why.
  • Run ls -l /etc | head and work out why some files are 644 and some are 777 or 600.
  • Run systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running | head.

16. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
AccountsOne admin account for everythingNamed accounts per person, shared credentials banned
AccessPassword over SSH or RDPKeys or VPN, MFA, no direct root
PermissionsWhatever makes it workLeast privilege, reviewed quarterly
ChangesTyped directly on the machineChange request, tested, automated, audited
ConfigEdited by hand in placeManaged as code, rolled out by tooling
PatchingWhen you rememberScheduled, prioritised by severity, with a window
BackupsOccasional manual copyAutomated, monitored, restore-tested
LogsRead after the user complainsCentralised and alerted on before users notice
InventoryRemembered or a spreadsheetAutomated discovery, reconciled regularly
LinuxLearn on one distributionStandardise on one, know the differences

17. Key Takeaways

  • The concepts are identical on Linux and Windows; only the commands differ.
  • enable means start at boot, start means right now.
  • Windows inherits permissions from the parent folder, which explains most "Access is denied" problems.
  • Work from the outside in: reachability, service, port, logs, resources.
  • A backup you have never restored is not a backup.
  • Standardise. Fewer operating system variants means fewer surprises.

chapters.title: SDLC, Agile and Scrum
chapters.html:
1. What is the SDLC?

The Software Development Life Cycle is the set of stages a project passes through, from an idea to something running in production. Every team uses one, even if they never name it.

Idea -> Requirements -> Design -> Build -> Test -> Deploy -> Maintain -> Repeat

Why it matters: the SDLC exists to answer three questions before they become expensive. What are we building, who needs it, and how do we know it works?

2. The Lifecycle Models Compared

ModelHow work is dividedFeedback arrivesBest whenBiggest risk
WaterfallOne phase at a time, in orderAt the very endRegulated, fixed-scope projectsDiscovering it is wrong after building it
IterativeRepeating cycles of design, build, testEvery cycleRequirements are moderately clearScope and schedule drift
AgileShort sprints of working softwareEvery sprintRequirements change oftenDocumentation gaps, scope creep
DevOpsContinuous integration, delivery and feedbackContinuouslyRunning services in productionProcess overhead if done badly
LeanEliminate waste, maximise flowContinuouslyStruggling to deliver valueTeams feel rushed without context
KanbanA continuous flow of work, no sprintsContinuouslySupport and maintenance queuesStale work builds up silently

Memory trick: Waterfall is Water all at once, Agile is a fast Iteration loop, DevOps is the engine that keeps shipping. In real companies they are often used together, not chosen between.

3. Waterfall, in Case You Meet It

1. Requirements   -> a document describing what to build
2. Design         -> architecture, database schema, mockups
3. Development    -> writing the code
4. Testing        -> QA finds the bugs
5. Deployment     -> release to production
6. Maintenance    -> fix and enhance

Each phase has a defined exit gate. The problem is not that phases exist, it is that all the uncertainty is front-loaded into a document written before anyone builds anything.

Where you will still meet it: government contracts, hardware and safety-critical systems, and any project where the regulatory authority demands written sign-off at each stage.

4. Agile Manifesto

Published in 2001, four sentences that reversed the traditional priorities:

We valueOverBecause
Working softwareComprehensive documentationSoftware is the point, the document supports it
Welcoming changeFollowing a planChange arrives; a plan that cannot bend fails
Customer collaborationContract negotiationThe customer learns what they want from the product
Delivering valueProducing artefacts and processesProgress is only real if something useful ships

Memory trick: the four "over" words are documentation, plan, contract negotiation, artifact and process. Agile still writes documents and follows plans, it just does not value them above shipping.

5. Agile Principles in Plain English

  • Deliver early and often. Waiting months to see anything is the biggest source of wasted work.
  • Welcome changing requirements. Change late is cheaper than change never, because it is cheap while you are still building.
  • Deliver working software frequently. Monthly beats yearly.
  • Business people and developers work together daily. Not once at the start.
  • Build projects around motivated individuals. Give people the problem and trust them.
  • Working software is the primary measure of progress. Not task completion.
  • Sustainable pace. Teams that work 70 hours a week for a quarter produce less over a year than teams working 40.
  • Technical excellence and good design. Technical debt is paid for by every future sprint.
  • Simplicity, the art of maximising work not done.
  • Self-organising teams. Someone decides how, the team decides what.
  • Regular reflection and tuning. Change the way you work based on what you learn.

6. Scrum - The Full Framework

Scrum is the most widely used Agile framework. It is deliberately simple: three roles, five events, three artefacts. Everything else is detail.

RoleWhoAccountable forThe one question they ask
Product OwnerOne person, not a committeeMaximising product value and ordering the backlog"What should we build next?"
Scrum MasterOne person, often not a managerTeam effectiveness and the framework itself"What is stopping the team?"
DevelopersWhoever builds it, 3 to 9 peopleCreating a usable increment every sprint"How will we build it?"

Memory trick: the Product Owner owns the what and the order, the Scrum Master owns the how the team works, the Developers own the how they build. One decision owner each, which is what makes Scrum work.

7. The Five Scrum Events

EventDurationPurposeKey question
Sprint1 to 4 weeks, fixed lengthThe container for all other events"What will we finish this sprint?"
Sprint PlanningMax 8 hoursAgree the goal and pick work"Why are we doing this, and what is the goal?"
Daily Scrum15 minutes, every dayRe-plan the day toward the goal"What will I do today, and is anything in the way?"
Sprint ReviewMax 4 hoursShow working software and gather feedback"What did we build, and what should change?"
Sprint RetrospectiveMax 3 hoursImprove how the team works"What should we stop, start and try?"

Memory trick for the flow: Plan in the morning of day one, Daily every day, Review the product with stakeholders at the end, Retro on ourselves right after. And every event has a timebox in proportional hours, which is worth memorising.

The Sprint, the Goal, and the Increment

The Sprint is a fixed-length container. The Sprint Goal is the single objective for it. The Increment is the working product added to the product, and it must be usable, not "90 percent done".

Sprint length is a commitment. Two weeks is the most common. Shorter gives faster feedback but less work per sprint; longer wastes more if the goal is wrong.

The Daily Scrum in detail

Fifteen minutes, standing, same time and place every day, focused on the goal. Everyone answers three questions:

  • What have I done since the last Daily Scrum?
  • What will I do before the next one?
  • What is blocking my progress?

If there are deeper problems, discuss them after. The Daily Scrum is not a status report to a manager.

Review versus Retrospective - the classic confusion

AspectSprint ReviewSprint Retrospective
AudienceStakeholders and the whole teamThe team only
SubjectThe product, the increment, the roadmapThe people and the process
Question"What did we build and what do you think?""How did we work and what will we change?"
OutputUpdated Product BacklogOne or two concrete improvements

Memory trick: Review is about the product, Retro is about the team.

8. The Three Artefacts

ArtefactOwnerRefined inCommitted toPurpose
Product BacklogProduct OwnerContinuousProduct GoalEverything wanted, ordered by value
Sprint BacklogDevelopersDuring PlanningSprint GoalWhat the team will do this sprint, with a plan
IncrementDevelopersEvery sprintSprint GoalUsable product added to the previous one

How a story travels

Epic        -> Product Owner writes it in the Product Backlog
  Story     -> A slice of that epic, with value and acceptance criteria
    Task    -> A technical step the Developers split it into
      Commit -> An actual line of code change

Memory trick: Epic is big, Story is deliverable in one sprint, Task is smaller still. A story that cannot be finished in a sprint is too big.

User Stories and Acceptance Criteria

As a shop owner
I want to see daily sales totals
So that I know whether to restock

Acceptance criteria:
  - Totals load within 2 seconds
  - Shows today, yesterday and last week
  - Exports to CSV
  - Empty state shown when there are no sales

Memory trick: as a, I want, so that. The "so that" is the most important part, because it states the value. Criteria are written by the team and are really a conversation starter.

Definition of Done

The team's shared checklist for what "finished" means. It usually includes code reviewed, tests written and passing, no known security issues, documentation updated, deployed to staging, and monitored. A story is only done when it meets this, regardless of what the sprint board says.

Memory trick: "Done" is a definition, not a feeling. If two people disagree about whether something is done, the DoD is missing.

9. Estimation and Forecasting

TechniqueHow it worksGood forWatch out for
Story pointsRelative size: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21Agile backlogs, sizing relative effortNot hours, and not comparable across teams
T-shirt sizingSmall, medium, large, XLRough sizing without precisionToo coarse for forecasting
HoursDirect developer estimatesFixed, well-understood workDevelopers estimate optimistically, then overrun
Planning pokerTeam estimates together, then revealsSurfacing disagreement and assumptionsTakes time every sprint

Memory trick: the Fibonacci sequence is used because the gap between 8 and 13 is deliberately large, signalling "this is much bigger". A 6 is not offered.

Velocity

Velocity is the sum of story points completed per sprint. It is a forecasting tool for this team, not a productivity score to compare teams with. The usual question is not "what is your velocity" but "how much of the backlog can we finish by this date".

Burndown and Burnup

ChartShowsUse it to
BurndownRemaining work against timeSpot scope creep and whether the goal is still reachable
BurnupCompleted work against timeSee added and removed scope, and true throughput
Cumulative flowWork in each state over timeSpot a bottleneck and over-polishing

10. Anti-Patterns - How Teams Break Scrum

Anti-patternWhat it looks likeWhy it is wrongThe fix
Sprint as a waterfallDesign, then code, then test, all inside the sprintNo feedback until the sprint endsTest as you build; demo working software weekly
Sprint of choresSprint Goal is "clear the tech debt"Deliverable value is not the goalPair cleanup with user value
Shu, shu, shuTeam says Scrum but nothing changesProcess without purposeScrum Master exists to change the system
Too many Scrum MastersCoordinators across teamsCreates overhead, fragments accountabilityOne per team; scale across teams instead
Product Owner as figureheadPO never actually decidesBacklog ordering is a popularity contestGive the PO real authority and time
Sprint Goal as a list"Do login, fix search, update profile"Tasks, not an outcomeWrite a sentence describing the change users see
Committed, not doneWork moved to the next sprint repeatedlyNo real forecast, no trustSplit stories so they fit; reduce Sprint Goal
Scrum but the org is a projectFixed scope, date and budgetAgile cannot absorb thatMake the three fixed: time, quality, scope flexes

Memory trick: if a sprint produces no working software that a real user could touch, it was not Scrum.

11. Scrum versus Kanban versus SAFe

AspectScrumKanbanSAFe
CadenceFixed sprintsContinuous flowProgram increments, often quarterly
RolesThree, definedNone requiredMany: Product Owner, Team, System Architect, Scrum Master, Programme Management
Work in progressLimited by the Sprint BacklogExplicit WIP limit per columnPer team
ChangeBacklog can change any timeAny timeChange is managed with Product Backlog and trains
Best forProduct development with regular deliverySupport, maintenance, continuous flowVery large organisations, many teams
RiskCeremony for teams that do not need itWork stalls silently without limitsBureaucracy and slow decisions

Memory trick: Scrum works in sprints with defined roles; Kanban works as a flow with WIP limits and no roles; SAFe is Scrum scaled to many teams.

12. How Scrum Connects to CI/CD

Scrum and DevOps are complementary. Scrum decides what to build and when. CI/CD decides how reliably that work ships. Together they form a feedback loop from idea to production to customer feedback.

Product Owner     Backlog        Sprint Planning       Sprint
  prioritises      ordered by     team commits to a     Developers build
  value            value          Sprint Goal           every day

  Sprint Review -> demo working software in staging
  Sprint Retrospective -> improve how the team works

Every commit -> CI builds and tests automatically
Green build   -> CD deploys to staging automatically
Staging OK    -> promote to production
Production    -> metrics feed back to the backlog
Agile conceptDevOps counterpartShared goal
Definition of DonePipeline passes all quality gatesBoth mean "finished and verified"
Sprint Review demoDeployment to stagingReal feedback on real software
Product BacklogInfrastructure backlogBoth need prioritisation and grooming
Sprint GoalRelease milestoneBoth are dated commitments of value
Retrospective action itemPipeline improvement, such as adding a test gateBoth close the loop by improving the system

Memory trick: Scrum is the plan, CI/CD is the pipes. You need both. A sprint without a pipeline ships by hand, and a pipeline without a sprint ships random changes.

Common scaling situations

SituationWhat is often missingWhat usually helps
Two teams sharing one codebaseOwnership and merge coordinationClear code ownership, trunk-based development, small PRs
Five teams, one releaseA release train or planExplicit release cadence agreed up front
Sprints with frequent releasesNothing, this is good practiceKeep it; releasing per sprint is the goal

13. Try It Yourself (45 minutes)

  • Write one epic with three stories beneath it, each with acceptance criteria and a "so that" clause.
  • Run a 15-minute Daily Scrum on your own work, using the three questions.
  • Estimate ten tasks in story points, then rank them. Notice how much harder relative sizing is than hours.
  • Plot a burndown for your current project and see whether scope grew.
  • Write a Definition of Done for a small project and check whether it removes ambiguity.
  • Map a recent project onto the five Scrum events and notice what was missing.
  • Take one anti-pattern from the table and think about how to fix it in a team you have worked in.

14. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
FrameworksScrum, because it teaches the ideasWhatever fits; the principles matter more than the ceremonies
Sprint lengthOne week, to see results fastOne or two weeks, matched to release cadence
EstimationStory points, to learn themStill common; some teams prefer hours on well-understood work
VelocityTracked and displayed proudlyUsed privately for forecasting, never compared between teams
MeetingsAttended happilyTimeboxed, with agendas and recorded actions
ScopeFixed by the backlog owner informallyOne accountable Product Owner, backlog ordered by value
Definition of DoneLoose, "it works on my machine"Automated gates in the pipeline: tests, scans, reviews
RetrospectiveSometimes skippedHeld every sprint, with tracked action items
ShippingManual deploys at the endAutomated CD, deploying per sprint or more often
MetricsStory points and burndownDORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, failure rate, recovery time

15. Key Takeaways

  • The SDLC is a set of stages; the model you pick changes when you get feedback.
  • Agile values working software over documentation, and change over a plan.
  • Scrum is three roles, five events, three artefacts, nothing more.
  • The Product Owner owns the what, the Scrum Master owns the process, the Developers own the how.
  • Review is about the product; Retrospective is about the team.
  • Done is a shared definition, not a feeling.
  • Story points are relative and not comparable across teams.
  • Scrum is the plan, CI/CD is the pipes; you need both.

chapters.title: AWS (2026)
chapters.html:
1. What AWS Actually Is

AWS is the largest cloud provider: you rent servers, storage and databases over the internet instead of buying hardware. You pay for what you use and turn things off when you stop using them.

The mental model that makes AWS click: everything you create is a resource. Resources live inside a region, and access to them is controlled by IAM. Nearly every AWS question is really one of these three.

PillarWhat it isWhy it matters
RegionsIsolated geographic areas, for example eu-west-1Where your data physically lives
Availability ZonesSeparate datacentres inside a regionSurvive a single-site failure
ResourcesEC2 instances, S3 buckets, RDS databasesThe things you actually build
IAMIdentity and Access ManagementWho may do what, the single biggest security lever
Shared responsibilityAWS secures the cloud, you secure your dataExplains why misconfiguration is the top breach cause

Memory trick: a Region is a city, an Availability Zone is a separate data centre in that city. Two AZs means one data centre can burn down without taking you offline.

2. Regions, Availability Zones and Naming

CodeRegionLocation
us-east-1US East, N. VirginiaUSA
eu-west-1Europe, IrelandIreland
ap-south-1Asia Pacific, MumbaiIndia
us-east-2US East, OhioUSA

Read a region code right to left: the continent, then the direction, then a number. eu-west-1 is Europe, west, first region.

The three availability zone types

TypeWhat you getUse it when
Availability ZonesIndependent datacentres, low latency between themAlmost always; this is the default choice
Local ZonesOne zone, big cities, low latency from usersMedia, gaming, need city-level closeness
Wavelength ZonesInside 5G/mobile networksProcessing right at the mobile edge

3. The AWS Console and Naming Rules

Almost every AWS service uses the same naming pattern. Learn it once and you can predict resource names before you ever open the console.

abbreviation-environment-account          e.g. dockeybe-prod-483920
myapp-prod-iam-role
dockeybe-prod-1-subnet-public

Shared responsibility in one line each

AWS is responsible forYou are responsible for
Security of the physical datacentresYour IAM permissions
The hypervisor and host OS patchesThe guest OS and its packages
Storage durability of the disksYour bucket policies and encryption
Managed service patchingYour application code and its secrets

Memory trick: the biggest cause of cloud breaches is not AWS failing, it is a customer leaving a bucket public. That is your job.

4. IAM - The Most Important Service

IAM controls who can do what to which resources, and when. Get this right and most security problems disappear.

The building blocks

Building blockIs it a person or a thing?What it holds
UserA humanLong-term credentials, which you should almost never create
RoleA service, an app or a third partyShort-lived credentials
GroupA set of usersAttach policies to many people at once
PolicyNeitherThe permissions themselves, as JSON

Memory trick: users and groups are for people. Roles are for software. If a machine has an identity, it should be a role.

Policy anatomy

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/reports/*",
    "Condition": {
      "IpAddress": { "aws:SourceIp": "203.0.113.0/24" }
    }
  }]
}
ElementMeaning
EffectAllow or Deny. An explicit Deny always wins
ActionWhat is permitted, such as s3:GetObject, or * for everything
ResourceWhich thing, written as an ARN
ConditionExtra rules such as source IP, time or MFA

The rules that keep you safe

  • Never use * for Action. Grant the specific call you need.
  • Scope every resource. A role that can do anything anywhere is a role that will eventually do anything somewhere.
  • No long-lived users. Use IAM Identity Centre and temporary credentials.
  • Deny by default. An identity with no policy can do nothing.
  • Rotate and audit. Use CloudTrail and Access Analyzer.
# The single most useful IAM commands
aws iam list-users
aws iam list-roles
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws iam get-policy --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3FullAccess

5. Networking - VPC, Subnet, Security Group

A VPC is your private network inside AWS. Everything you launch lives in one.

ConceptWhat it isAnalogy
VPCYour private networkThe whole city
SubnetA smaller slice of the VPCA street
Route tableWhere traffic from a subnet goesSignposts
Internet GatewayThe door to the internetThe city gate
NAT GatewayAllows outbound onlyA one-way exit
Security GroupFirewall attached to a resourceA guard on each door
Network ACLFirewall attached to a subnetA checkpoint at the street entrance

Public vs private subnets - the key decision

AspectPublic subnetPrivate subnet
Route to the internetDirect via an Internet GatewayOnly outbound, via a NAT Gateway
Reachable from the internetYes, if a security group allows itNo, ever
HoldsLoad balancersDatabases, internal apps, workers
WhyNeeds to accept inbound trafficMust not be exposed to attackers

Memory trick: a database never goes in a public subnet. This one rule prevents a large share of real-world data breaches.

Security groups vs network ACLs

AspectSecurity GroupNetwork ACL
Applies toIndividual resourcesWhole subnet
StatefulYes, return traffic is automaticNo, you must allow both directions
OrderNo rules, just allow and denyEvaluated in numbered order
Change effectOnly affects new connectionsCan kill live traffic instantly

CIDR blocks to remember

CIDRMeansIs it safe?
0.0.0.0/0Everywhere on the internetOnly for public resources such as a load balancer
10.0.0.0/8All private 10.x addressesAcceptable for internal traffic
203.0.113.0/24One small public office networkYes, this is scoped

Warning: opening port 22 or 3389 to 0.0.0.0/0 is scanned within minutes of being created. Never do it.

# AWS CLI network commands
aws ec2 describe-vpcs
aws ec2 describe-subnets
aws ec2 describe-security-groups
aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16

6. S3 - Object Storage

S3 stores files as objects in buckets. You can think of it as an infinitely large hard drive you access over the web, though it behaves nothing like a filesystem.

Storage classes - pick by how often you read

ClassBuilt forRetrieval costTypical use
StandardFrequent accessNoneActive application data
Standard-IAInfrequent but quickSmallData lake, analytics
Intelligent-TieringUnknown or changing patternNoneWhen you cannot predict usage
Glacier InstantRarely, needs minutesSmallVersioned backups
Glacier FlexibleRarely, needs hoursModerateQuarterly archives
Deep ArchiveAlmost neverHigherCompliance, 7 to 10 year retention

Memory trick: colder storage is cheaper to keep and more expensive to fetch. Move data down tiers as it ages.

Lifecycle rules

Transition objects automatically: to Standard-IA at 30 days, to Glacier at 90, and delete at 365. This is how real buckets stay affordable.

Block Public Access

Four settings, all of which should be ON for almost every bucket. This is the single most effective S3 security control.

  • Block all public access
  • Ignore public ACLs
  • Block public bucket policies
  • Restrict public bucket ACLs
# Useful S3 commands
aws s3 ls
aws s3 cp report.csv s3://my-bucket/
aws s3 sync ./dist s3://my-bucket/ --delete
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket my-bucket
aws s3 presign "s3://my-bucket/report.pdf" --expires-in 3600

S3 Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
Public accessBucket left public so you can read itBlock Public Access on, signed URLs or CloudFront
EncryptionDefault onlySSE-KMS with a customer-managed key
VersioningOffOn, with a lifecycle policy to expire old versions
Deletingconsole deleteNever; rely on versioning and lifecycle rules
AccessAccess keys on your laptopIAM roles, ideally temporary credentials

7. Compute - EC2 and Beyond

ServiceYou manageAWS managesStart timeUse when
EC2The whole OS and its patchesThe physical hostMinutesYou need full control or unusual software
ECSContainers and scalingThe serversMinutesYou already run Docker
EKSKubernetesThe control planeAbout 10 minutesYou already run Kubernetes
FargateNothing but the containerServers and containersSecondsSpiky or unpredictable load
LambdaOnly the functionEverything elseUnder a secondEvent-driven, short tasks

Memory trick: each step up the table removes one more thing you must patch and monitor. Choose the highest level you can comfortably operate.

EC2 things to know

  • AMI - the template for an instance. Never use latest, because it changes under you.
  • Instance types - t3.micro is cheap and burstable, m7g.large is general purpose, c7g.xlarge is compute optimised, r7g.large is memory optimised.
  • Key pairs - SSH keys for Linux, not for Windows.
  • Placement groups - how instances are spread across AZs.

Serverless - Lambda

You upload a function, AWS runs it per request and you pay per invocation. Watch three limits:

LimitTypical valueWhat it means
TimeoutUp to 15 minutesLonger work needs Step Functions or ECS
Memory128 MB to 10 GBPower scales with memory, not CPU
Package size250 MB zippedLarge dependencies must sit in a layer
Cold startUnder a second usuallyFirst call on a new container is slower

8. Databases

ServiceModelManaged by AWSScales byUse when
RDS MySQL or PostgresRelational, SQLYes, including patchingVertically, with read replicasYour data has relationships
AuroraRelational, MySQL or Postgres compatibleYes, with 6 copies across 3 AZsStorage separates from computeYou need high availability by default
DynamoDBKey-value, NoSQLFully serverlessAutomatically, on partition keyTraffic is spiky and unpredictable
ElastiCacheIn-memory cacheYesNode size and shard countTo remove a database bottleneck
RedshiftData warehouse, columnarYesNode count and concurrencyReporting and analytics over huge data

Memory trick: relational and fixed-shape data is RDS. Spiky, key-value and enormous traffic is DynamoDB.

RDS decisions that matter

  • Multi-AZ is standby replication for failure, not for speed.
  • Read replicas are for read-heavy load.
  • Backups are automatic and kept for a window you set.
  • Never put a database in a public subnet.

9. DNS, Load Balancing and Scaling

Route 53

Route 53 is AWS's DNS. Beyond simple records it is a full traffic router, which makes failover surprisingly simple.

Record typePoints toTypical use
AAn IPv4 addressNormal web traffic
AAAAAn IPv6 addressModern clients
CNAMEAnother hostnamewww pointing to example.com
ALIASAn AWS resource such as an S3 bucketApex domains, with no extra charge
WeightedSeveral records split by weightBlue and green, or a 10 percent canary
FailoverPrimary with a health-checked backupAutomatic disaster recovery
LatencyThe fastest healthy regionUsers spread around the world

Load balancers

TypeLayerRoutes onExample
Application LB7, HTTPPath, host, headersexample.com to /api or /web
Network LB4, TCPPort and IP onlyUltra low latency, gaming, TLS offload
Gateway LB3IP and port across many serversFirewalls and intrusion detection appliances

Memory trick: ALB for HTTP rules, NLB for raw TCP speed, GWLB for appliances. ALB is the default choice for web applications.

Auto Scaling

Auto Scaling keeps a minimum instance count, adds instances when CPU or a custom metric rises, and removes them when load falls. Always pair it with a load balancer and health checks, or it will cheerfully scale to zero healthy nodes.

10. The Well-Architected Pillars

PillarOne-line summaryThe question it asks
Operational excellenceRun and monitor systems continuouslyWill we learn from every change?
SecurityProtect data, systems and assetsWho can do what, and did we audit it?
ReliabilityRecover from failure and meet demandWhat happens when this component dies?
Performance efficiencyUse resources efficientlyAre we using the right size or shape?
Cost optimisationDeliver value at the lowest priceWhat are we paying for and not using?
SustainabilityMinimise environmental impactAre we burning more compute than the task needs?

Memory trick: Operational excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance, Cost, Sustainability. Every AWS certification exam maps onto these.

11. Cost Control - Where Money Is Lost

Common mistakeHow to spot itThe fix
An idle EC2 left runningCost Explorer, grouped by serviceStop it, or schedule it for the hours it is used
Unassociated Elastic IPsThey are billed even with nothing attachedRelease them
Forgotten test environmentsCost by tag or by accountTag everything and automate teardown
Cold S3 data in StandardLarge buckets that are rarely readLifecycle rules moving data to Glacier
Data transfer out of AWSA surprising NAT Gateway or S3 billCache with CloudFront, or keep traffic inside AWS
Oversized databasesLow CPU on a large instance classDownsize and enable storage autoscaling
# Cost and audit commands
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-01-01,End=2026-02-01 --granularity MONTHLY
aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=instance-state-name,Values=running"
aws budget create-budget --budget-name Monthly --budget-type COST --limit Amount=100,Unit=USD
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=DeleteTrail

Memory trick: a bill spike is almost always an unused resource. Tag everything, set budget alerts, and review Cost Explorer monthly.

12. What Is New in 2026

AreaWhat changedWhy it matters
Generative AIAmazon Bedrock offers managed access to many models with no vendor lock-inBuild AI features without training or hosting a model
EKS Auto ModeA fully managed Kubernetes node lifecycleNo more hand-built node groups
Elastic disaster recoveryCross-region recovery as a managed serviceA regional failure becomes a non-event
S3 Express One ZoneSingle-zone storage at very high throughputFor data processing, not long-term storage
OpenTelemetry in AWSOTel-native in CloudWatch, X-Ray and ECSVendor-neutral observability
Savings Plans and GravitonCommit to usage, and use ARM chips for up to 40 percent lessThe two biggest levers on monthly cost
IPv6 by defaultNew VPCs and services now prefer IPv6Plan for dual stack from the start

13. Try It Yourself (60 minutes)

  • Create an AWS account and set up a second factor. Do not skip this even on the free tier.
  • In IAM, create a role for EC2 that may only read one S3 bucket. Attach no wildcards.
  • Create a VPC with two subnets in different availability zones, one public and one private.
  • Create a security group allowing SSH only from your own IP, never 0.0.0.0/0.
  • Launch an EC2 instance with a pinned AMI and a key pair. Terminate it when done.
  • Create an S3 bucket, upload a file, and confirm Block Public Access is on.
  • Run aws sts get-caller-identity and aws ce get-cost-and-usage.
  • Set a monthly budget with an alert at 50 percent.

14. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
Access keysLong-lived keys on your laptopIAM roles and Identity Centre, never stored keys
AMIsThe latest Amazon LinuxPinned version, patched by a scheduled pipeline
Regionsus-east-1 onlyAt least two, with tested failover
AvailabilityA single instanceMulti-AZ behind an autoscaling group
InfrastructureClicking in the consoleAll of it in code, reviewed and applied by pipeline
SecretsPlaintext in a config fileSecrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store, encrypted
TaggingNoneEnvironment, owner and cost centre on everything
TeardownDeleting in the consoleAutomated destruction of ephemeral environments
LoggingDefault onlyCloudTrail everywhere, centralised and alerted
GuardrailsYour own disciplineSCPs, Config rules and Control Tower accounts

15. Key Takeaways

  • Everything is a resource, in a region, governed by IAM. That is the model.
  • A region is a city; an availability zone is a separate data centre in it.
  • Users are for people, roles are for software.
  • Never put a database in a public subnet, and never open 22 or 3389 to the world.
  • Block Public Access on every S3 bucket.
  • A bill spike is almost always an idle resource. Tag, budget, review.
  • Infrastructure should live in code, not in console clicks.

chapters.title: Delivery Tooling: CI/CD, Actions, Jenkins, Terraform, Ansible
chapters.html:
1. What a CI/CD Pipeline Actually Is

A pipeline is an automated sequence that takes code from a commit to something running in production. It replaces the instruction "it builds on my machine" with "it built successfully, twice, on a clean machine".

commit -> build -> test -> package -> security scan -> deploy staging
       -> smoke test -> deploy production -> monitor
TermMeansDetail
CI, Continuous IntegrationMerge often, build automaticallyEvery push is compiled and tested
CD, Continuous DeliveryAlways ready to releaseA human approves the production release
Continuous DeploymentReleases with no human stepGreen build goes straight to production
PipelineThe whole automated processDefined as code, usually YAML
Pipeline as codeThe pipeline lives in version controlReviewable, versioned, auditable

Memory trick: Continuous Integration is about code, Delivery is about being ready, Deployment is about actually doing it.

2. The Standard Pipeline Stages

StageWhat it doesTypical gate
SourceClone, check out the exact commitFails if the branch is protected
BuildCompile, bundle, resolve dependenciesBuild errors stop everything
Unit testFast tests, no external servicesMust pass 100 percent
Code qualityLint, format, coverage thresholdBlocks on new violations
Security scanDependency CVEs, secrets, SASTBlocks critical findings
PackageBuild a container image, tag itImage must be reproducible
Integration testReal databases, real servicesMust pass before deploy
Deploy stagingAutomatic, no approvalAlways automatic
Smoke testIs the app actually alive?Blocks production on failure
Deploy productionPromotion, canary or blue-greenManual or automatic by policy
Verify and monitorHealth checks and metricsAutomatic rollback on failure

Memory trick: fail fast and cheap. A unit test failure costs seconds; a production failure costs hours. Put the cheap gates first.

3. Deployment Strategies

StrategyHow it worksRollbackDowntimeCost
RecreateStop the old, start the newRedeploy the old versionYesCheapest
RollingReplace instances a few at a timeRedeploy the previous imageNoLow
Blue-greenRun both, then cut traffic overFlip traffic back instantlyNoDouble capacity briefly
CanarySend a small percentage of traffic to the new versionRoute 100 percent back to oldNoNeeds real traffic splitting
Rolling canaryCanary plus continuous automated analysisAutomatic on metric regressionNoMost tooling and effort

Memory trick: Recreate is Risky, Blue-green is Backup, Canary is a small Canary bird that tests the mine. Rolling sits in between.

4. Pipeline Security Essentials

PracticeWhy it mattersWhere it lives
Least-privilege token permissionsA leaked token should do minimal damagepermissions: in the workflow
Pin third-party actions to a SHATags can be moved to malicious codeuses: org/action@sha256:...
OIDC instead of stored keysNo long-lived cloud secrets in GitHubCloud provider role assumption
Protect the main branchNobody should push straight to productionBranch protection rules
Signed images and commitsProves nothing was altered in transitCosign, Sigstore
Never echo secretsLogs are readable by everyone with accessMasked secrets in CI

Memory trick: if a credential lives in a config file, assume it will end up on the internet. Use short-lived, scoped credentials instead.

5. GitHub Actions - Workflow Anatomy

A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/. It has triggers (on:), one or more jobs, and steps inside each job.

name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest -q
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}
KeyMeaningNote
nameWorkflow name shown in the UIYour only real documentation
on:When it runspush, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch
permissions:The token's allowed actionsAlways set this, even to read-only
runs-on:Which runnerPin the version for reproducibility
steps:Ordered commands in the same shellThe last one determines success
uses:Call an action or repositoryPin third-party actions to a commit SHA
with:Inputs to an actionSame idea as function arguments
env:Environment variablesUse secrets, never literal values
secrets.XA stored secretMasked in logs, but still treat carefully

Memory trick: the workflow file is the pipeline as code. Reviewing a change to it is reviewing a change to how you ship.

Jobs, dependencies and matrices

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python: ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest -q

  deploy:
    needs: build          # waits for build to succeed
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh
FeatureWhat it doesUse when
needsMakes one job wait for anotherStage ordering: build then deploy
if:Runs the job only when trueDeploy only from main, or only on failure
strategy.matrixRuns the same job many times in parallelTest against many versions or operating systems
continue-on-errorDoes not fail the job on errorOptional, non-blocking checks
timeout-minutesHard limit on a jobStops hung builds wasting minutes

Useful gh CLI commands

gh workflow list
gh workflow run ci.yml
gh run list --limit 10
gh run view 1234567 --log-failed
gh run rerun 1234567 --failed
gh secret set API_KEY
act -l                # list workflow jobs locally
act -j test           # run one job locally with Docker

Memory trick: act runs a GitHub Actions workflow on your own machine before you push. It is the fastest way to debug a pipeline.

6. Jenkins - The Self-Hosted Automation Server

Jenkins is a self-hosted automation server. It is older than GitHub Actions and is still common in companies that need it on their own infrastructure. It is the reference implementation for the idea of a pipeline.

TermMeaning
ControllerThe Jenkins server itself, with the UI and webhooks on port 8080
Node or agentA machine that actually runs the build steps
JobA single automated task
PipelineA job whose steps are defined as code in a Jenkinsfile
Freestyle projectThe old click-and-configure job type
Shared libraryReusable pipeline code stored in a Git repository
PluginExtends Jenkins for most integrations

Memory trick: the controller is the manager, agents are the workers. Scale builds by adding agents, not controllers.

Jenkinsfile, the declarative way

pipeline {
    agent any
    environment {
        IMAGE = 'myapp'
    }
    stages {
        stage('Checkout') {
            steps { checkout scm }
        }
        stage('Build') {
            steps { sh 'docker build -t $IMAGE .' }
        }
        stage('Test') {
            steps { sh 'docker run --rm $IMAGE pytest -q' }
        }
        stage('Deploy') {
            when { branch 'main' }
            steps { sh 'docker push $IMAGE:latest' }
        }
    }
    post {
        always  { echo 'Finished' }
        failure { mail to: 'team@example.com', subject: 'Build failed' }
    }
}
BlockPurpose
pipeline {}Top level, required
agentWhere the build runs: any, none, docker, or a label
environmentVariables available to every stage
stagesThe ordered steps, each visible in the UI
stepsThe commands, such as sh or bat
whenConditions such as branch or environment
postalways, success, failure, unstable, cleanup
sh versus batShell command on Linux and Mac, or on Windows

Memory trick: Jenkins is Java-based, runs on port 8080, and its agent inbound port is 50000. Those three facts solve most Jenkins networking problems.

Running Jenkins locally

docker run -d --name jenkins -p 8080:8080 -p 50000:50000   -v jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk17
docker exec jenkins cat /var/jenkins_home/secrets/initialAdminPassword
docker logs -f jenkins
docker restart jenkins

7. Terraform - Infrastructure as Code

Terraform declares the infrastructure you want in HCL files, then works out the API calls needed to reach it. It is not configuration management for machines; it creates cloud resources.

The four commands that matter

CommandWhat it doesSafe?
terraform initDownloads providers, prepares the .terraform folderYes
terraform planShows what would change, changing nothingYes, always read it
terraform applyMakes reality match the planIt creates and destroys real resources
terraform destroyRemoves everything the configuration managesExtremely dangerous

Memory trick: plan is the rehearsal, apply is the performance. Never run apply without reading plan first.

State

State is Terraform's memory of what exists. It is usually a single JSON file and it is the most important thing to protect.

terraform state list
terraform state show aws_instance.web
terraform state rm aws_instance.web
terraform state push backup.tfstate
RuleReason
Commit state to a locked remote backendA lost state file means orphaned, unmanaged resources
Enable locking on the backendTwo engineers applying at once corrupts state
Never edit state by handTerraform will not expect it
Split state per environmentStaging state and production state must never merge

Workspaces

Workspaces let one configuration manage several states: development, staging and production from the same files.

terraform workspace list
terraform workspace new staging
terraform workspace select staging
terraform workspace delete staging

8. Ansible - Configuration Management

Ansible connects over SSH and makes machines match a description. There is no agent to install, which is why it is called agentless. Where Terraform creates resources, Ansible configures things that already exist.

TermMeaning
InventoryThe list of machines and groups you manage
PlaybookA YAML file of plays, listing tasks to run against groups
PlayA group of hosts with a set of tasks
TaskOne action using one module
ModuleThe unit of work: copy, apt, service, template, lineinfile
RoleA reusable directory of tasks, variables, handlers and templates
CollectionA package of roles, such as community.general
HandlerA task that runs only when notified, usually a service restart

Memory trick: Inventory says where, playbook says what, module says how.

Idempotency - the whole point

Running a playbook twice must leave the system in the same state as running it once. A playbook that installs a package when missing is idempotent; one that appends a line to a config file every run is not, and will eventually break something.

ansible all -m ping
ansible webservers -m ping
ansible all -m setup | grep ansible_distribution

A simple playbook

- name: Configure web servers
  hosts: webservers
  become: true
  vars:
    http_port: 80
  tasks:
    - name: Update apt cache
      ansible.builtin.apt:
        update_cache: true
      tags: [always]

    - name: Install nginx
      ansible.builtin.apt:
        name: nginx
        state: present
      notify: Restart nginx
      tags: [install]

    - name: Ensure nginx is running
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true

  handlers:
    - name: Restart nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: restarted
KeywordMeaning
hostsWhich group from the inventory this play targets
becomeRun with sudo
varsVariables for this play
tasksThe ordered actions
notifyTrigger a handler when this task changes something
handlersRuns once at the end, only if notified
tagsRun only some tasks with --tags
state: presentEnsure installed, without upgrading if already there

The commands worth memorising

ansible all -m ping
ansible-playbook site.yml --check --diff    # show what would change
ansible-playbook site.yml --syntax-check    # validate before running
ansible-playbook site.yml --limit webservers
ansible-playbook site.yml --tags deploy
ansible-playbook site.yml --start-at-task "Install nginx"
ansible-inventory --graph
ansible-vault create secrets.yml
ansible-galaxy collection install community.general

Memory trick: always run with --check first. It reports what would change without changing anything, which is exactly what you want before touching production.

9. The Four Tools Side by Side

ToolPurposeDescribesRuns whereIdempotent
GitHub ActionsCI/CD pipelineSteps to build, test, deployGitHub or self-hosted runnersYes, if written well
JenkinsCI/CD pipelineA Jenkinsfile in the repoYour own controller and agentsYes, if written well
TerraformProvision infrastructureCloud resources in HCLAgainst the cloud APIYes, by design
AnsibleConfigure machinesTasks and modules in YAMLOver SSH to existing hostsYes, by design

Memory trick: GitHub Actions and Jenkins move code, Terraform creates infrastructure, Ansible configures machines.

10. Try It Yourself (60 minutes)

  • Create a repository and add a GitHub Actions workflow with a build job, a test job and a needs dependency between them.
  • Add a matrix so the test job runs on three Python versions.
  • Install the gh CLI, run gh auth login and gh workflow list.
  • Run a Jenkins container in Docker, unlock it with the printed admin password, and create a pipeline job using the Jenkinsfile above.
  • Install Terraform and run init, validate and plan on the main.tf template in this app.
  • Install Ansible, write a playbook that creates a user and installs a package, then run it with --check before running it for real.
  • Wire them together: have Terraform output the server IP, and feed it into the Ansible inventory.

11. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
Pipeline definitionOne workflow file, edited freelyReviewed, versioned, with required status checks
RunnerGitHub-hosted, ubuntu-latestPinned image, or self-hosted for network access
DeploymentsManual button pressProgressive rollout with automatic rollback
SecretsRepository secretsEnvironment-scoped, rotated, short-lived OIDC
Terraform stateLocal terraform.tfstateRemote, locked backend, per environment
Terraform applyFrom your laptopFrom the pipeline, after plan review
Ansible inventoryA few IPs in a text fileDynamic inventory from the cloud provider
Ansible runsStraight to productionStaging first, then a limited canary group
JenkinsLatest image tagPinned version, patched, with a shared library
FailuresFix it and push againAlerted, with a runbook and a post-mortem

12. Key Takeaways

  • A pipeline replaces "it works on my machine" with reproducible verification.
  • Put the cheap, fast checks first, and fail early.
  • Recreate is risky, blue-green is backup, canary is a small test.
  • Pin third-party actions to a SHA and set token permissions explicitly.
  • Jenkins runs on 8080 with agents inbound on 50000.
  • Terraform plan is a rehearsal; state is the memory and must be locked and remote.
  • Ansible is agentless and idempotent, so always run --check first.
  • Actions and Jenkins move code, Terraform creates infrastructure, Ansible configures machines.

chapters.title: DevOps and Cloud
chapters.html:
1. What Is DevOps?

DevOps removes the wall between writing software and running it. Developers own their code in production, and operations teams write code. The goal is small, frequent, reversible changes.

Memory trick for the golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Monitor those four and you know whether your service is healthy.

2. Containers - Docker

A container packages your application with its dependencies into a single image that runs identically everywhere. That removes the classic "works on my machine" problem.

docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web myapp:1.0
docker ps
docker logs -f web
docker exec -it web sh
docker stop web && docker rm web
ConceptMeaningAnalogy
ImageAn immutable template with the app and its dependenciesA recipe
ContainerA running instance of an imageA cooked meal from the recipe
DockerfileThe build instructions for an imageThe written recipe
VolumeStorage that survives container deletionA hard drive, not RAM
RegistryWhere images are stored and sharedA library

Containers versus virtual machines: a VM emulates hardware and ships a full OS kernel, so it is large and slow to boot. A container shares the host kernel, so it is small and starts almost instantly.

3. Kubernetes - Scheduling Containers

Kubernetes keeps a desired number of containers running. If one dies it is replaced; if traffic rises it scales out. You describe the desired state and the controller makes it happen.

ObjectWhat it doesUse it for
PodThe smallest runnable unitAnything, but rarely created by hand
DeploymentManages a stateless replicated workloadWeb servers, APIs, workers
StatefulSetStable identity and storage per replicaDatabases, anything needing a fixed disk
ServiceA stable virtual IP in front of changing podsNetworking, always
IngressRoutes outside HTTP traffic by path or hostOne entry point for many services
ConfigMapNon-secret configurationEnvironment specific settings
SecretSensitive values such as passwordsCredentials and tokens
PVCA request for persistent storageAnything that must keep data

Memory trick: Deployment for things that can be thrown away, StatefulSet for things that cannot.

kubectl apply -f app.yaml
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod <name>
kubectl logs -f deployment/myapp
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh
kubectl port-forward svc/myapp 8080:80
kubectl scale deployment/myapp --replicas=3
kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp
kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp
kubectl delete -f app.yaml

4. Containers versus Virtual Machines

AspectVirtual machineContainer
ContainsA full OS with its own kernelJust the app and its libraries
SizeGigabytesMegabytes
Start timeMinutesMilliseconds
IsolationStrong, separate kernelWeaker, shares the host kernel
DensityDozens per hostHundreds per host
Best forFull OS, strong isolation, legacy appsMicroservices, scale out, fast deploys

5. Where to Go Deeper

The tool mechanics live in their own chapters so this chapter stays about mindset. Use these pointers when you need the detail.

TopicGo toWhy it is separate
CI/CD pipelines, GitHub ActionsChapter 13, Delivery ToolingWorkflow syntax, matrices, caching and runners need room
Jenkins pipelinesChapter 13, Delivery ToolingJenkinsfile, agents and plugins are a large topic
Terraform and AnsibleChapter 13, Delivery ToolingState, backends, modules and roles need proper explanation
Scrum, Agile and the SDLCChapter 11, SDLC, Agile and ScrumRoles, events and artefacts deserve their own treatment
AWS services in depthChapter 12, AWSRegions, IAM, VPC, S3, EC2 and cost control
Linux and Windows commandsChapters 8 and 10Full command references with permissions and services

Memory trick: this chapter answers what DevOps is and why it exists. Chapter 13 answers how to run the delivery pipeline.

gh workflow list
gh run list --limit 10
gh run view <id> --log-failed
gh workflow run deploy.yml --ref main
act -l              # run workflows locally before pushing

6. Version Control with Git
