JWTA signed token carrying claims, with an expiry
MFAA second factor: something you know, have, or are
SSOOne identity provider for many applications
OAuthLet a third party grant limited access without your password
OpenID ConnectOAuth with an identity token, so the app knows who signed in

Memory trick: authentication is the door, authorisation is what is inside the room. A locked door with no locks on the cupboards is still a security problem, and that is the most common real-world flaw.

Sessions versus tokens: a session stores state on the server and the browser holds an opaque id, so you can revoke it instantly. A JWT is self-contained and verified without a database call, which is fast but cannot be revoked before it expires. That single trade-off explains most authentication design decisions.

10. CORS - Why The Browser Blocks Things

CORS, the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing rules, exists for one reason: to stop another website from using your logged-in session to send actions as you.

You open your bank in one tab and an attacker's page in another. Without CORS, JavaScript on the attacker's page could quietly call your bank's API, and the browser would attach your cookies, because it cannot tell your request from a forged one.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://myapp.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: POST, GET
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
RuleMeaning
Same-originSame scheme, host and port. No CORS involved.
Simple requestGET, POST or HEAD with simple headers. Sent, then blocked on the reply.
PreflightThe browser asks permission with OPTIONS before the real request.
No wildcard with credentialsYou cannot send cookies and allow every origin
CORS is not server securityOnly browsers enforce it. A curl script ignores it entirely

Memory trick: CORS protects the browser, not your API. Your server must still check authorisation on every request, because any program can ignore CORS.

11. CSRF - The Attack CORS Prevents

Cross-site request forgery works because of how cookies behave. Cookies are sent by the browser automatically to any matching domain, without the page's JavaScript asking.

So if you are logged in to your bank, a page anywhere else can contain a form that silently submits a transfer, and your browser will attach your session cookie to it.

DefenceHow it works
SameSite cookiesThe strongest and simplest fix: do not send the cookie on cross-site requests
CSRF tokenA hidden random value per form, checked by the server against the session
Double submit cookieToken in the form and in a cookie; the attacker can read neither to match them
Never use GET for changesA GET can be triggered by an image tag, with no script at all
Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax

Memory trick: CSRF is about cookies being sent when you did not intend it. SameSite cookies solve it by not sending them.

12. The Rest Of The Web Security Vocabulary

TermMeans
XSSInjecting script into a page the user views. Steals sessions.
SQL injectionUser input treated as SQL code, letting an attacker read or change the database
ClickjackingAn invisible page layered over a button you meant to click
Open redirectA login link that sends you to an attacker's site afterwards
SSL or TLSEncrypting the connection. HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS.
HSTSTelling browsers to refuse plain HTTP for your domain
Rate limitingCapping requests per user or IP to stop brute force
Least privilegeGive the minimum access needed, and nothing more
Input validationNever trust anything arriving from outside the system

Memory trick: most web vulnerabilities come from trusting input. Validate at the edge, escape on output, and parameterise every query, and most of this table stops applying to you.

13. Common Rules Worth Knowing

  • An order is never stored by trusting the price the browser sent. Re-price it.
  • Stock is decremented atomically, never read then written.
  • Money is stored as an integer of minor units, never a float.
  • A refund is a new transaction, never a deletion or an edit of the original.
  • Every payment endpoint takes an idempotency key.
  • Every state-changing request is authorised on the server, every time.
  • Every cookie holding a session is HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite.

Try it yourself: take the shop journey above and write down the database tables it needs. Basket, order, line item, product, inventory, payment, refund and customer, plus the relationship between each. When you have done that, most application design problems stop being mysterious.

Learning vs production: a small shop runs a single till and one database, and the rules above are enough. Production adds concurrency, multiple tills, tax jurisdictions, partial refunds, chargebacks, payment retries, reconciliation and an audit trail. The rules do not change; the number of ways they can be violated does.

chapters.title: Software Testing
chapters.html:
1. What Testing Really Buys You

A test is a machine that answers one question: does the code still do what we think it does? Writing it down as code means the answer arrives in seconds, forever, without a human having to remember what the feature used to do.

Memory trick: bugs found in requirements cost 1x to fix, in design 5x, in code 10x, in production 100x. Every cheap test you write moves a bug left, where it is cheap.

2. The Test Levels, The Order You Do Them, And The Phase They Run In

Tests are written and run in a fixed order, fastest first. If a unit test cannot pass, there is no point starting the integration test behind it.

LevelWhat it exercisesOrder you do itPhase it runs inSpeedTypical tool
Unit testOne function or class, alone, with its neighbours faked1st - written while you code, minutes after the codeEvery save (pre-commit) and every commitMillisecondspytest, unittest, Jest
Integration testTwo or more real parts together: API + database, app + queue2nd - once units are greenEvery push / pull request in CISecondspytest + TestClient, Testcontainers
System / end-to-endThe whole running system, driven like a user3rd - after integration passesMerge to main, nightly, or pre-releaseMinutesPlaywright, Selenium, Cypress
Regression testEvery bug that ever shipped, re-checked foreverContinuous - each fix adds a caseEvery pipeline run, foreverSame as the level the bug lived atAny suite; golden/snapshot files
Acceptance testWhether the software satisfies the agreed requirementsLast - before sign-offPre-release, UAT, alpha/betaHoursCucumber, manual UAT scripts

Memory trick: Unit, Integration, System, Acceptance - UISA. Write them in that order, run them in that order, and stop the pipeline at the first red stage.

3. The Test Pyramid

        /  E2E   \          few, slow, expensive, brittle
       /------------\ 
      / Integration  \      medium count, medium speed
     /----------------\ 
    /     Unit tests    \   many, fast, cheap, precise
   /______________________\

Wide base, narrow top. A suite that is mostly end-to-end tests is slow and flaky; a suite with no end-to-end tests never checks that the parts actually connect. Aim for roughly 70% unit, 20% integration, 10% end-to-end - the ratios matter less than the shape.

4. Unit Tests

A unit test calls one thing with given inputs and asserts the output. It touches no network, no disk, no database, no real clock. The three-part shape is Arrange, Act, Assert.

def test_discount_applies_above_threshold():
    # Arrange
    cart = Cart(items=[Item(price=50), Item(price=30)])
    # Act
    total = cart.total(discount=0.1)
    # Assert
    assert total == 72.0   # (50 + 30) - 10%


def test_empty_cart_is_free():
    assert Cart(items=[]).total() == 0

Good unit tests are FIRST: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely. If two tests cannot run in any order, they are coupled and one of them will lie to you.

What not to test: private helpers you might rename tomorrow, third-party library behaviour, or framework boilerplate. Test your decisions, not your syntax.

5. Integration Tests

Units can all pass while the app is broken - the wiring is wrong, the query is misspelled, the config key does not exist. Integration tests run real pieces together.

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from app.main import app   # your FastAPI application

client = TestClient(app)

def test_create_order_persists():
    response = client.post("/orders", json={"sku": "A1", "qty": 2})
    assert response.status_code == 201
    body = response.json()
    # The database must really contain it, not just the response.
    stored = client.get(f"/orders/{body['id']}")
    assert stored.json()["qty"] == 2

Learning vs reality: while learning you point tests at a local database. In production CI, each job spins its own throwaway database (Testcontainers starts a Docker container per run) so jobs never collide.

6. System, End-to-End And Acceptance

TypeQuestion it answersWho owns itFailure means
System / E2EDoes the whole stack work for a real user journey?Developers + QASomething between the parts is broken
UAT (user acceptance)Is this the software the business asked for?Product / customerWrong feature, missing requirement
Alpha / betaDoes it survive real users and real data?Real usersAssumptions that no test could anticipate
Smoke testAfter a deploy: is the site up and login works?PipelineRoll back immediately

7. Regression Testing

Regression means an old thing that worked is broken now. Regression testing is not a separate tool - it is the discipline of turning every bug fix into a permanent test so the bug can never come back.

# The bug: applying a coupon twice gave money back.
def test_coupon_applies_only_once():
    cart = Cart(coupon="SAVE10")
    first = cart.total()
    second = cart.total()        # calling again must not re-apply
    assert first == second

Golden (snapshot) files are regression tests for output shape: dump the JSON, the rendered HTML, the CLI help text to a file; the test compares and fails on any diff; a human approves intentional changes. Most regression failures are accidental side effects you never considered - that is exactly what they are for.

Memory trick: a bug fixed without a test is a bug on parole.

8. Black-Box Testing - Testing From The Outside

Black box means the tester cannot see the code. Judgement comes only from the requirements and the inputs and outputs. Anyone can do it: a manual tester, a customer, an automated script written from the spec.

TechniqueHow it worksExample (field: age, valid 18-120)
Equivalence partitioningSplit inputs into classes that should behave the same; test one from eachOne case each: 17 (too young), 30 (valid), 121 (too old)
Boundary value analysisOff-by-one bugs live on the edges, so test the edges and their neighbours17, 18, 19, 119, 120, 121
Decision tableList every combination of conditions as rowslogged in x subscribed x premium -> expected outcome
State transitionWalk the states and the legal/illegal moves between themorder: new -> paid -> shipped; what about new -> shipped?
Error guessingTry what always breaks: empty string, 0, negative, huge, SQL quotes, emoji, nullage = -1, age = 999999999, age = "twenty"
Use case / exploratoryScript a realistic user goal, then improvise around itRegister, add card, buy, refund, buy again
# Black-box in code: no knowledge of internals, only the contract.
def test_age_boundaries():
    assert validate_age(18) is True     # just inside
    assert validate_age(17) is False    # just outside
    assert validate_age(120) is True
    assert validate_age(121) is False

9. White-Box Testing - Testing From The Inside

White box (glass box / structural) means you can see the source, and you design tests to execute its paths. The tester is usually the developer.

Coverage typeQuestion it answersExample where it catches a gap
StatementDid every line run?An error branch never entered
BranchDid both outcomes of every if/else run?if user: ... else: ... - the else never tested
PathDid every route through the function run?Combination of two conditions never exercised together
ConditionDid each sub-condition get true and false?if a and b: - only a=True, b=True tested
Cyclomatic complexityHow many independent paths exist? (decisions + 1)A function with complexity 12 needs ~12 tests to cover it
# White-box: the branch exists, so both sides must be tested.
def tax_for(price, is_member):
    if is_member and price > 100:      # two conditions, one branch
        return price * 0.05
    return price * 0.10

# Covering branch (both outcomes) implies:
assert tax_for(200, True)  == 10.0
assert tax_for(50,  True)  == 5.0
assert tax_for(200, False) == 20.0
Black boxWhite box
Sees the code?NoYes
Designed fromRequirements, specificationSource, control flow, branches
Who does itQA, customers, anyoneDevelopers
Best atMissing features, wrong behaviour, usabilityUntested branches, dead code, complexity
Blind spotCannot know which paths were never writtenAssumes the code is the spec - it may be wrong

Memory trick: black box asks "is the right software built?" white box asks "is the software built right?" You need both.

10. Coverage - What It Measures And What It Does Not

pytest --cov=app --cov-report=term-missing
# Name       Stmts   Miss  Cover   Missing
# app/orders.py    80      6    92%   41-46
  • Coverage counts lines executed, not correctness. 100% coverage with dumb assertions proves nothing.
  • Treat it as a gap detector: read the missing lines and ask why they are untested.
  • Branch coverage is a better target than line coverage.
  • A practical gate for most teams: 80% overall, 100% on money, auth and other critical paths.

11. TDD, BDD And The Pipeline

Red     - write a test that fails (you have not written the code yet)
Green   - write the smallest code that makes it pass
Refactor- improve the code, tests stay green
Repeat  - one behaviour per cycle, minutes not hours

BDD (behaviour-driven development) writes the same idea in plain language: Given a logged-in user, When they click Buy, Then an order is created. The sentence becomes an automated test, so business and code stay in the same document.

Pipeline stageRunsGate
Pre-commit hookLint, format, fast unit testsCannot commit broken code
Pull requestAll unit + integration tests, coverage, SASTReview blocked until green
Merge / mainFull suite + a few E2E journeysDeploy blocked until green
NightlySlow E2E, load tests, full regressionFailure opens a ticket
Pre-releaseSmoke + acceptance + UAT sign-offRelease blocked until green
Post-deploySmoke test against productionAutomatic rollback on failure

12. A/B Testing - Experiments On Real Users

Unit tests tell you whether the code works. A/B testing tells you which version works better for humans: split users at random into A (control) and B (variant), measure the same metric on both, and keep the winner.

StepWhat you doClassic mistake
1. Hypothesis"Changing the button to green will raise clicks"Running a test with no stated hypothesis
2. MetricOne primary metric (click-through, conversion) + guardrails (latency, refunds)Choosing the metric after seeing results
3. RandomisationAssign users randomly, 50/50, sticky per userRe-randomising per page view, splitting a team
4. Sample sizeDecide up front how many users you need (power analysis)Stopping as soon as it looks good
5. SignificanceRun a full business cycle (a week, incl. weekends); check p < 0.05 or a confidence interval excluding zeroPeeking daily and stopping early - this inflates false positives
6. DecideShip, iterate, or kill; document the resultShipping variant B because the CEO prefers it
import math

def ab_summary(visitors_a, conversions_a, visitors_b, conversions_b):
    pa, pb = conversions_a / visitors_a, conversions_b / visitors_b
    pooled = (conversions_a + conversions_b) / (visitors_a + visitors_b)
    # Standard error of the difference between two proportions.
    se = math.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1/visitors_a + 1/visitors_b))
    z = (pb - pa) / se if se else 0
    lift = (pb - pa) / pa * 100 if pa else float("inf")
    return {"control": pa, "variant": pb, "lift_pct": lift, "z": z}

# |z| > 1.96 means the difference is significant at 95% confidence.
print(ab_summary(10_000, 320, 10_000, 372))

Memory trick: an A/B test is a measurement, not a vote. Decide the metric and duration before you look, and never peek-and-stop.

13. Non-Functional Tests

KindQuestionTools
Performance / loadHow many users before it falls over?k6, JMeter, Locust,wrk
SecurityCan an attacker make it do the wrong thing?SAST: bandit - DAST: OWASP ZAP
AccessibilityCan a screen-reader user complete the task?axe, Lighthouse
Resilience / chaosWhat happens when a dependency dies?Chaos Monkey, toxiproxy
UsabilityCan a human figure it out without instructions?Five users, one moderator

14. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
Tests you writeA few happy pathsHappy paths + boundaries + every past bug
SpeedRun them by handAutomated in seconds on every push
FakesMock everything, tests are trivialFake only the slow/unstable edges; test the real database
CoverageNot measuredReported, gated on critical paths
Flaky testsRe-run until greenQuarantined and fixed - a flaky test is treated as a broken build
Manual QAYou click aroundExploratory testing for what scripts cannot express; scripts own the rest
A/B testsNot applicableHypothesis, metric, sample size and significance decided up front

15. Key Takeaways

  • Unit, Integration, System, Acceptance - write and run them in that order; stop the pipeline at the first red stage.
  • Regression testing turns every bug fix into a permanent test. A bug fixed without a test is a bug on parole.
  • Black box tests the specification; white box tests the code. Both are necessary.
  • Coverage finds gaps; it does not prove correctness.
  • A/B testing is a controlled experiment: hypothesis, metric, random assignment, sample size, significance - in that order.
  • Keep the pyramid wide at the bottom; end-to-end tests are the slowest and the most brittle.

Exercise: take any function you have written and add one equivalence-partition test, one boundary-value test and one branch-coverage test. Run pytest -not -v and count how many lines the new tests uncovered.

chapters.title: Deployment Strategies
chapters.html:
1. What A Deployment Strategy Actually Is

Deployment strategy is the answer to one question: how do new code users get from the old version to the new one without the business stopping? The code is already tested; this is about the minutes or hours when both versions exist at once.

Memory trick: every strategy is a trade between three things - speed (how fast the new code arrives), risk (how many users are hit if it is broken) and cost (how much extra infrastructure runs during the switch).

2. The Strategies Compared

StrategyHow it worksDowntimeRisk blast radiusRollbackBest when
Big bangStop old, deploy new everywhere at onceYes, usually100% of users, instantlyRe-deploy the old version (slow)Demos, internal tools, first deploy ever
RollingReplace a few instances at a time until all are newNoThe batch size, e.g. 25%Easy - stop the rollout, roll back batchesStateless services, Kubernetes, VM fleets
Blue-greenTwo identical environments; traffic switches from blue (old) to green (new) in one stepNo100% at the switch, but instant and reversibleFlip the switch back - secondsReleases that need a hard cut-over, schema checks
CanarySend 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% of traffic to the new version, watching metrics between each stepNoStarts at 1% of usersStop early, most users never noticedAnything customer-facing, high risk
Phased (staged)Roll out by group: internal staff -> one region -> one customer tier -> everyoneNoOne group at a timeFreeze the phase, fix, resumeMobile apps, multi-region, enterprise cohorts
ShadowSend real traffic to both versions; only the old one answers users, compare outputsNoZero (new version answers nobody)Simply delete itValidating a rewrite or a risky change
Feature flagNew code ships dark; a runtime switch turns behaviour on per user/segmentNoWhatever the flag targetsTurn the flag off - no redeployContinuous delivery, dark launches, experiments

3. The Topologies, Drawn

ROLLING              BLUE-GREEN
                     load balancer
old old old new         |            switch!
 [batch 1][2][3]       v
                     [ BLUE (v1) ]  ----+----> users (today)
replace 1..n until      |
all are new           [ GREEN (v2) ] ---+----> users (after switch)

CANARY                       PHASED / COHORT
        traffic
         |                    Phase 1: staff
    +----+----+               Phase 2: region EU
    v    v    v               Phase 3: all customers
  [v1] [v1] [v2]  <- start 1% on v2
              |
      1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% on v2, watching metrics

4. A Canary Step By Step

# 1. Deploy the new version alongside the old (nobody routed to it yet)
kubectl apply -f app-v2.yaml          # or: docker compose up -d app-v2

# 2. Move 1% of traffic to it
kubectl patch virtualservice app \
  --type merge -p '{"spec":{"http":[{"route":[{"destination":{"host":"app","subset":"v1","weight":95}},{"destination":{"host":"app","subset":"v2","weight":5}}]}}]}'

# 3. Watch the canary signals for the soak period (5-30 minutes)
#    error rate, p95 latency, saturation - compare v2 against v1
kubectl top pod -l version=v2

# 4. Good? Increase weight: 5 -> 25 -> 50 -> 100.  Bad? Roll back:
kubectl patch virtualservice app --type merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"http":[{"route":[{"destination":{"host":"app","subset":"v1","weight":100}}]}}]}'

Memory trick: a canary was the coal-miner's bird. If the bird dies, you leave the mine. If the 1% deployment's error rate moves, you stop - before the rest of the users are involved.

5. Rollback, Runbooks And The Safety Net

MechanismWhat it doesRule
Instant rollbackRe-point traffic at the previous artefact (blue, or previous image tag)Must be one command, tested before you need it
Database migrationsSchema changes outlive deploymentsExpand - migrate - contract: add columns first, backfill, only later remove. Never deploy code that needs a column the old version lacks
Health checksAutomatic rollback trigger5xx rate or latency over threshold during canary -> abort
RunbookThe written steps: what changed, how to verify, how to roll backIf it is not written, it is 3am and nobody remembers
Smoke testPost-deploy: login, browse, buyRuns automatically; failure rolls back for you

6. Choosing A Strategy

Risk to users of being wrong is HIGH (payments, auth, anything public)?
  yes -> canary or phased, with feature flags inside
  no  -> is the app stateless and replicated?
           yes -> rolling (simplest default on Kubernetes)
           no   -> blue-green (instant, clean rollback)

Need to test behaviour before showing it?        -> feature flag
Doubtful rewrite, want production data?          -> shadow
Just want the demo working today?                -> big bang

Microservices usually combine them: rolling deploys of each service, canary at the edge, feature flags inside the code.

7. What Breaks Deployments (And How Strategies Handle It)

FailureBig bangRolling / canaryBlue-green
Bad binaryEveryone down until fixedCanary catches it at 1%; rolling halts mid-wayFlip back in seconds
Config errorOutageContained to the batchOld env untouched
Incompatible schemaOutage + data riskMixed versions collide - use expand/contract migrationsBoth versions share one database - same rule applies
Missed dependencyFull rollbackStop the rolloutFlip back

8. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
StrategyBig bang: stop, replace, startRolling or canary, automated by Argo Rollouts / Spinnaker / ECS
RollbackRedeploy the old build if you still have itOne command, rehearsed, under a minute (SLO)
Signals"Looks fine"Error rate, latency, saturation compared per version
Flagsif statements in codeFlag service (LaunchDarkly, Unleash) with owners and expiry dates
SchemaEdit the table by handVersioned migrations, expand/contract, reversible
ApprovalYou press the buttonPipeline gates: tests green, review, then progressive rollout

9. Key Takeaways

  • Speed, risk and cost - every strategy trades between those three.
  • Rolling is the Kubernetes default; blue-green buys an instant hard cut-over; canary keeps blast radius to 1% while you watch real metrics.
  • Phased rollouts are canaries across groups of people instead of percentages of traffic.
  • Feature flags separate deploying from releasing: code ships dark, behaviour turns on later, rollback is a switch not a redeploy.
  • Migrations must be safe for both versions at once: expand, migrate, contract.
  • If rollback has never been rehearsed, you do not have one.

Exercise: write a one-page runbook for your own project: what ships, which strategy it should use, the exact rollback command, and the three metrics that prove it worked.

chapters.title: Authentication and TLS
chapters.html:
1. How Your Data Actually Transfers

Before any token can be trusted, the wire it travels on has to be safe. One page load is a chain of handshakes.

User                    CDN/ISP             DNS             Server
 |                        |                  |                |
 | 1. https://shop.com    |                  |                |
 |------DNS query---------+----------------->|                |
 |<----shop.com = 93.184.x.x-----------------+                |
 |                        |                  |                |
 | 2. TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) ---------->|
 | 3. TLS handshake:                             --------------|
 |    client hello (cipher suites)  ---------->               |
 |    server hello + certificate   <-----------  proves the   |
 |    key exchange (ECDHE)  ------->            server IS shop|
 |    both derive a session key                   |            |
 |    encrypt everything from here on <=========>|            |
 | 4. GET /index.html  (HTTP inside TLS) ------->             |
 |<--- 200 OK + HTML  (encrypted) ---------------             |
LayerJobBreaks if missing
DNSNames the destination IPCache-poisoning sends users to an attacker
TCPReliable, ordered deliveryLost or reordered packets
TLSEncryption, integrity, server identityAnyone on the Wi-Fi reads your password and tokens
HTTPThe request/response itself-

Memory trick: DNS finds the house, TCP knocks the door, TLS agrees on a secret language, HTTP says what you want. HTTPS = HTTP spoken inside TLS.

2. Sessions Versus Tokens

Server-side sessionToken (JWT)
Where state livesServer memory/database; cookie holds only a session idInside the token itself; server keeps nothing
Scales horizontallyNeeds sticky sessions or shared store (Redis)Any server can verify it alone
Logout / revokeInstant - delete the sessionHard - the token stays valid until it expires
Best forClassic web apps, admin panelsAPIs, mobile, microservices

3. What A JWT Is

A JSON Web Token is three base64url parts joined by dots. It carries its own claims, is signed (not encrypted by default), and any holder can verify it without asking the issuer.

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9 . eyJzdWIiOiI0MiIsInJvbGUiOiJhZG1pbiIsImV4cCI6MTcz… . SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c
|______ header ______| |________________ payload ________________| |_______ signature ______|
 {alg: HS256, typ: JWT}   {sub: 42, role: admin, exp: 173…}          HMAC(server_secret, header.payload)
PartContentsProtects against
HeaderAlgorithm and token typeNothing itself - which is why alg must be pinned when verifying
Payload (claims)sub (who), exp (expiry), iat (issued), aud (audience), iss (issuer), plus custom dataCarries identity so the server needs no session lookup
SignatureHMAC or RSA over header.payloadTampering: change one character of the payload and verification fails

Critical: base64 is encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode the payload. Never put passwords or secrets in a JWT - only what you are happy to expose.

4. Signing And Verifying (Real Code)

# pip install pyjwt
import datetime
import jwt

SECRET = "change-me-in-a-secret-manager"

def issue_token(user_id, role="user"):
    payload = {
        "sub": str(user_id),
        "role": role,
        "iat": datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc),
        "exp": datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)
               + datetime.timedelta(minutes=15),
        "iss": "dockeybe-api",
        "aud": "dockeybe-web",
    }
    return jwt.encode(payload, SECRET, algorithm="HS256")

def verify_token(token: str):
    # algorithms=[...] is mandatory: it stops the alg:none attack where an
    # attacker strips the signature and re-sends the token.
    return jwt.decode(token, SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"],
                      issuer="dockeybe-api", audience="dockeybe-web")

# FastAPI dependency
from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer

scheme = HTTPBearer()

def current_user(cred = Depends(scheme)):
    try:
        claims = verify_token(cred.credentials)
    except jwt.PyJWTError:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
                            detail="invalid or expired token")
    return claims
ThreatThe defence
Tampered payloadSignature check fails
alg: none (signature stripped)Pin algorithms=[...] on verify
Replayed after logoutShort expiry (5-15 min) + refresh tokens, or a server-side deny list
Stolen secret = forge anythingRS256/ES256: public key verifies, only the auth server holds the private key
Token from another serviceCheck aud and iss on every verify
Long-lived tokensexp 15 min + rotating refresh token in an httpOnly cookie

HS256 vs RS256: HS256 shares one secret (both sign and verify) - every service holding the secret can mint tokens. RS256 is asymmetric: the auth server signs with the private key, everyone else verifies with the public key, so a compromised API server cannot forge identity.

5. OAuth 2.0 - Delegated Authorization

OAuth 2.0 answers a different question: not "who are you" but "let this app do one thing on my behalf, without giving it my password". Four roles:

RoleWhat it isExample
Resource ownerThe human who owns the dataYou, your Google Drive
ClientThe app asking for accessA third-party photo editor
Authorization serverIssues the tokens after consentaccounts.google.com
Resource serverThe API holding the datawww.googleapis.com/drive

The flow you will actually implement is the authorization code flow with PKCE. OAuth is about authorization; OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a thin layer on top that adds authentication (who is the user) via the id_token. Google Sign-In is OIDC.

Authorization Code Flow (with PKCE)

You (browser)            Your app (FastAPI)          Google (authorization server)
    |                          |                                |
    | 1. click "Sign in"       |                                |
    |------------------------->|                                |
    | 2. redirect to Google    |                                |
    |    /authorize?client_id=..&redirect_uri=..&state=..      |
    |    &scope=openid email   |                                |
    |    &code_challenge=..    |                                |
    |--------------------------------------------------------->|
    | 3. user logs in and consents (only Google sees the password)
    |<---------------------------------------------------------|
    | 4. redirect back with ?code=ABC&state=xyz                |
    |------------------------->|                                |
    | 5. POST /token  code=ABC + code_verifier + client_secret  |
    |                          |------------------------------>|
    |                          | 6. {access_token, id_token,    |
    |                          |     refresh_token}             |
    |                          |<------------------------------|
    | 7. set session cookie    |                                |
    |<-------------------------|                                |
    | 8. API calls carry the token (Authorization: Bearer ...)  |
    |-------------------------> resource APIs                   |
ElementPurpose
client_id / client_secretIdentifies your app; the secret proves it is really you at /token
redirect_uriMust be pre-registered - otherwise codes can be stolen by an open redirect
scopeLeast privilege: "email" not "everything"
stateRandom value round-tripped through the browser; blocks CSRF / login CSRF
PKCE (code_challenge / verifier)Saves public clients (SPAs, mobile) from needing a secret: the code is worthless without the verifier
access_tokenShort-lived key to the API (minutes)
refresh_tokenLong-lived, used only at the token endpoint to get new access tokens; rotate it on every use
Authorization codeSingle-use, seconds-lived, TLS-protected stepping stone

Grant types and when to use them: authorization code (humans via browser - the default), client credentials (machine-to-machine, no user), device code (TVs and CLI tools). Implicit and password grants are legacy - do not build them.

6. Google Sign-In (OIDC), End To End

# pip install google-auth httpx
import httpx

GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID = "...apps.googleusercontent.com"
GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET = "..."
GOOGLE_DISCOVERY = "https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration"

async def exchange_code(code: str, redirect_uri: str, code_verifier: str):
    # Step 6: swap the authorization code for tokens
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        token_resp = await client.post(GOOGLE_DISCOVERY + "/token", data={
            "code": code,
            "client_id": GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID,
            "client_secret": GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET,
            "redirect_uri": redirect_uri,
            "grant_type": "authorization_code",
            "code_verifier": code_verifier,      # PKCE
        })
        tokens = token_resp.json()

        # Verify the id_token signature with Google's public keys -- never
        # trust its payload without checking the signature, aud and exp.
        userinfo = await client.get(
            "https://oauth2.googleapis.com/tokeninfo?id_token="
            + tokens["id_token"])
        claims = userinfo.json()
        assert claims["aud"] == GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID
        return claims   # {sub, email, name, picture, ...}
  1. Front end generates state + code_verifier, stores them, redirects to Google's /authorize with the code challenge.
  2. Google authenticates the human and asks for consent per scope.
  3. Back at your redirect URI: exchange code + verifier for tokens.
  4. Verify the id_token (signature, aud, exp, iss), then issue your own session or JWT for your app.
  5. Google's access token is for Google's APIs - keep it server-side if you need it, never expose your client secret in the browser.

7. Where To Keep The Token

StorageProsCons
httpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Lax cookieJavaScript cannot read it; SameSite blunts CSRFNeeds CSRF defence for state-changing requests
localStorage / sessionStorageSimple for SPAsAny XSS steals the token instantly; no expiry control
In-memory (variable)Not persisted at allLost on refresh; still XSS-reachable

Memory trick: cookies for web pages, Authorization header for APIs you call yourself, and always TLS - a token on a plain HTTP connection is a bearer token anyone on the path can spend.

8. The Whole Toolkit, Compared

ToolAnswersShape
Password + sessionWho are you, on this site?Cookie holds an id; server holds the state
JWTWho are you, for any service?Signed self-contained token, stateless verification
OAuth 2.0What may this app do for me?Delegated access with scopes, no password sharing
OIDC / Google Sign-InWho is this human, proven by someone I trust?OAuth + verified id_token with profile claims
mTLS / API keysWhich machine is calling?Service identity, not human identity

9. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
SecretsHard-coded in the fileSecret manager / env vars, rotated, never in git
Token lifetime30 days so it never annoys you15-minute access tokens, rotating refresh tokens
RevocationIgnoredDeny list or short TTL + refresh revoke
Sign-inYour own password tableOIDC provider (Google, Azure AD) + MFA
CORS*Exact origins with credentials
HTTPSlocalhost is fineTLS everywhere, HSTS, redirect HTTP to HTTPS

10. Key Takeaways

  • DNS finds, TCP connects, TLS protects, HTTP speaks - HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS.
  • A JWT is signed, not encrypted: base64 payload is public; sign it, pin the algorithm, keep exp short.
  • HS256 shares a secret; RS256 keeps the signing key on the auth server only.
  • OAuth 2.0 delegates access with scopes and never shares the password; OIDC adds verified identity on top - that is Google Sign-In.
  • state and PKCE are not optional: they are the CSRF and code-theft defences.
  • httpOnly cookie for browsers, Authorization header for APIs, TLS always.

Exercise: decode a JWT at jwt.io, then build the issue and verify pair from section 4. Tamper with one character of the payload and watch verification fail.

chapters.title: Advanced Python
chapters.html:
1. Lambda - Small Anonymous Functions

A lambda is a one-expression function with no name. It exists for the moments when you need a tiny function right here, usually as an argument.

square = lambda x: x * x                 # works, but def square(x) is better

# The four places lambda genuinely earns its keep:
sorted(orders, key=lambda o: o["total"], reverse=True)
players.sort(key=lambda p: (-p["score"], p["name"]))
items = list(filter(lambda x: x > 0, raw))
buttons = [ctk.CTkButton(win, text=n, command=lambda n=n: open(n)) for n in names]
RuleWhy
One expression onlyNo loops, no assignments - if you need those, write a def
Name it with def when reusedkey=age_of reads better than a lambda in a stack trace
Loop variables need bindinglambda: i captures the variable, not the value - use lambda i=i: i or functools.partial
Never assign to a name twicePEP 8: lambda should be where you need an expression, not a def in disguise

2. map, filter, reduce And Comprehensions

names  = list(map(str.upper, users))                 # apply to every item
emails = list(filter(lambda u: u.active, users))     # keep matching items
from functools import reduce
total  = reduce(lambda a, b: a + b.price, cart.items, 0)

# The same three, as comprehensions - usually preferred:
names  = [u.name.upper() for u in users]
emails = [u.email for u in users if u.active]
total  = sum(item.price for item in cart.items)

# Dict and set comprehensions too:
by_id = {u.id: u for u in users}
sizes = {len(word) for word in words}
ToolReads asPrefer when
map(f, xs)"apply f to each"f already exists as a function; chains lazily with map
filter(p, xs)"keep where p"predicate exists; comprehension is clearer otherwise
reduce(f, xs)"fold into one value"almost never - sum()/any()/all()/min() are clearer
comprehension"build this list"default choice: readable, Pythonic, fast

Memory trick: map transforms, filter selects, reduce folds. If you have to reread it, use a comprehension instead.

3. itertools - Loops Without Loops

from itertools import chain, groupby, islice, count, product

merged   = chain(list_a, list_b)                    # lazy concatenation
first_10 = islice(rows, 10)                         # head of an iterator
for key, group in groupby(sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r.city), key=lambda r: r.city):
    print(key, list(group))                         # grouped runs
pairs    = product(colors, sizes)                   # cartesian product
infinite = islice(count(0, 2), 5)                   # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]

4. Threads - Concurrent I/O In One Process

A thread is a second stream of execution inside the same program, sharing the same memory. Python has a Global Interpreter Lock (GIL): only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, so threads do not speed up number crunching - they hide waiting. Waiting on a network, a disk, an API: threads win. Pure computation: use processes (Chapter 28) or NumPy.

import threading
import time

def fetch(url):
    print(f"start {url} on {threading.current_thread().name}")
    time.sleep(1)            # stands in for a network call
    print(f"done  {url}")

# 1. Raw threads
threads = [threading.Thread(target=fetch, args=(u,), name=f"t{i}")
           for i, u in enumerate(urls)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()          # wait for all; without join the main
                                    # thread exits and kills them

# 2. The pool you should actually use
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool:
    futures = {pool.submit(fetch, u): u for u in urls}
    for future in as_completed(futures):
        result = future.result()    # raises here if the task raised

5. Shared Memory Needs A Lock

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def bump():
    global counter
    with lock:                 # only one thread at a time inside
        counter += 1           # read-modify-write is not atomic

# Rules:
# - with lock:  is always safer than lock.acquire() (exception-safe)
# - hold the lock for the shortest possible time
# - queue.Queue is often better than a lock: producers put, consumers get
# - daemon=True threads die with the program - fine for background pings,
#   wrong for work that must finish
ToolUse for
threading.ThreadOne-off background jobs
ThreadPoolExecutorMany similar I/O tasks - the default choice
threading.Lock / RLockProtecting a shared variable
queue.QueueHanding work between threads safely (producer/consumer)
threading.EventSignalling "stop now" to a worker
concurrent.futuresFutures, timeouts, error propagation

Memory trick: GIL means threads share one CPU core for Python code - pick threads to wait, processes to compute.

6. Pydantic v2 - model_dump() And Validation

Pydantic validates at the boundary and gives you typed objects inside. model_dump() turns the object back into plain data for JSON, databases or logs.

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field, ValidationError

class UserIn(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=80)
    age: int = Field(ge=0, le=130)
    tags: list[str] = []

# Validate at the edge - bad input raises before your code runs:
try:
    user = UserIn.model_validate({"email": "a@b.co", "name": "Ada", "age": 36})
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.errors())            # structured, JSON-serialisable errors

user = UserIn(email="a@b.co", name="Ada", age=36)

user.model_dump()                  # {"email": "a@b.co", "name": "Ada", ...}
user.model_dump(mode="json")       # JSON-safe types (datetime -> str)
user.model_dump(exclude={"tags"})  # leave fields out
user.model_dump(by_alias=True)     # send database field names
user.model_dump_json()             # straight to a JSON string
user.model_copy(update={"age": 37})  # immutable-ish update
UserIn.model_validate_json(raw)    # validate straight from bytes
MethodDirectionUse it for
model_validate / model_validate_jsonoutside -> objectAPI request bodies, config files, webhooks
model_dump / model_dump_jsonobject -> outsideResponses, caching, logs
model_fieldsintrospectionGenerating docs or forms

model_dump vs dict(): v2's model_dump() is the supported way; dict(user) is the v1 habit and hides options like mode="json" and exclude=. FastAPI itself calls model_dump when serialising your response models.

7. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
LambdaEverywhere it fitsOnly for one-line keys; named functions everywhere else
ThreadsOne thread, hope for the bestPools with bounded workers, timeouts, graceful shutdown
Shared stateGlobals and hopeQueues and locks, or no shared state at all
Validationif checks scattered in the routeOne Pydantic model at every boundary
Serialisationjson.dumps(dict(obj))model_dump(mode="json") - typed, tested, consistent

8. Key Takeaways

  • Lambda is an expression for one-off callbacks, not a function style.
  • map/filter/reduce exist; comprehensions and sum()/any() are usually clearer.
  • The GIL makes threads good at waiting and useless at computing - use ThreadPoolExecutor for I/O, processes for CPU.
  • Always join your threads, or bound them with an executor.
  • Validate at the boundary with Pydantic; serialise with model_dump(mode="json").

Exercise: write a script that fetches five URLs with sequential requests, then with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=5), and compare the wall-clock times with time.perf_counter().

chapters.title: Python Internals
chapters.html:
1. Metaclasses - The Class Of A Class

Every class is an instance of something. type builds normal classes; a metaclass is a class whose instances are classes. Control __new__ of the metaclass and you control how classes are constructed: validate fields, register plugins, inject methods.

class Meta(type):
    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, ns):
        # Runs at class-definition time, before the class exists.
        registry[name] = ns.get("kind", name)     # auto-register plugins
        for key, value in ns.items():
            if key.startswith("field_") and not isinstance(value, property):
                raise TypeError(f"{name}.{key} must be a property")
        return super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, ns)

    def __init__(cls, name, bases, ns):
        cls.schema = {k: v.type for k, v in ns.items() if isinstance(v, property)}

class Model(metaclass=Meta):
    kind = "base"

class User(Model):
    kind = "user"                                 # registry["User"] == "user"

# You already use metaclasses: ABCMeta (abstractmethod) and ORM models like
# SQLAlchemy declarative bases are built on them.

Memory trick: __init__ of a class initialises an instance; Meta.__init__ initialises a class.

2. Descriptors - The Engine Under property

A descriptor is any object with __get__ (and optionally __set__/__delete__) that lives in a class body. Every attribute lookup on an instance checks the type's MRO for a data descriptor first - which is exactly how property, classmethod and staticmethod work.

class Validated:                       # a data descriptor
    def __init__(self, name, kind=str, required=True):
        self.name, self.kind, self.required = name, kind, required
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):      # called once at class creation
        self.private = "_" + name
    def __get__(self, obj, owner=None):
        if obj is None: return self
        return getattr(obj, self.private, None)
    def __set__(self, obj, value):            # validation happens HERE
        if not isinstance(value, self.kind):
            raise TypeError(f"{self.name} must be {self.kind.__name__}")
        if self.required and value in (None, ""):
            raise ValueError(f"{self.name} is required")
        setattr(obj, self.private, value)

class Account:
    owner = Validated("owner", str)
    email = Validated("email", str)

a = Account(); a.owner = "Ada"        # every assignment validated, no code in Account

# property is the built-in descriptor shortcut:
class Temp:
    def __init__(self, c): self._c = c
    @property
    def f(self): return self._c * 9 / 5 + 32      # __get__
    @f.setter
    def f(self, v): self._c = (v - 32) * 5 / 9     # __set__
DescriptorHasControls
Non-data (only __get__)__get__Reads; instance dict wins if present
Data (__get__ + __set__)__get__, __set__Reads AND writes; shadows the instance dict

3. Advanced Decorators - Classes, Arguments, Wrapping

# A class-based decorator (anything callable with __call__ works):
class CountCalls:
    def __init__(self, func): self.func, self.calls = func, 0
    def __call__(self, *a, **kw):
        self.calls += 1
        return self.func(*a, **kw)

# A decorator THAT TAKES ARGUMENTS - the shape that confuses everyone.
# Three nested functions: outer receives the arguments, middle receives the
# function, inner receives the call.
def retries(max_attempts=3, delay=0.5):
    def decorator(func):
        import functools, time
        @functools.wraps(func)                # keep __name__, __doc__!
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
                try:
                    return func(*args, **kwargs)
                except Exception:
                    if attempt == max_attempts: raise
                    time.sleep(delay * attempt)      # exponential-ish backoff
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@retries(max_attempts=3, delay=0.2)
def call_api(url): ...

# Stacking: decorators apply bottom-up.
@login_required            # runs second (outermost)
@cache(ttl=60)             # runs first (innermost)
def get_report(month): ...

Memory trick: @decorator is sugar for f = decorator(f); @decorator(x) is sugar for f = decorator(x)(f) - one call returns the real decorator.

4. Coroutines And asyncio - Concurrency Without Threads

An async def function is a coroutine: it can pause at await and let the event loop run something else. One thread, no GIL fight, thousands of concurrent I/O operations.

import asyncio, httpx

async def fetch(client, url):           # coroutine function
    r = await client.get(url)           # PAUSES here; loop does other work
    return r.status_code

async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        urls = [f"https://httpbin.org/get?i={i}" for i in range(20)]
        tasks = [asyncio.create_task(fetch(client, u)) for u in urls]
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)   # run all, collect in order
        # return_exceptions=True would put failures in the list instead
        print(results)

asyncio.run(main())                     # builds the loop, runs, cleans up
ToolChoose it when
asyncio + gatherThousands of socket/HTTP waits, one process, FastAPI endpoints
ThreadPoolExecutorBlocking libraries you cannot make async
ProcessPoolExecutorCPU-heavy work (see next section)
Background tasks (asyncio.create_task)Fire-and-forget work after a response

Rules: never await in a non-async function; never call a blocking library inside async code (it freezes the whole loop - use asyncio.to_thread); gather for fan-out, Queue for producer/consumer, wait_for for timeouts.

5. Multiprocessing - Real Cores, Real Isolation

The GIL means one Python bytecode at a time per process. Multiprocessing spawns separate OS processes, each with its own interpreter, GIL and memory - true parallelism on every core, at the cost of pickling data across process boundaries.

from multiprocessing import Process, Pool
import os

def cpu_job(n):                        # must be importable (top level)
    return sum(i * i for i in range(n))

if __name__ == "__main__":             # REQUIRED on Windows/macOS:
    #     without it every child re-imports __main__ and re-runs the app.
    with Pool(processes=4) as pool:
        results = pool.map(cpu_job, [10_000_000] * 8)   # 8 jobs on 4 cores
        # pool.imap for lazy results, pool.apply_async for fire-and-collect
ThreadProcess
Shares memoryYes (needs locks)No - picklable args only
Parallel CPU workNo (GIL)Yes
Startup costMicrosecondsMilliseconds
Failure isolationOne crash kills allSeparate address spaces
Use forNetwork/disk waitsCompute, sandboxes, native libs that release memory

6. Generators And Iterators - Lazy Data

An iterator is anything with __iter__ and __next__. A generator is the easiest way to write one: yield suspends and hands a value back, keeping its local state, so nothing is computed until you ask.

def read_large_file(path):              # constant memory on a 100 GB file
    with open(path) as fh:
        for line in fh:
            if line.startswith("ERROR"):
                yield line.rstrip()

errors = read_large_file("app.log")     # nothing read yet
count = sum(1 for _ in errors)          # now it streams

# Infinite sequence, bounded by islice:
def natural():
    n = 0
    while True:
        n += 1
        yield n
first_even = (x for x in natural() if x % 2 == 0)   # generator expression
import itertools
print(list(islice(first_even, 5)))      # [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]

# send(): coroutines get their data back in - the root of async/await:
def accumulator():
    total = 0
    while True:
        value = yield total              # pause; receive via .send()
        if value is None: return
        total += value
ConceptMeans
Lazy evaluationCompute on demand; a generator expression of a million rows costs one row at a time
One-shotA generator is exhausted after one pass - wrap with a function that recreates it if you need repeats
yield fromDelegates to a sub-generator, flattening the pipeline
BackpressureThe consumer drives: stop pulling and production stops - natural flow control for streams

7. CPython Memory Management

MechanismWhat it does
Reference countingEvery object has a count; +1 when referenced, -1 when dropped; hitting 0 frees it immediately
Cyclesa refers to b refers to a - counts never reach 0
Generational GCgc module periodically finds unreachable cycles; 3 generations, scanned every 700/10/10 allocations
AllocatorsSmall objects: per-size pools (pymalloc). Large: malloc directly
InterningSmall ints (-5..256) and short identifiers are shared, so they are the same object
sys.getrefcountShows the count (one higher than you expect - the argument reference counts too)
import gc, sys

a = []; b = [a]; a.append(b)     # cycle: neither reaches refcount 0
print(sys.getrefcount(a))        # inspect
print(gc.collect())              # force the cycle collector; returns freed count

class Expensive:
    def __init__(self): self.buf = bytearray(10_000_000)
    def __del__(self): print("freed")     # called when refs hit 0 (usually)

# Finding leaks: objgraph.show_backrefs() or tracemalloc - take two snapshots
import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()
snap1 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
... # suspected leak code ...
snap2 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for stat in snap2.compare_to(snap1, "lineno")[:5]:
    print(stat)                  # who allocated the memory that stayed

Memory trick: refcounting frees acyclic objects instantly; the generational collector exists only for cycles. Real "memory leaks" in Python are almost always a list or cache that keeps a reference alive.

8. MRO - Method Resolution Order

With multiple inheritance, which foo() runs? Python uses C3 linearization: a deterministic order that respects local precedence (your base list order) and monotonicity (a class never appears before its own bases).

class A:    def who(self): return "A"
class B(A): def who(self): return "B"
class C(A): def who(self): return "C"
class D(B, C): pass

print(D.__mro__)
# (<class 'D'>, <class 'B'>, <class 'C'>, <class 'A'>, <class 'object'>)
print(D().who())          # "B" - leftmost base wins

# super() walks the MRO, not "the parent":
class Base:
    def render(self): return "base"
class Left(Base):
    def render(self): return "[" + super().render() + "]"
class Right(Base):
    def render(self): return "{" + super().render() + "}"
class Both(Left, Right):
    def render(self): return "<" + super().render() + ">"

Both().render()   # "<[{base}]>" - super() follows Both.__mro__ precisely

Diamond problem: A is a base of both B and C - without a single linear order, A.method could run twice. C3 guarantees each class appears exactly once. TypeError: Cannot create a consistent MRO means you asked for an impossible ordering (usually conflicting base lists).

9. Dunder Methods - making your objects act like built-ins

class Money:
    def __init__(self, amount, currency="EUR"):
        self.amount, self.currency = amount, currency
    def __add__(self, other):  return Money(self.amount + other.amount)      # a + b
    def __iadd__(self, other): self.amount += other.amount; return self      # a += b
    def __eq__(self, other):   return self.amount == other.amount            # a == b
    def __lt__(self, other):   return self.amount < other.amount             # sorted(a)
    def __bool__(self):        return self.amount != 0                       # if a:
    def __len__(self):         return len(str(self.amount))                  # len(a)
    def __contains__(self, x): return x in str(self.amount)                  # x in a
    def __getitem__(self, i):  return str(self.amount)[i]                    # a[i]
    def __iter__(self):        return iter(str(self.amount))                 # for x in a
    def __repr__(self):        return f"Money({self.amount})"                # f-string, logs
    def __str__(self):         return f"{self.amount} {self.currency}"       # print(a)
    def __call__(self):        return self.amount * 2                        # a()
    def __enter__(self): ...; def __exit__(self, *e): ...                    # with a:
    def __new__(cls, *a):      ...                                           # control creation
    def __slots__ = ("amount", "currency")   # fixed layout, no __dict__, saves RAM

# Type-specific hooks you will meet:
# __hash__      dict/set keys (define __eq__ without __hash__ and the object
#               becomes unhashable)
# __format__    format(m, ",.2f")
# __index__     range(m) / list[m]
# __matmul__    the @ operator (NumPy matmul)
# __del__       last reference dropped (do not rely on it for cleanup)

Memory trick: dunder methods are protocols, not inheritance: if your object does the operations, Python will call them. That is "duck typing" written down.

10. Custom Context Managers - Guaranteed Cleanup

# The class form - two methods, no exceptions swallowed:
class OpenDB:
    def __init__(self, dsn): self.dsn = dsn
    def __enter__(self):
        self.conn = connect(self.dsn)
        return self.conn                  # bound to the 'as' name
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        self.conn.close()
        return False                      # False: let exceptions propagate
                                           # True: swallow them (rarely right)

with OpenDB(dsn) as conn:
    conn.execute(...)

# The generator form - shorter, uses finally implicitly:
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def temp_cd(path):
    import os
    old = os.getcwd()
    os.chdir(path)
    try:
        yield os.getcwd()                 # everything before yield = __enter__
    finally:
        os.chdir(old)                     # everything after = __exit__

with temp_cd("/tmp/build") as cwd:
    ...

# Also in the toolbox:
# contextlib.suppress(KeyError)   - ignore specific exceptions
# contextlib.redirect_stdout(...) - capture prints
# contextlib.ExitStack            - enter many managed resources dynamically
# contextlib.closing(obj)         - call obj.close() on exit for anything

Why it matters: files, locks, sockets, transactions and temporary directories all have an "acquire now, release no matter what" shape. The with statement is the only thing that runs cleanup when the body raises.

11. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
Metaclasses / descriptorsCool demosORMs, validation frameworks, plugin registries - use them, rarely write them
asyncioasync def because it looks modernasync at the edges only; sync in the core, no blocking calls in the loop
MultiprocessingForgotten __main__ guard crashes WindowsPools sized to cores, chunks for big data, timeouts on every task
GeneratorsLists of everythingStreams: pipelines of generators over logs, rows, events
MemoryTrust the GCtracemalloc snapshots, bounded caches, __slots__ on hot objects
Context managerstry/finally you forget to writeEvery resource goes through with - including timing and tracing spans

12. Key Takeaways

  • Metaclasses run when a class is created; descriptors run on every attribute access - property is a descriptor.
  • A decorator with arguments is three nested functions; functools.wraps keeps the metadata.
  • asyncio hides waiting on one thread; multiprocessing gets real cores - and needs the if __name__ == "__main__" guard on Windows.
  • Generators give lazy, constant-memory, backpressure-aware pipelines.
  • Reference counting frees acyclic objects instantly; the GC only exists for cycles.
  • MRO is C3 linearisation: deterministic, leftmost-first, each class once; super() walks that exact list.
  • Dunder methods are the protocols that make objects work with operators, loops and with-statements.

Exercise: build a validated Model with a metaclass that forbids mutable class attributes, then a generator that streams a 1 GB file and counts matches while staying under 50 MB RSS (watch with task manager or ps).

chapters.title: FastAPI
chapters.html:
1. Why FastAPI

PropertyWhat it means
Fast (ASGI)Uvicorn + async - near Node/Go speed for I/O workloads
TypedPydantic models validate input and serialise output automatically
Documented/docs (Swagger) and /redoc generated from your type hints - for free
Standards-basedOpenAPI, JSON Schema, OAuth2, HTTP standards
Async-nativeasync def endpoints run concurrently; sync endpoints get a thread pool
pip install fastapi uvicorn[standard] pydantic-settings sqlalchemy

# main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI(title="DocKube API", version="1.3.0")

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}

uvicorn main:app --reload                      # development
uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --workers 4    # production

2. Routes, Parameters, Validation

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Query
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class ItemIn(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=80)
    price: float = Field(gt=0)

class ItemOut(ItemIn):
    id: int

@app.post("/items", response_model=ItemOut, status_code=201)
async def create_item(body: ItemIn):          # body validated by Pydantic
    return {**body.model_dump(), "id": 1}

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")                  # path parameter
def get_item(item_id: int,                   # FastAPI converts and validates
             q: str | None = Query(None, max_length=20),
             verbose: bool = False):
    if item_id not in DB:
        raise HTTPException(404, detail="item not found")
    return DB[item_id]
You declareFastAPI does
path param typed intConverts "abc" -> 422 automatically, adds it to OpenAPI
body: ItemInParses JSON, validates every field, returns 422 with exact errors
response_model=ItemOutFilters leaked fields, serialises, documents the response
async defRuns on the event loop - never block it
def (sync)Runs in a threadpool - safe for blocking DB drivers

3. The Folder Structure - Python Terms

Spring calls them controllers, services, DAOs/repositories and DTOs. Python projects with FastAPI use the same layering under these names:

Spring termPython / FastAPI termIts job
ControllerRouter (routers/)HTTP only: parse request, call service, return response
ServiceService (services/)Business rules; no FastAPI imports here
DAO / RepositoryRepository (repositories/)All SQL / ORM access; returns domain objects
DTOSchema (schemas/)Pydantic models for request/response shapes
EntityModel (models/)SQLAlchemy table mapping
Bean / DI containerDepends() dependency injectionFastAPI builds and injects dependencies per request
application.yml.env + Settings (core/config.py)Typed configuration
Interceptor / FilterMiddlewareLogging, request ids, CORS - runs around every request
@ControllerAdviceexception_handlersCentral error -> JSON mapping
app/
|-- main.py                 # app factory, middleware, exception handlers
|-- core/
|   |-- config.py           # Settings(BaseSettings) loaded from .env
|   |-- security.py         # password hashing, JWT create/verify
|   `-- logging.py          # structured logging setup
|-- db.py                   # engine, SessionLocal, Base, get_db()
|-- dependencies.py         # get_db, get_current_user - reusable Depends
|-- schemas/                # Pydantic DTOs (what the API speaks)
|   |-- item.py             # ItemIn, ItemOut, ItemUpdate
|   `-- user.py
|-- models/                 # SQLAlchemy tables (what the DB stores)
|   `-- item.py
|-- repositories/           # the ONLY place with SQL and queries
|   `-- item_repo.py
|-- services/               # business logic and transactions
|   `-- item_service.py
|-- routers/                # HTTP layer only
|   |-- items.py
|   `-- auth.py
|-- tests/
|   |-- conftest.py         # test app + throwaway database fixtures
|   `-- test_items.py
|-- .env.example
`-- requirements.txt

Memory trick: a request flows router -> service -> repository -> database, and each layer only talks to the next. If you ever import FastAPI inside a service or repository, the layering has leaked.

4. One Feature, All Layers

# schemas/item.py - what crosses the wire
class ItemCreate(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1)
    price: float = Field(gt=0)

class ItemOut(ItemCreate):
    id: int
    owner_id: int
    model_config = {"from_attributes": True}    # ORM object -> model

# repositories/item_repo.py - the only file that knows SQL
def create(db: Session, data: ItemCreate, owner_id: int):
    row = models.Item(**data.model_dump(), owner_id=owner_id)
    db.add(row)
    db.commit()
    db.refresh(row)
    return row

def get(db: Session, item_id: int):
    return db.get(models.Item, item_id)

# services/item_service.py - rules, not HTTP
class ItemService:
    def __init__(self, db: Session):
        self.db = db

    def create(self, data: ItemCreate, owner_id: int):
        taken = (self.db.query(models.Item)
                    .filter_by(name=data.name, owner_id=owner_id).first())
        if taken:
            raise DomainError("you already have an item called that")
        return item_repo.create(self.db, data, owner_id)

# routers/items.py - HTTP only
router = APIRouter(prefix="/items", tags=["items"])

def get_service(db: Session = Depends(get_db),
                user = Depends(get_current_user)):
    return ItemService(db)                      # built per request

@router.post("", response_model=ItemOut, status_code=201)
def create(body: ItemCreate, svc = Depends(get_service)):
    try:
        return svc.create(body, user["sub"])
    except DomainError as exc:
        raise HTTPException(409, detail=str(exc))

# main.py - assemble the app
from routers import items, auth
app.include_router(items.router)
app.include_router(auth.router)

5. Configuration, Middleware And Error Handling

# core/config.py - typed settings, never os.environ scattered around
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str
    jwt_secret: str
    redis_url: str = "redis://localhost:6379/0"
    model_config = {"env_file": ".env"}

settings = Settings()          # app refuses to start with missing keys

# main.py - middleware wraps EVERY request (order matters: first added = outermost)
from fastapi import Request
import time, uuid, logging

@app.middleware("http")
async def request_context(request: Request, call_next):
    rid = request.headers.get("x-request-id", uuid.uuid4().hex[:12])
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["x-request-id"] = rid
    logging.info("%s %s %s %.1fms rid=%s", request.method,
                 request.url.path, response.status_code,
                 (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000, rid)
    return response

@app.exception_handler(DomainError)
async def domain_errors(request: Request, exc: DomainError):
    # One JSON shape for every failure: {error: {code, message}}
    return JSONResponse(status_code=409,
                        content={"error": {"code": "conflict", "message": str(exc)}})

# CORS - exact origins, never *
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
app.add_middleware(CORSMiddleware,
                   allow_origins=["https://app.example.com"],
                   allow_credentials=True,
                   allow_methods=["GET", "POST"],
                   allow_headers=["authorization", "content-type"])

6. Testing The App

# tests/conftest.py
import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from app.main import app
from app.db import override_get_db

app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = override_get_db   # throwaway database

@pytest.fixture
def client():
    with TestClient(app) as c:                  # runs startup/shutdown hooks
        yield c

# tests/test_items.py
def test_create_and_read(client):
    r = client.post("/items", json={"name": "desk", "price": 120})
    assert r.status_code == 201
    item_id = r.json()["id"]
    assert client.get(f"/items/{item_id}").json()["name"] == "desk"

def test_rejects_bad_input(client):
    r = client.post("/items", json={"name": "", "price": -1})
    assert r.status_code == 422        # validation is FastAPI's job

# Run: pytest -q --cov=app
Test typeToolCovers
UnitpytestService and repository logic in isolation
Integration (API)TestClient + real databaseRouting, validation, persistence together
Contractschemathesis (generated from /openapi.json)Every endpoint against the documented schema
End-to-endPlaywrightFront end against the real stack

7. Deploying

# Dockerfile (slim, non-root)
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /srv
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN useradd -r appuser && chown -R appuser /srv
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--workers", "4"]

# Behind a proxy: uvicorn workers are the app servers; nginx or the cloud
# load balancer terminates TLS. Migrations run BEFORE the new pods start:
alembic upgrade head && uvicorn app.main:app

8. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
StructureEverything in main.pyrouters / services / repositories / schemas, one feature per folder
ConfigHard-coded stringsBaseSettings + .env, validated at boot, secrets from a manager
ErrorsHTTPException sprinkled everywhereDomain exceptions + one central handler with a stable JSON shape
DatabaseOne global engine, sessions created by handget_db dependency, pooling, Alembic migrations, repository isolation
DocsHand-written/docs is the contract, checked in CI with schemathesis
Process--reloadMultiple uvicorn workers behind a proxy, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM

9. Key Takeaways

  • FastAPI turns type hints into validation, documentation and serialisation - the schema IS the contract.
  • Python's names for the Spring layers: router (controller), service, repository (DAO), schema (DTO), model (entity), Depends (DI), middleware (interceptor).
  • Requests flow router -> service -> repository; each layer imports only the next.
  • async endpoints must never block; sync endpoints get a threadpool for free.
  • Centralise errors, type your settings, test with TestClient against a throwaway database.

Exercise: scaffold the structure above with a single Item resource and every layer filled in; add one test per layer and run pytest -q --cov=app.

chapters.title: Email Systems
chapters.html:
1. The Three Ways To Send Mail

WayHowUse when
SMTP relayYour code speaks SMTP to a server (yours or a provider's)You already have mail infrastructure
HTTP mail APIPOST JSON to SendGrid/Mailgun/Resend/etc with an API keyThe default today: better deliverability, dashboards, webhooks
Local sendmailHand the message to /usr/sbin/sendmailContainers and legacy boxes, rarely on Windows

Memory trick: SMTP is how servers talk to each other; mail APIs are how YOUR app talks to a provider that then speaks SMTP for you. Home ISPs and cloud providers block port 25 - you almost always need a provider anyway.

2. Sending Over SMTP - Standard Library

import smtplib
from email.message import EmailMessage
from email.utils import make_msgid

def send_welcome(to: str, name: str):
    msg = EmailMessage()
    msg["From"] = "DocKube <no-reply@dockeybe.dev>"
    msg["To"] = to
    msg["Subject"] = "Welcome to DocKube"
    msg.set_content(f"Hi {name},\n\nYour account is ready.\n-- The team")
    html = f"<h1>Welcome, {name}!</h1>"
    html += "<p>Your account is ready.</p>"
    msg.add_alternative(html, subtype="html")

    # host, port, username, password, TLS
    with smtplib.SMTP_SSL("smtp.example.com", 465, timeout=10) as smtp:
        smtp.login("apikey-or-user", "secret")
        smtp.send_message(msg)

# StartTLS variant: smtplib.SMTP(host, 587) then smtp.starttls() then login.

# Async version for FastAPI - blocking SMTP in a coroutine freezes the loop
import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
_executor = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4)

@app.post("/notifications/welcome")
async def welcome(to: EmailStr):
    # run_in_executor wraps the blocking send like any other thread task
    await asyncio.get_running_loop().run_in_executor(
        _executor, send_welcome, to, "friend")
    return {"queued": True}

3. HTML Mail, Templates And Attachments

from email.message import EmailMessage

def send_invoice(to: str, pdf: bytes, rows: list):
    msg = EmailMessage()
    msg["Subject"] = "Your invoice"
    # Inline styles only: Gmail and friends strip <style> blocks.
    rows_html = "".join(
        f"<tr><td>{r['item']}</td><td align='right'>{r['price']:.2f}</td></tr>"
        for r in rows)
    msg.add_alternative(
        f"<table cellpadding='6' style='border-collapse:collapse'>{rows_html}</table>",
        subtype="html")
    msg.add_attachment(pdf, maintype="application", subtype="pdf",
                       filename="invoice.pdf")
    return msg

# Templates: keep the subject/body in files (Jinja2) so writers can edit
# them without a deploy: env.render("welcome", name=name)
RuleWhy
multipart/alternative (text + html)Some clients only render text
Inline CSSMajor clients strip style tags
One-click unsubscribe + List-Unsubscribe headerSpam law (CAN-SPAM, GDPR) and inbox placement
Never interpolate user input into raw HTMLHTML injection / phishing via your domain
Send async and return 202A slow SMTP server must not hold the request open

4. The Mail APIs Compared

ProviderHow you call itFree tierKnown for
SMTP + any relaysmtplib to port 465/587VariesNo dashboard, no webhooks
SendGridPOST /v3/mail/send + Bearer key100 emails/dayTemplates, analytics, industry default
MailgunPOST /v3/.../messages (API or SMTP)1000/month (trial)Developer ergonomics, receiving mail
AWS SESPOST via SigV4, or SMTP creds3000/month from EC2Cheapest at scale, AWS-native
PostmarkPOST /email100/month (trial)Transactional speed and deliverability
ResendPOST /emails + React Email templates3000/monthModern DX, loved by Next.js apps
Brevo (ex-Sendinblue)POST /v3/smtp/email300/dayCheap bulk + marketing
SMTP2GOAPI or SMTP1000/monthDeliverability reporting

5. Calling A Mail API From FastAPI

# pip install httpx
import httpx
from fastapi import BackgroundTasks

SENDGRID_KEY = settings.sendgrid_key
SENDGRID_FROM = "DocKube <no-reply@dockeybe.dev>"

async def sendgrid_send(to: str, subject: str, html: str):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
        r = await client.post(
            "https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/mail/send",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {SENDGRID_KEY}"},
            json={
                "personalizations": [{"to": [{"email": to}]}],
                "from": {"email": "no-reply@dockeybe.dev"},
                "subject": subject,
                "content": [{"type": "text/html", "value": html}],
            },
        )
        r.raise_for_status()          # 202 Accepted means queued
        return r.status_code

@app.post("/notifications/reset")
async def reset_email(body: ResetIn, tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    # Fire after the response: the user never waits on a mail provider.
    tasks.add_task(sendgrid_send, body.email,
                   "Reset your password", render_reset(body.token))
    return {"queued": True}          # always 202, never leak if an account exists
ConceptMeaning
Transactional vs bulkPassword resets (immediate, low volume) vs campaigns (batched, throttled)
SPFDNS record listing which servers may send as your domain
DKIMCryptographic signature on the message, verified against DNS
DMARCPolicy telling receivers what to do when SPF/DKIM fail (none -> quarantine -> reject)
WebhooksProvider POSTs delivery, bounce and open events back to your endpoint
Suppression listBounced or complained addresses you must stop mailing

Memory trick: without SPF + DKIM + DMARC your perfect email lands in spam. Set the three records before you send your first message, then warm up the volume gradually.

6. Learning vs Production

AspectWhile learningIn production
ProviderMailtrap / Ethereal (fake inbox)SendGrid or SES with dedicated IP warm-up
SendingInline in the request - slow, and retried twice = two mailsBackground task or queue with idempotency key + retries
FailuresException bubbles to the userQueued, retried with backoff, dead-lettered, alerted
SecretsKey in the sourceEnvironment / secret manager, scoped, rotatable
TrackingNoneWebhooks for delivered/bounced/complained, suppression honoured
Contentf-strings in codeVersioned templates with a preview and review

7. Key Takeaways

  • SMTP for server-to-server, HTTP mail APIs for your app - port 25 is blocked almost everywhere.
  • Never block the event loop on SMTP: BackgroundTasks or a thread executor.
  • multipart text + HTML, inline styles, unsubscribe header, escape user input.
  • SPF, DKIM and DMARC are the difference between the inbox and the spam folder.
  • Send asynchronously, retry idempotently, honour bounces.

Exercise: wire a /notifications endpoint that queues a SendGrid (or Mailtrap) send with BackgroundTasks, then check the provider dashboard shows a 202 and a delivered event.

chapters.title: Cryptography
chapters.html:
1. Four Words People Mix Up

TermDoesReversible?Examples
EncodingRepresents data in another formatYes, triviallybase64, UTF-8, URL encoding
HashingOne-way fingerprint of any length -> fixed digestNo (by design)SHA-256, bcrypt, Argon2
EncryptionTwo-way scrambling with a keyYes, with the keyAES-GCM, Fernet, RSA, ChaCha20
TokenisationReplaces a value with a random referenceOnly via the mapping storePayment tokens, session ids

Memory trick: hashing is a fingerprint (cannot be reversed, proves equality), encryption is a locked box (the key opens it). Passwords get hashed, card numbers in a database get tokenised, data on the wire gets encrypted.

2. Symmetric Encryption - One Key Both Ways

# pip install cryptography
from cryptography.fernet import Fernet

key = Fernet.generate_key()              # store in a secret manager, never in git
cipher = Fernet(key)

token  = cipher.encrypt(b"card 4242 4242 4242 4242")
plain  = cipher.decrypt(token)            # b'card 4242...'

# Fernet also authenticates: tampered ciphertext raises InvalidToken.
# Envelope encryption: encrypt the data with a random data key, then
# encrypt the data key with the master key (KMS) - so you rotate rarely.

# AES-GCM (what most APIs use - authenticated encryption)
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
import os

aes_key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)
aes     = AESGCM(aes_key)
nonce   = os.urandom(12)                 # never reuse a nonce with a key!
cipher  = aes.encrypt(nonce, b"payload", b"aad-header")
plain   = aes.decrypt(nonce, cipher, b"aad-header")

3. Asymmetric Encryption - Two Keys

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa, padding

private = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
public  = private.public_key()

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes

blob = public.encrypt(b"session-key",
    padding.OAEP(mgf=padding.MGF1(hashes.SHA256),
                 algorithm=hashes.SHA256, label=None))
plain = private.decrypt(blob,
    padding.OAEP(mgf=padding.MGF1(hashes.SHA256),
                 algorithm=hashes.SHA256, label=None))
